title: Targets
text:
This project uses the targets package for pipeline management in R. The targets package helps to automate the workflow by defining a series of steps (targets) that depend on each other. Each target represents a piece of data or a computation, and targets ensures that only the necessary parts of the pipeline are re-executed when changes occur.
Here is a visual network showing the relationships between the targets in this project:


+ gcm_ts_plot declared [5 branches]
+ niwa_met_daily declared [7 branches]
+ gcm_monthly_deltas declared [7 branches]
+ rotorua_inflow_list_matrix declared [1 branches]
+ gcm_point_data declared [34 branches]
+ gcm_point_data_std declared [34 branches]
+ aeme_glm4 declared [1 branches]

title: Staged PEST++ Calibration of GLM-AED
text:
The Lake Rotorua GLM-AED model was calibrated in stages with aemetools and PEST++ (pestpp-ies): (1) water balance, (2) water temperature, (3) AED biogeochemistry, (4) alum with FRP and chlorophyll-a. This page reports the run that used the updated daily temperature and oxygen observations and the corrected calibration pipeline.

Water level and temperature are well calibrated (level KGE 0.81, RMSE 8 cm; temperature KGE 0.98, RMSE 0.54 °C on 38,000 daily observations).
Oxygen is now reasonably simulated (KGE 0.69, RMSE 1.25 mg/L, r = 0.84). Chlorophyll-a has some skill (KGE 0.20, r = 0.24), FRP is unbiased but weakly correlated (r = 0.19), and ammonium and nitrate are still poor.
Alum has a modest effect on modelled FRP in the calibrated model. With the stage 3 parameters, removing the dose raises mean FRP from 0.0034 to 0.0044 mg/L (about 30%) and leaves the FRP error unchanged, and the alum parameters barely change the fit within their ranges. FRP is low in the model with or without alum, and only 56 to 73 observations, mostly near the detection limit, constrain it.
An earlier version of this page was wrong for oxygen, FRP, ammonium and nitrate. A unit-conversion bug in the calibration (below) made PEST compare observations with values 30 to 70 times too small. The results here were rerun after fixing it.

title: Staged PEST++ Calibration of GLM-AED
section: 2 What changed since the first cut
text:
2 What changed since the first cut







Change
Effect




Double unit conversion fixed. aemetools multiplied simulated oxygen, FRP, ammonium and nitrate by their conversion factor (0.032, 0.031, 0.014) after AEME::read_model_outputs() had already converted them. PEST therefore scored observations against values about 1/32 of the true model value.
Earlier stage 3 and 4 results for these variables were invalid and are discarded. The fix is in a private copy of aemetools (calibration/lib_aemetools_patched); the same change is needed in the upstream package.


Rainfall units fixed in the forcing (about 42 times too little rain)
Applied in build_calib_base_aeme(); the same fix is needed at source in era5_corrected_hourly


Daily temperature and oxygen observations (updated by you)
Used for stages 2 to 4; any sub-daily duplicates are averaged to daily by thin_lake_obs()


Bottom-water anoxia added as a target (CHM_oxynal, number of anoxic layers)
Scored with weight 2


Surface oxygen down-weighted (weight 0.1)
Surface oxygen follows air–water exchange and temperature, which the calibrated parameters barely move


One FRP group over the whole column and all months
Split into surface and bottom summer groups the two held only 5 and 9 observations at the detection limit, and one of them carried a weight of 431


log1p scoring for chlorophyll-a
Reduces the pull of bloom peaks; needs the patched aemetools


Sediment oxygen demand range opened to 8 times the measured values
The measured values could not draw bottom water down in the model (see Stage 3)


Simulation window set with set_time() only
Earlier runs simulated the full 2011 to 2022 record each time because suggest_sim_period() overrode the window; runs are now 3 to 4 times faster

text:
3 Approach
The calibration is a set of scripts in calibration/, run from the project root, rather than targets targets: PEST++ runs are long, stochastic and stateful, and each stage needs a human check of the previous one. targets supplies the baseline Aeme object (aeme_base_file, R/build_calib_base_aeme.R).

Script
Targets

2

stage 1 parameters narrowed to their posterior, plus Kw, radiation and air-temperature factors, coef_mix_hyp, per-zone sediment temperature


3

4

PHS_frp, PHY_tchla (log1p), with aed_alum on

5
05_apply_posterior.R
all
final parameter sets, forward runs, performance tables and plots



Settings: stages 1 and 2 used 40 realisations and 4 iterations (10 workers); stage 3 used 30 realisations, 4 iterations and 4 workers, simulating 2017 to 2020 and scoring 2019 to 2020; stage 4 used 24 realisations, 3 iterations and 4 workers, simulating 5 years and scoring 3. Each stage reads the previous stage’s checkpoint. The PEST machinery (building, localisation, carry/narrow hand-offs) is reused from scripts/pest_funs.R.
Assumptions:

The measured sediment flux study has five zones; the deepest pit was removed from the hypsograph, so measured zones 2 to 5 map to model zones 1 to 4.
Measured fluxes replace the generic values in aed_sa_calib_params.csv (10 to 100 times too large for Rotorua).
Outflow is the Ōhau weir rating curve, so the outflow multiplier is not calibrated.
No suspended-solids observations exist, so aed_noncohesive stays at its defaults.
Stage 3 was calibrated with no alum, although the lake was dosed throughout. Stage 4 re-fits FRP and chlorophyll-a with alum on, but nitrogen and oxygen parameters are not re-fitted.

title: Staged PEST++ Calibration of GLM-AED
text:
11 Ammonium and nitrate
Ammonium and nitrate are the weakest variables. What the data and a set of forward runs show (stage 3 best fit, 2017 to 2020, bottom water = 17 m and deeper, December to April):

Observed ammonium is high through the lower water column in summer, not only at the bed: the mean is 0.11 mg/L at 10 to 17 m, 0.12 at 17 to 21 m and 0.16 at 21 to 25 m (maximum 0.73), against about 0.003 mg/L everywhere in the model.
Total N is also short in the model (0.26 mg/L at the bottom against 0.44 observed, and about 0.25 against 0.30 at the surface).
Bottom nitrate is 2 to 3 times too high in the model (0.041 against 0.017 mg/L), consistent with ammonium being nitrified rather than accumulating.




Bottom-water (17 m and deeper), December to April means (mg/L) when sediment ammonium release, oxygen demand, nitrification and organic N breakdown are scaled from the stage 3 best fit. Observed means: ammonium 0.177, nitrate 0.017, total N 0.435.

More sediment ammonium release does not produce the observed ammonium. Scaling the flux 10, 30 and 70 times raises bottom ammonium only from 0.003 to 0.003, 0.004 and 0.007 mg/L (total N rises from 0.26 to 0.31, so the nitrogen enters the model but not as ammonium). Adding two or three times the oxygen demand (bottom oxygen then matches the observed 5.8 mg/L) gives at most 0.009 mg/L, and lowering the oxygen half-saturation for release changes nothing.
The released ammonium does not accumulate. In the 30 times run the bottom layer is anoxic (below 1 mg/L) on 11% of days and the flux (0.9 mmol m-2 d-1) adds about 0.7 mmol m-3 d-1 to the 1.2 m bottom layer, yet its ammonium on those days averages 0.004 mg/L. Anoxic spells in the model are short, so it is mixed away and lost (denitrification in the bottom layer averages about 0.7 mmol m-3 d-1); the observations imply weeks of isolation.
Faster breakdown of organic N does not help. Raising rpon_hydrol 10 to 20 times lowers total N (to 0.16 to 0.19 mg/L) and leaves ammonium at 0.006 mg/L; the extra nitrogen is lost.

A nitrogen-only calibration with wide ranges confirmed this. I ran a separate pestpp-ies step (80 model runs, everything else held at the joint stage 3 result) that opened the levers above: sediment ammonium flux by zone from 0.5 to 150 times the measured value (up to 2.7 to 5.9 mmol m-2 d-1 in the ensemble), ksed_amm, rnitrif, knitrif, rdenit, kdenit and f_an, scored on ammonium and nitrate in three depth bands over December to April. The error score did not improve (9.42 at the start, 9.44, 9.90 and 9.69 in later iterations; the best realisation was one of the starting ensemble). Across the starting ensemble, which spans those very wide ranges, the bottom and mid-depth ammonium groups changed by only 10 to 20%. So the ammonium shortfall is not a parameter problem: these parameters cannot make the model hold ammonium in the lower water column.
Likely causes, in the order I would check them:

Units of the measured sediment fluxes. The measured ammonium flux (0.011 to 0.039) is in the range expected for g N m-2 d-1 (0.8 to 2.8 mmol m-2 d-1), but AED takes mmol m-2 d-1. If the study reported grams, the ammonium flux is entered about 70 times too small (the FRP flux about 30 times). This is unconfirmed: the study’s units need checking against its source. The nitrogen step above covered fluxes of that size and still could not fit ammonium, so correcting the units may be right but would not fix ammonium on its own.
Structure and mixing (the most likely cause now). See the next section: the calibrated wind scaling is 1.64 and the model cannot combine moderate stratification with the observed anoxia and ammonium. The model also has no deep pit (hyps_no_hole, 21.5 m deep) while the observed ammonium is highest at 21 to 25 m, and the model hypolimnion is not isolated for long enough. Also check denitrification (rdenit is 15 of a range to 20) and the external N load, given the 0.05 to 0.18 mg/L total N deficit.

title: Staged PEST++ Calibration of GLM-AED
text:
12 Mixing and stratification
The checks above point to mixing. The question is whether the model’s lower water column is mixed too strongly to hold ammonium. The answer is more awkward than “too strong”.
The calibrated wind scaling is very high. Stage 2 settled on a wind scaling of 1.64 (limit 2.0) applied to an ERA5 series that is already bias-corrected. That series averages about 5.2 m/s (2017 to 2020), against 4.6 m/s measured at the buoy (2022 to 2026), so the model is driven by a mean wind of about 8.6 m/s. Mixing energy goes with the cube of wind speed, so this is about 4 times the stirring of the corrected forcing. The wind scaling was fitted to the heat and water budget, not to mixing, so it is acting as a compensating parameter.
The model needs that wind to avoid over-stratifying. The table re-runs the stage 3 best fit (with the sediment ammonium flux 30 times higher, so that release is not the limit) at lower wind scaling and with weaker hypolimnetic mixing (coef_mix_hyp). At the calibrated wind the model is already more stratified than the lake (53% of days against 39%, mean ΔT 1.4 against 1.0 °C), yet bottom oxygen drops below 2 mg/L on only 2% of days (10% observed) and bottom ammonium stays at 0.003 mg/L (0.18 observed).
Lowering the wind makes stratification far too strong long before ammonium gets close. At a scaling of 1.3, 70% of days are stratified (ΔT 2.4 °C) and 36% of days are anoxic; at 1.0 the model is stratified on 92% of days with a ΔT of 6.6 °C, a bottom temperature 1.6 °C too cold and anoxia on 87% of days, and bottom ammonium only reaches 0.075 mg/L.
Weaker hypolimnetic mixing alone (coef_mix_hyp 0.1) changes little (anoxia 14% of days, ammonium 0.007 mg/L).

So the model cannot reproduce what the lake does: moderate stratification, anoxia on about 10% of days, and ammonium of 0.18 mg/L together. Ammonium only accumulates in the model when most of the days are anoxic, which is far from the observed 10%. Two things follow:

Wind scaling cannot be used to fit the heat budget. It is hiding a heat or evaporation error and, through the cubed dependence of mixing on wind, it sets the stratification. The wind scaling should be fixed near the buoy-based value, and the heat and evaporation terms (ce, ch, cd, radiation and humidity factors) and the mixing coefficients (coef_mix_conv, coef_mix_shear, coef_mix_turb, coef_mix_KH) should carry that error instead.
Stratification should be a calibration target. The current temperature targets (surface, bottom, metalimnion bands) fit the temperatures well but leave the surface-to-bottom difference, Schmidt stability and thermocline depth unconstrained (KGE about −0.2 and −0.1 in the first cut).

title: Staged PEST++ Calibration of GLM-AED
text:
13 Issues and next steps

Ammonium and nitrate are poorly simulated for structural or unit reasons, not because of tuning (see the section above). First confirm the units of the measured sediment fluxes, then re-open the ammonium flux range and use total N as a target to constrain the budget.
Alum parameters are weakly identified. FRP is dominated by the dose and the efficiency; treat alum efficiency and settling as scenario dimensions, not fitted values, in any projection. Only 56 to 73 FRP observations fall in the windows, mostly near the detection limit.
TLI4 depends on total P, total N and Secchi, none of which are calibration targets yet. Add them before using LKE_tli4 (see the climate strategy).
Stage 3 was calibrated without alum. Consider running stage 3 with alum on from the start, using the dosing history.
Parameters at their bounds in stages 2 and 3 (wind scaling, crest elevation, sediment temperature amplitude, rpoc_hydrol, diatom R_growth) suggest compensating errors; test whether the projections are sensitive to them.
Fix the upstream bugs: the double unit conversion in aemetools and the rainfall units in the era5_corrected_hourly target.
Housekeeping. The large PEST working directories (pest/, pest_smoke/, pest_diag/), the test folders in calibration/ and aeme_base_prerainfix.rds can be deleted. Archived (invalid) results are in calibration/checkpoints/archive_prevdata/.

Dadi et al. (2023)
Sudden eutrophication of an aluminum sulphate treated lake due to abrupt increase of internal phosphorus loading after three decades of mesotrophy. PDF


Click to expand: Summary

Key Findings - Lake Barleber (Germany), an artificial gravel pit lake successfully remediated with aluminium sulphate in 1986, remained mesotrophic for nearly 30 years before undergoing sudden re-eutrophication in 2016–2017, with TP increasing from ~40 µg L⁻¹ to ~270 µg L⁻¹ and massive cyanobacterial blooms developing. - Internal P loading from sediments was identified as the primary driver of re-eutrophication; estimated P release for 2017 was approximately 600 kg for the whole lake, consistent with sediment incubation experiments showing significant P release only under anoxic conditions. - The reducible (redox-dependent, Fe/Mn-bound) P fraction (BD-P) constituted 37–58% of total P in surface sediments, indicating high sensitivity to reductive release under anoxia. - Temperature and anoxia acted synergistically: anoxic high-temperature incubations produced SRP release rates approximately five times higher than anoxic low-temperature treatments (0.94 ± 0.23 vs ~0.17 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹), confirming temperature as a major amplifying factor. - Multiple P-retention indicators (NaOH-Al:NaOH-P, NaOH-Al:(NH₄Cl+BD)-P, and Sum-Al:Sum-Fe ratios) were all below recommended thresholds, demonstrating that the Al adsorption capacity of the sediment had been substantially exhausted after three decades. - Sediment focusing and low sedimentation rates (estimated at ~0.9 cm yr⁻¹) in this closed, autochthonous lake are proposed as factors that prolonged initial treatment effectiveness by keeping the Al-rich layer near the sediment surface.
Aluminium Sulphate Treatment: Results - The 1986 treatment applied 480 tonnes of aluminium sulphate (36 g Al m⁻², 5.7 mg Al L⁻¹ volumetric dosage), which successfully restored the lake to clear water within one year, with macrophytes re-establishing and TP remaining low (173–373 kg lake-wide) for nearly 30 years — well above the mean treatment longevity of ~11 years reported for Al-treated lakes globally. - P fractionation of the 40 cm sediment core identified a distinct NaOH-Al and NaOH-P peak at 28–34 cm depth, consistent with the depth expected for the 1986 Al application given the estimated sedimentation rate, confirming that the Al layer persisted in the sediment but had been progressively buried and diluted. - NaOH-Al:NaOH-P molar ratios across the sediment column (3–6) were uniformly below the recommended thresholds of 10 (Rydin and Welch 2000) and 12.6 (de Vicente et al. 2008), indicating that Al adsorption capacity had been exhausted relative to the P pool. - The Sum-Al:Sum-Fe ratio decreased approximately 5-fold from its value at the time of Al application, falling below the threshold of >3 proposed as necessary to prevent P release, and the NaOH-Al:(NH₄Cl+BD)-P ratio of ~3 in the upper sediment was far below the recommended threshold of >25. - High background sulphate concentrations (~500 mg L⁻¹ before treatment, rising after Al addition) promoted sulphide formation, which permanently immobilised Fe as iron sulphides and reduced the active iron pool competing with Al for P binding — a mechanism specific to aluminium sulphate treatment that would not apply to poly-aluminium chloride. - Al floc formed during treatment is susceptible to resuspension by wind and benthivorous fish activity (both documented at Lake Barleber), meaning the Al-rich layer was continuously mixed with new, lower-P-binding sediment rather than remaining as a discrete buried stratum, further eroding treatment effectiveness over time. - The tipping point towards re-eutrophication followed a three-stage mechanism: (1) gradual exhaustion of Al adsorption capacity causes non-bound P to accumulate in the BD-P pool; (2) the BD-P pool approaches saturation, making the system vulnerable to anoxic release; (3) wind mixing events rapidly transport released P from the hypolimnion to the photic zone, triggering bloom formation that then self-reinforces through elevated sediment oxygen demand and further SRP accumulation.
Implications & Recommendations - Al treatment of lakes is not a permanent solution; longevity depends on Al dose/area, hydraulic residence time, lake morphology (Osgood index), sedimentation rate, and background sulfate concentrations — the latter promoting sulphide formation that immobilises Fe and reduces the active iron pool available for P binding. - Re-eutrophication risk is likely to increase under climate warming, as longer and more intense stratification periods will extend anoxic conditions and raise hypolimnetic temperatures, accelerating organic matter mineralisation and internal P loading. - Regular post-treatment monitoring of sediment P fractionation and Al retention molar ratios in the upper 5 cm is essential to detect declining P adsorption capacity before re-eutrophication occurs. - Poly-aluminium chloride is recommended in preference to aluminium sulphate, given that the high background sulphate concentration in Lake Barleber contributed to sulphide formation and loss of the active iron P-binding pool. - Many treated lakes will require repeated aluminium application to sustain acceptable water quality; this should be planned as part of long-term lake management rather than treated as a one-off intervention.

title: Resources
text:
2022

Hamill (2022)
Trend and State of Nutrients in Lake Rotorua Streams 2002–2022.
River Lake Ltd for Bay of Plenty Regional Council.
PDF


Click to expand: Summary

The report focuses on nine major streams contributing to Lake Rotorua’s water quality. - Nutrient trends were assessed using the seasonal Kendall test over three periods: 2002-2022, 2002-2010, and 2010-2019. - The analysis includes total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), and dissolved reactive phosphorus (DRP) concentrations and loads.
Nutrient Concentrations and Stream Flows This section details the mean flow rates and nutrient concentrations in the streams entering Lake Rotorua.

The mean flow to Lake Rotorua from 2002-2022 was 11.8 m³/s, with Hamurana being the largest contributor at 2.63 m³/s.
The highest total nitrogen concentrations were found in Waiohewa (2839 mg/m³) and the highest total phosphorus concentrations in Waingaehe (123 mg/m³).
Streams like Hamurana, Awahou, and Waingaehe showed high concentrations of dissolved reactive phosphorus (DRP), with ratios of DRP to TP between 80-90%.

Trends in Nutrient Concentrations Over Time This section discusses the observed trends in nutrient concentrations across the monitored streams.

From 2002 to 2022, TN concentrations increased in Hamurana, Awahou, and Waiteti, particularly in Awahou and Waiteti since 2010.
TN concentrations decreased in Puarenga and possibly Ngongotaha, but this trend did not continue post-2010.
TP concentrations increased in Hamurana, Ngongotaha, Utuhina, Puarenga, Waingaehe, and Waiohewa, with trends continuing since 2010 in all but Waingaehe.

Nutrient Loads to Lake Rotorua

The nine main streams transported an average of 410 t/y of nitrogen and 28 t/y of phosphorus from 2002-2022.
The highest TN loads came from Awahou (71.1 t/y), Puarenga (67.4 t/y), and Hamurana (66.5 t/y).
TP loads were primarily contributed by Hamurana (7.5 t/y), Puarenga (5.1 t/y), and Awahou (3.9 t/y).




Mangeya (2022)
Groundwater Modelling Report.
Jacobs for Bay of Plenty Regional Council (Toi Moana).


Click to expand: Summary

Project Background and Objectives
The Bay of Plenty Regional Council engaged Jacobs to develop a groundwater flow model for the Rotorua Water Management Area to enhance water management practices. The Rotorua Water Management Area covers approximately 1,100 km². The model aims to improve understanding of groundwater systems and surface water interactions. It will inform groundwater allocation limits and assess various abstraction scenarios.
Scope of Work for Groundwater Modelling
The project involved several key tasks to develop and document the groundwater model.

Analyze available data and create a conceptual hydrogeological model.
Develop and calibrate a transient three-dimensional numerical groundwater flow model using MODFLOW.
Simulate predictive scenarios and document the model development and predictions.
Deliver the numerical model and associated files to the Bay of Plenty Regional Council.

Limitations of the Groundwater Modelling

The model does not account for certain factors that could affect groundwater and surface water quality.
Excludes the impact of groundwater extraction on water quality. Does not consider density effects from variable groundwater salinity or temperature. Ignores two-phase fluids in the active geothermal reservoir.

Importance and Context

Rotorua Te Arawa Lakes are culturally, historically, and ecologically significant.
Water quality varies with catchment characteristics: undeveloped (e.g., Tikitapu, Okataina) vs. highly developed agricultural/forestry (e.g., Rotorua, Rerewhakaaitu, Okaro).

Methodology for Nutrient Loads

Used updated export coefficient approach and Overseer® modelling for nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P).
Land use areas calculated for surface and groundwater catchments.
Nutrient loss rates estimated per land use, accounting for local factors (e.g., pest impacts, forest removal).
Additional sources included geothermal inputs, septic systems, municipal wastewater, atmospheric deposition, and hydrological connections among lakes.
Attenuation estimated from physiography to produce a consistent regional nutrient budget.

Key Findings and Implications

Agricultural land contributes disproportionately to N and P loads.
Geothermal, atmospheric, and connected-lake sources are significant in some catchments.
Many catchments exceed ‘reference’ nutrient loads by 2–3×, complicating restoration.
Provides basis for assessing internal lake loading and guiding catchment/lake management strategies.

title: Resources
text:
2016

Smith et al. (2016)
Phosphorus and nitrogen loading restraints are essential for successful eutrophication control of Lake Rotorua, New Zealand. PDF


Click to expand: Summary

Key Findings - Generalised additive models applied to a 14-year (2001–2015) dataset from Lake Rotorua found highly significant (p < 0.001) declines in total phosphorus (TP), total nitrogen (TN), and chlorophyll a (Chl-a) in surface waters, refuting claims that water quality had continued to decline despite mitigation. - Alum dosing in the Utuhina and Puarenga Stream inflows had a highly significant reducing effect on TP and Chl-a (p < 0.001), with near 4-fold reductions in Chl-a at maximum dosing rates, but no significant effect on TN. - Correlations of Chl-a with both TP and TN were highly significant, and the difference between the two correlation coefficients was not significant, indicating that algal productivity responds to both nutrients rather than either alone. - Bioassay studies in Lake Rotorua consistently demonstrated co-limitation of phytoplankton growth by both N and P, with spatial and temporal variation in which nutrient was more limiting. - Policies focused solely on reducing N loads risk stimulating dominance by heterocystous, N₂-fixing cyanobacteria (e.g. Dolichospermum, Aphanizomenon), whose bloom concentrations are strongly correlated with water column TP.
Implications & Recommendations - Both N and P loads to Lake Rotorua must be controlled simultaneously for effective eutrophication management; a single-nutrient strategy is insufficient and potentially counterproductive. - Alum dosing in tributary inflows is effective for short-term P reduction but is not recommended as a perpetual measure; its continuation should be contingent on progress in catchment-scale land-use change and nutrient runoff mitigation. - Achieving the target Trophic Level Index of 4.2 requires TN loads below 435 t y⁻¹ and TP loads below 37 t y⁻¹ — major reductions from current inputs dominated by agricultural land use (~75% of N load, ~45% of P load). - “Legacy P” stored in fertilised soils and streambed sediments, and long groundwater residence times (decades to over a century), mean that water quality responses to catchment management will be substantially lagged and require long-term commitment. - Continued monitoring of nutrients, Chl-a, and cyanobacterial biovolume should be maintained to track restoration trajectories and evaluate the relative contributions of alum dosing versus catchment management.

title: Resources
text:

Abell et al. (2015)
Lake Rotorua Treated Wastewater Discharge: Environmental Effects Study ERI Report 80, University of Waikato. PDF


Click to expand: Summary

Key Findings

The treated wastewater discharge contributes a measurable nutrient load to Lake Rotorua, which may influence the lake’s trophic status, algal growth, and water-quality trends.
There is evidence of spatial variability in how the discharge impacts the lake — e.g., nearer to the discharge site showing different water quality versus more remote parts of the lake.
The effectiveness of the current wastewater treatment and discharge regime is assessed and found to have limitations: even treated wastewater can contribute significant nutrient inputs if volumes are large and/or treatment is not optimised.
The report discusses the lake’s capacity to assimilate or dilute the nutrient load, and whether it is being exceeded or approaching thresholds that may degrade ecological health.

Implications & Recommendations

Management of wastewater inputs to Lake Rotorua must account not just for concentration of nutrients in the effluent but for volume of discharge and how that interacts with lake hydrodynamics (mixing, stratification, residence time).
Upgrading treatment processes, reducing nutrient concentrations further, or reducing the volume of discharge may be necessary to protect lake health.
Monitoring of water quality and ecological responses (algal blooms, oxygen levels, benthic habitat) should continue and be linked explicitly to discharge data to evaluate trends.
Lake management strategies should take a holistic view: catchment land-use, inflows, internal nutrient cycling, and wastewater discharges all interact to determine lake condition.

Click to expand: Summary

Lake Rotorua’s Water Quality Challenges Lake Rotorua has faced significant water quality decline due to nutrient loads and land use changes, necessitating a comprehensive management strategy.

Lake area: 80 km², mean depth: 10 m.
Cultural significance to the Te Arawa people and vital for tourism and recreation.
Water quality deterioration began in the 1960s, linked to treated wastewater inputs and land use changes from forest to pasture.
Urban wastewater discharge ceased in 1991, but ongoing pastoral expansion, especially dairy farming, has continued to impact water quality.
Legacy effects from historical land use and nutrient pools in sediments complicate current management efforts.

Modelling Approach for Water Quality Management A modelling approach is essential for assessing the impacts of land use, climate change, and management actions on Lake Rotorua’s water quality.

Integrated multiple models: SimCLIM, ROTAN, CLUES, DYRESM-CAEDYM.
SimCLIM predicts climate data (temperature, rainfall) for the Rotorua catchment up to 2100.
ROTAN simulates streamflows and nitrate transport between surface water and groundwater.
CLUES estimates annual average phosphorus loads in streams.
DYRESM-CAEDYM models vertical distribution of water temperature and nutrient cycling relevant to trophic state.

Nutrient Load Reduction Requirements To improve water quality, significant reductions in nitrogen and phosphorus loads are necessary.

At least 350 tonnes of nitrogen and a similar amount of phosphorus must be removed annually.
Target Trophic Level Index (TLI) value set at 4.2 to restore water quality.
Climate change is expected to exacerbate challenges, increasing stratification and internal nutrient loading.
Internal nutrient release from sediments is comparable to external loads, complicating management.

Internal Nutrient Loading and Management Strategies Addressing internal nutrient loading is critical for achieving long-term water quality goals in Lake Rotorua.

Internal loading from sediments contributes significantly to nutrient levels, especially during stratification.
Chemical flocculants may reduce internal loading but have limited duration of effectiveness (approximately four years).
Effective sediment capping can offset water quality deterioration but requires prior reduction of catchment nutrient loads.

title: Lake Rotorua V4 - GLM-AED output plots
text:
0. Helpers
profile_vars/zone_vars are read straight off the NetCDF file’s dimensions (AEME has no catalogue of “every variable in this output” — it only knows the variables it has a name mapping for), so this is the one place raw ncdf4 is used outside the sediment-heat section. get_var() happily accepts either the AED name ("OXY_oxy") or AEME’s own name ("CHM_oxy") for everything found this way.


Code
nc <- nc_open(outfile)
var_dims <- sapply(names(nc$var), function(v) sapply(nc$var[[v]]$dim, `[[`, "name"))

profile_vars <- names(var_dims)[sapply(var_dims, function(d) "z" %in% d)]
zone_vars    <- names(var_dims)[sapply(var_dims, function(d) {
  "nzones" %in% d && !"z" %in% d && !"sed_layers" %in% d
})]

long_name <- function(var) {
  v <- nc$var[[var]]
  if (is.null(v)) return(var)
  sprintf("%s (%s)", if (nzchar(v$longname)) v$longname else var, v$units)
}

cat(sprintf("%d profile variables, %d zone variables\n", length(profile_vars), length(zone_vars)))


160 profile variables, 37 zone variables


Code
# A handful of AED variable names aren't recognised by AEME's fuzzy matcher even
# though they're just renamed internally (e.g. dissolved oxygen is `CHM_oxy`, not
# `OXY_oxy`) - resolve those explicitly rather than letting get_var() error.
var_alias <- c(OXY_oxy = "CHM_oxy")
resolve_var <- function(var) unname(ifelse(var %in% names(var_alias), var_alias[var], var))

#' GLM writes each layer against a moving Lagrangian grid, so `get_var()`'s depths
#' don't line up day to day - interpolate onto a common depth-below-surface grid
#' before tiling, or the heatmap comes out as sparse, misaligned slivers.
grid_profile <- function(df, nz = 150) {
  depths <- seq(0, max(df$depth, na.rm = TRUE), length.out = nz)
  df |>
    group_by(Date) |>
    group_modify(~ data.frame(depth = depths,
                               value = approx(.x$depth, .x$value, xout = depths, rule = 2)$y)) |>
    ungroup()
}

#' Depth-time heatmap for a (lon, lat, z, time) variable, via AEME::get_var()
plot_profile <- function(var, cmap = "viridis") {
  df <- get_var(aeme, model = "glm_aed", var_sim = resolve_var(var), remove_spin_up = FALSE) |>
    grid_profile()
  ggplot(df, aes(x = Date, y = depth, fill = value)) +
    geom_raster() +
    scale_y_reverse() +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = cmap, na.value = NA) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "depth (m)", fill = NULL, title = var,
         subtitle = long_name(var)) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8))
}

plot_zone <- function(var) {

    geom_line(linewidth = 0.4) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = "zone", title = var, subtitle = long_name(var)) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 9), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 7),
          legend.position = "bottom")
}

title: Meeting Notes
text:
Meeting with DO – 11 August 2026
Data & Setup The team reviewed data inputs for Lake Rotorua modelling, including a hypsograph (excluding the hole), hourly met data from NIWA (sourced from the airport), and existing inflow data. The plan is to calibrate against the historical period (2000–2010) and validate against contemporary data (2011–2026), with a water balance assessment using GLM v4’s diagnostic residual outflow.
Calibration Strategy (to be discussed further with Matt) Calibration will cover physical and biological parameters, including phytoplankton dynamics modelled across three groups: cyanobacteria (positively buoyant), diatoms, and chlorophytes (winter-dominant). Buoy data will be integrated to separate signal from noise, drawing on parameters from an old CAEDYM version.
Calibration Benchmarks Key performance indicators were identified, framed as important for climate adaptation conversations: - Trophic Level Index (TLI) and its components — TN, TP, chlorophyll-a, and Secchi depth - Anoxic duration, temperature, and stratification metrics - Phytoplankton timing - Outflow nutrient concentrations to the Ohau Channel - Alum dosing module — accounting for pH effects, TLI impact, and cost implications - Consideration of whether a simplified approach could achieve comparable results
Sediment Processes Discussion around fixed vs. dynamic sediment loading, potential looping of the spin-up period, and the associated trade-offs.
Other - Slides prepared for the MH update — to be retained for ongoing monthly meetings - Longwave radiation to be estimated using an algorithm

28/04/26 - BoP PC10 Meeting

Summary: This PC10 meeting covered the science, monitoring, and economic dimensions of managing water quality in Lake Rotorua under climate change pressures. Key discussions centred on nitrogen reduction targets, groundwater lags, and the costs of mitigation options including constructed wetlands and riparian restoration. Data consistency, groundwater monitoring integration, and the validity of the TLI 4.2 target were debated, alongside updated nutrient accounting, internal loading measurements, and emerging restoration techniques such as ultrasonic cyanobacteria removal. An economic review and spatial planning work are ongoing to identify the most cost-effective pathways to meeting PC10 objectives. TALT engagement (via William) is ongoing with an update to follow, and strong turnout from the Rotorua Pastoral Collective reflects positive MoU partner engagement. 2007–present (~19 yr, two loggers)
On-lake met station: temp, RH, wind, pressure, rain; shortwave radiation on the new buoy only
The only source actually measured over the lake surface — the ground truth for lake-effect corrections. The two loggers agree closely where they can be compared (see below), so they splice into one record
Old buoy has no shortwave radiation; ~15% of hourly records missing for some variables; rain gauge is noisy


Airport (NIWA #1770)
niwa_met_hourly_aeme
1981–2025 (44 yr)
Nominally a full met suite at a fixed land station
Longest record; good temperature/RH
Wind and radiation have little or no overlap with the buoy window; daily rain is incomplete (~250 mm/yr); land-station bias vs. the lake


Airport (MetService NZROA)
airport_met_aeme (from airport_met)
Jan 1993 – Jun 2023 (30 yr)
Hourly temp, RH, station pressure, rain, shortwave radiation, wind speed and direction
Complete, independent hourly record with a real rain gauge, shortwave and wind; overlaps the old buoy for 16 years
Ends June 2023; wind, rain and radiation are hour-ending values; station pressure missing for ~32 % of hours; land station


ERA5-Land (reanalysis)
era5_hourly_met
2011–present
Gridded reanalysis, full met suite
Continuous, gap-free, extends into the future for scenario work
Coarse grid cell (not lake-specific); its own biases need correcting against real observations


PC10 / BOPRC stations
pc10_climate_met
Temp/RH: 2006–present (Edmund Rd); Rain: 1901–present (Whakarewarewa)
Temp, RH, rain only — no radiation or wind
Rain record is by far the longest of any source here; independent of NIWA’s instrumentation
No radiation/wind; weaker correlation with the buoy than the airport (see comparison below)



The airport and PC10 stations were chosen from BOPRC/NIWA’s larger station networks by longest, most complete overlapping record rather than by raw distance to the lake — see the PC10 extraction notes for the full station comparison (pc10_climate_station_summary()); for Lake Rotorua, every realistic candidate station already sits close to the lake, so record length matters more than the last kilometre of proximity.

title: Meteorological Data Sources & Forcing Comparison
section: Comparing the raw sources against the buoy
text:
Comparing the raw sources against the buoy
met_source_comparison aggregates all five sources to daily values and scores the NIWA airport, MetService airport, ERA5 and PC10 against the buoy — the only source with a direct claim to being “true” lake conditions — over whatever window each pair overlaps, for temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed, shortwave radiation and station pressure. Since the old buoy data were added (all_buoy_met_data), that window reaches back to mid-2007, so most comparisons rest on up to ~16 years of daily pairs.






Note



Wind units. Buoy wind is in m/s and is extrapolated to 10 m (from 2 m on the new buoy and 1.5 m on the old one). A duplicated knots→m/s conversion was being applied to buoy wind that was already in m/s, scaling it by 0.514; it was removed in buoy_to_aeme_met() (and the old-buoy equivalent) in October 2026. Before the fix the buoy’s mean 10 m wind was ~2.8 m/s; it is now ~5.4 m/s. That change moves ERA5’s apparent wind bias from ~−0.2 m/s to ~−2.8 m/s, so every wind result on this page reflects the corrected series, and earlier versions of this page that reported a small ERA5 wind bias were wrong. Separately, the buoy’s own rain had a unit bug, fixed in rotorua_buoy_met_data: before 2023-10-23 it logged rain in mm/10 min, while later records use mm.

Daily air temperature, relative humidity, rainfall and wind speed from all five sources, over the buoy’s record (2007–present).




What this shows:

Air temperature — every land/reanalysis source reads colder than the buoy: NIWA airport −0.95 °C, MetService airport −0.92 °C, PC10 −1.00 °C and ERA5 −1.48 °C on daily means. The offset is stable year to year (ERA5 − buoy is −1.3 to −1.7 °C in every year 2011–2025), so it is a real and consistent difference between lake-surface air and land/grid-cell air rather than drift. ERA5 tracks the buoy’s day-to-day shape best (r ≈ 0.99); both airports follow at r ≈ 0.98; PC10 is weakest (r ≈ 0.86, MAE ≈ 1.9 °C).
Relative humidity — all sources read more humid than the buoy: ERA5 +7.5 %, NIWA airport +6.4 %, MetService +6.1 %, PC10 +3.1 %. This is not simply a lake effect: the two land stations and ERA5 agree with each other (hourly ERA5 − MetService is only +0.6 %, r = 0.88), and the buoy’s offset is not constant — the annual ERA5 − buoy RH bias is +2–3 % in 2022–23, +9.5 % in 2024, +13 % in 2025 and +48 % in the 2026 data (buoy mean RH 47 %). The buoy RH sensor looks drifty or faulty, particularly from 2024 on (see the hourly section). PC10 RH has very weak correlation with the buoy (r ≈ 0.32).
Rainfall — mean daily totals agree well. The MetService gauge matches the buoy almost exactly (bias ≈ 0, r ≈ 0.86, the best rain agreement of any source), ERA5 is next (bias +0.0004 m/day, r ≈ 0.77), then the NIWA airport (r ≈ 0.59, biased low because its daily rain is incomplete), and PC10 is essentially uncorrelated day to day (r ≈ 0.06) despite agreeing on long-run totals — consistent with real small-scale spatial variability in rain rather than a PC10 error.
Wind speed — the buoy (10 m) averages ~5.4 m/s, well above every other source: MetService airport −1.7 m/s (r ≈ 0.89), NIWA airport −2.1 m/s (r ≈ 0.82, only 679 days), and ERA5 −2.8 m/s (r ≈ 0.89, 5,079 days), i.e. about 52 % below the buoy. Even against the land MetService station ERA5 is 1.2 m/s low on matched hours, so ERA5 under-reads wind generally and the buoy is windier than both land stations (open-water fetch plus the 2 m → 10 m extrapolation). PC10 has no wind station.
Shortwave radiation — only the MetService airport (r ≈ 0.97, bias −5 W/m² over 469 days of overlap with the new buoy, Feb 2022–Jun 2023) and ERA5 (r ≈ 0.84, bias −10 W/m² over 1,404 days) can be compared; the NIWA airport has no overlap with the buoy.
Station pressure — all sources differ from the buoy by a nearly constant offset (r ≥ 0.996): MetService −0.13 kPa, ERA5 −1.10 kPa and NIWA airport +3.29 kPa. MetService (station height 285 m) is by far the closest.


Hourly comparison: buoys, MetService airport and ERA5
The daily comparison scores sources against a single combined buoy series. This section looks at hourly resolution and brings in four series: the old buoy (2007–22), the new buoy (2022–), ERA5, and the MetService airport record (1993–Jun 2023), which is the only independent, complete hourly station in the set and overlaps the old buoy for 16 years. It answers three questions the daily view cannot: (1) can the two buoy loggers be treated as one record?, (2) what are ERA5’s biases on matched hours, variable by variable, including shortwave, pressure and wind direction? and (3) is the buoy itself a trustworthy reference for each variable? The old and new buoys never overlap in time, so they are compared with each other through their distributions and indirectly through ERA5 and MetService.
All series are floored to the hour (the old buoy logs every 15 minutes, so the :00 record is kept) and duplicate hours are dropped, keeping the first value so wind direction is never averaged arithmetically. MetService rain, wind and radiation are hour-ending values (they describe the hour preceding the stamp); MetService wind is the hourly mean where recorded and the 10-minute mean otherwise.


Code
era5_hourly_met          <- tar_read(era5_hourly_met)
airport_met_aeme         <- tar_read(airport_met_aeme)
old_buoy_met_hr_aeme     <- tar_read(old_buoy_met_hr_aeme)
rotorua_buoy_met_aeme_hr <- tar_read(rotorua_buoy_met_aeme_hr)

dfs <- list(
  "Buoy (new, 2022-)"   = rotorua_buoy_met_aeme_hr,
  "Buoy (old, 2007-22)" = old_buoy_met_hr_aeme,
  "ERA5"                = era5_hourly_met,
  "MetService airport"  = airport_met_aeme
)

# Variables shared by at least two sources (missing ones are filled with NA)
vars <- c("MET_tmpair", "MET_prsttn", "MET_wndspd", "MET_humrel",
          "MET_radswd", "MET_pprain", "MET_wnddir")

var_labels <- c(
  MET_tmpair = "Air temperature (°C)",
  MET_prsttn = "Station pressure (Pa)",
  MET_wndspd = "Wind speed (m/s)",
  MET_humrel = "Relative humidity (%)",
  MET_radswd = "Shortwave radiation (W/m²)",
  MET_pprain = "Rain (check units!)",
  MET_wnddir = "Wind direction (°)"
)

cols <- c("Buoy (new, 2022-)"   = "#1b9e77",
          "Buoy (old, 2007-22)" = "#d95f02",
          "ERA5"                = "#7570b3",
          "MetService airport"  = "#e7298a")

prep <- function(df) {
  for (v in setdiff(vars, names(df))) df[[v]] <- NA_real_
  out <- df |>
    mutate(Date = lubridate::floor_date(Date, "hour")) |>
    select(Date, all_of(vars)) |>
    arrange(Date)
  distinct(out, Date, .keep_all = TRUE)
}

dfs_h <- purrr::map(dfs, prep)

met_all <- dfs_h |>
  bind_rows(.id = "source") |>
  mutate(source = factor(source, levels = names(dfs)))

met_long <- met_all |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(all_of(vars), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = vars, labels = var_labels[vars]))

lin_vars <- setdiff(vars, c("MET_wnddir", "MET_pprain"))  # linear, non-rain
lin_long <- met_long |> filter(variable %in% var_labels[lin_vars])

# Timezone of each series (ERA5 starting at 13:00 hints at a UTC vs NZ offset)

  end    = do.call(c, lapply(dfs_h, \(d) max(d$Date)))
) |>

The two buoy loggers are statistically interchangeable for temperature, wind and pressure. Mean air temperature (14.0 °C both), 10 m wind speed (5.45 vs 5.34 m/s) and pressure (98.34 kPa both) match to within about 2 %, so there is no sign of a step change at the 2022 handover, and ERA5’s matched-hour offsets for these variables are nearly identical against each logger (below). Relative humidity is the exception (see the annual-bias table). The land and reanalysis series differ from the buoys in consistent ways: ERA5 is ~1.5 °C cooler, more humid (mean 83 % vs 75 %; median 87 % vs 77 %), has a wider temperature range (SD 4.6 vs 4.0 °C) and a much lower mean wind (2.48 vs ~5.4 m/s). The MetService airport sits in between on wind (3.58 m/s), is cooler than the buoys (12.7 °C, with a much wider range of −5 to 30 °C), is more humid (81 %), and reads 98.20 kPa station pressure (the buoys 98.34 kPa). Shortwave means agree across the three sources that measure it (new buoy 165, ERA5 170, MetService 167 W/m²).


Is the buoy a stable reference? Annual bias by year
Because ERA5 and the MetService airport are independent of the buoy and of each other, year-by-year bias against them shows whether a buoy sensor has drifted. A real, physical offset (such as lake vs. land air temperature) should be steady; sensor drift should not.


Code
b_all <- bind_rows(dfs_h[["Buoy (old, 2007-22)"]], dfs_h[["Buoy (new, 2022-)"]])
era5_h <- dfs_h[["ERA5"]]
ms_h   <- dfs_h[["MetService airport"]]

yr_bias <- function(ref, test, v, lab) {
  inner_join(select(ref, Date, ref = all_of(v)),
             select(test, Date, test = all_of(v)), by = "Date") |>
    filter(!is.na(ref), !is.na(test)) |>
    mutate(yr = lubridate::year(Date)) |>
    group_by(yr) |>
    summarise(bias = mean(test - ref), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(comparison = lab, variable = v)
}

annual_bias <- bind_rows(
  yr_bias(b_all, era5_h, "MET_tmpair", "ERA5 - buoy"),
  yr_bias(b_all, era5_h, "MET_humrel", "ERA5 - buoy"),
  yr_bias(b_all, era5_h, "MET_wndspd", "ERA5 - buoy"),
  yr_bias(ms_h,  era5_h, "MET_tmpair", "ERA5 - MetService"),
  yr_bias(ms_h,  era5_h, "MET_humrel", "ERA5 - MetService"),
  yr_bias(ms_h,  era5_h, "MET_wndspd", "ERA5 - MetService")
) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = vars, labels = var_labels[vars]))

annual_bias |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = comparison, values_from = bias) |>
  arrange(variable, yr) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Annual mean hourly bias of ERA5 against the buoys and against the MetService airport.")

Temperature and wind offsets are steady; the RH offset is not. ERA5 − buoy temperature stays between −1.3 and −1.7 °C every year (and ERA5 − MetService between −0.3 and −0.7 °C), and ERA5 − buoy wind between −2.6 and −3.4 m/s, so those are stable properties of the sources. ERA5 − MetService RH is within about ±1–2 % in every year. Against the buoy, however, the RH bias wanders from +5 % to +9.5 % through 2011–2020, falls to +2–3 % in 2022–23, then rises to +9.5 % (2024), +13 % (2025) and +48 % in 2026, when the buoy reports a mean RH of only 47 %. That pattern points to calibration drift or a failing sensor rather than a lake effect, and it matters because era5_bias_correction currently fits MET_humrel against this buoy record.

Matched-hour comparison: ERA5, MetService and the buoys
To remove sampling differences between periods, series are paired on hours where both have valid data: ERA5 against each buoy, ERA5 against the MetService airport, and MetService against each buoy. Bias is the second-named series minus the first-named reference, i.e. ERA5 − buoy, ERA5 − MetService, and MetService − buoy, so a negative wind bias means the first series reads low.


Code
paired <- function(ref, test, vars) {
  inner_join(
    ref  |> select(Date, all_of(vars)),
    test |> select(Date, all_of(vars)),
    by = "Date", suffix = c("_ref", "_test")
  ) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-Date, names_to = c("variable", "which"),
                        names_pattern = "(.*)_(ref|test)$", values_to = "value") |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = which, values_from = value) |>
    filter(!is.na(ref), !is.na(test))
}

lag_r <- function(ref, test, v, k) {
  t2 <- test
  t2$Date <- t2$Date - k * 3600
  d <- inner_join(select(ref, Date, a = all_of(v)), select(t2, Date, b = all_of(v)), by = "Date")
  d <- filter(d, !is.na(a), !is.na(b))
  cor(d$a, d$b)
}

A real bug this comparison caught
Running this comparison surfaced a unit mismatch that a single-source sanity check would have missed: ERA5-Land’s raw MET_pprain column is stored in mm/hour, while every other source in this pipeline (buoy, airport, PC10) is in m/hour/m-day, the AEME convention. Uncorrected, ERA5’s rainfall was reading roughly 1000x too high in the shared units (mean 0.18 vs. the buoy’s 0.0008 m/hr) — and because era5_bias_correction originally excluded MET_pprain from correction (rainfall was assumed to be a poor target due to buoy-gauge reliability, not a units problem), that inflated value would have flowed straight through era5_corrected_hourly into every scenario baseline.
Fixed in two places:

read_era5_hourly_met() now converts MET_pprain mm/hour → m/hour at read time, so the fix applies everywhere the ERA5 series is used, not just here.

Fixing ERA5 rainfall: quantile mapping vs. scaling
The default method = "scale" rain correction is only a monthly multiplier on totals, so it cannot touch the drizzle problem found above. metscale::fit_met_bias_correction() also offers empirical quantile mapping ("eqm") and quantile delta mapping ("qdm"), which remap the whole ERA5 distribution — zeros included — onto the buoy distribution month by month. Four ERA5 rain variants are compared here, all fit against all_buoy_met_data:

raw — uncorrected ERA5.
scale — the current era5_bias_correction approach (monthly multiplier).
eqm — quantile mapping (100 quantiles), which also adjusts wet-hour frequency and intensity.
eqm+scale — eqm, then a second monthly scale fit on the eqm output to put the total back on the buoy’s.

qdm was also fitted and gives numbers identical to eqm on the historical period (it only differs when extrapolating a trend), so it is not shown separately.

all_buoy_met_data <- tar_read(all_buoy_met_data)

fit_rain <- \(e, m) metscale::fit_met_bias_correction(
  e, all_buoy_met_data, vars = "MET_pprain", method = m,
  nquantiles = 100, verbose = FALSE)
apply_rain <- \(e, f) metscale::apply_met_bias_correction(e, f, verbose = FALSE)

f_scale <- fit_rain(era5_hourly_met, "scale")
f_eqm   <- fit_rain(era5_hourly_met, "eqm")
e_eqm   <- apply_rain(era5_hourly_met, f_eqm)
f_es    <- fit_rain(e_eqm, "scale")

rain_variants <- list(
  raw         = era5_hourly_met,
  scale       = apply_rain(era5_hourly_met, f_scale),
  eqm         = e_eqm,
  `eqm+scale` = apply_rain(e_eqm, f_es)
)

Its daily rainfall averages only 0.7 mm/day (~250 mm/yr) on days it is “valid”, roughly a fifth of every other gauge, so its rain series appears incomplete (many days probably contain only some of the 3-hourly observations) and cannot be used to judge totals or wet-day frequency. The MetService record now fills that role.

Recommendation (now implemented in the pipeline): use MET_pprain = "eqm" followed by a monthly scale for the historical ERA5 baseline. That fixes drizzle frequency, wet-hour intensity and the bulk of the tail, keeps the total on the buoy, and is consistent with the independent MetService total to within 1 % and PC10 to within ~4 %. Because the second stage is fit on the output of the first, it needs two chained calls rather than a single method = vector:
In _targets.R this is era5_rain_eqm_correction → era5_hourly_met_rainqm (stage 1), then era5_bias_correction fitted on era5_hourly_met_rainqm (stage 2, together with the other variables), with era5_corrected_hourly and era5_corrected_daily_baseline built from era5_hourly_met_rainqm. The equivalent standalone code is:


Code
# 1. quantile-map rain onto the buoy distribution
bc_rain_eqm <- metscale::fit_met_bias_correction(
  era5_hourly_met, all_buoy_met_data, vars = "MET_pprain",
  method = "eqm", nquantiles = 100, verbose = FALSE)
era5_eqm <- metscale::apply_met_bias_correction(era5_hourly_met, bc_rain_eqm)

# 2. restore the buoy's total with a monthly ratio
bc_rain_scale <- metscale::fit_met_bias_correction(
  era5_eqm, all_buoy_met_data, vars = "MET_pprain",
  method = "scale", by = "doy-loess", verbose = FALSE)
era5_rain_corrected <- metscale::apply_met_bias_correction(era5_eqm, bc_rain_scale)








Note



expand_met() rounding (fixed). metscale::expand_met() previously rounded every column to 3 decimals. Rain is in m/hr, so that quantised it to whole millimetres: in testing it cut the corrected wet-hour fraction from 15.2 % to 4.9 % and erased all the drizzle correction (and coarsened earlier era5_corrected_hourly rain). It now rounds to 6 decimals and the pipeline calls apply_met_bias_correction(expand = TRUE) directly. era5_corrected_daily_baseline rounds daily totals to 6 decimals too, so it is unaffected.


Caveats: hourly timing is unchanged (r stays ≈ 0.5) — this corrects the distribution, not when rain falls. The quantile map caps ERA5 extremes at the buoy’s observed maximum, and the extreme daily tail ends up somewhat heavier than the MetService gauge shows.




How this improves lake model forcing

The buoy reference is now ~19 years, not ~4.5. Adding the old buoy lets the day-of-year corrections in era5_bias_correction and niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction train on ~130,000 hourly pairs instead of ~40,000, and the hourly comparison shows the two loggers agree on temperature, wind and pressure.
Caught a forcing bug before it reached the model. The ERA5 rain unit error above would have meant every ERA5-driven scenario — including every future GCM projection, since deltas are applied to the ERA5 baseline — ran with rainfall roughly 3 orders of magnitude too high. A single-source pipeline has no way to notice this; comparing independent sources does.
Wind is the largest bias in the forcing, and it is now correctly sized. With the doubled unit conversion removed, ERA5 reads ~2.8 m/s (~52 %) below the buoy’s 10 m wind, not ~0.2 m/s. Wind drives mixing and surface heat flux directly, so era5_bias_correction’s MET_wndspd scale correction (cross-validated RMSE 3.52 → 2.06 m/s, KGE 0.19 → 0.72) is one of the most consequential steps in the pipeline. The land stations cannot substitute: the MetService airport also reads 1.7 m/s below the buoy, so the correction really is a land/reanalysis → lake transfer and depends on the buoy’s 2 m/1.5 m → 10 m extrapolation being right.
The buoy → airport extension helps temperature and humidity, less so wind. niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction trains on the full buoy overlap (2007–present) and cuts NIWA-airport-vs-buoy RMSE from 2.02 → 1.74 °C (temperature) while humidity, which uses the 2022–23 buoy only in this fit, shows no cross-validated gain (RMSE 5.7 → 6.6 %; in-sample 5.7 → 5.5 %); wind is corrected for bias (−2.3 → −0.1 m/s) but with only modest gains in RMSE (3.18 → 2.94 m/s) and weak correlation (r ≈ 0.63). era5_bias_correction_extended cuts ERA5 temperature RMSE from 2.08 → 1.45 °C and humidity from 7.3 → 7.0 %.
A second, independent hourly station is now available. The MetService airport record (1993–Jun 2023) has a real rain gauge, shortwave and wind, and agrees with ERA5 on temperature (−0.5 °C), humidity (+0.6 %) and shortwave (−2 W/m²). It validates the rain correction independently of the buoy, exposes the buoy RH drift, and is a candidate for extending reference records back before 2007 (for variables where it agrees well with the buoy: temperature, pressure, rain).
PC10’s 1901–present rainfall record is the longest available context for Rotorua rainfall, over 40 years longer than the airports’. That’s directly useful for summarise_climate_extremes.R / climate-extreme-events.qmd’s historical-extremes framing, and as a long-run independent check on whatever ERA5 rainfall climatology ends up driving the historical baseline and scenario deltas. Its weak daily correlation with the buoy for RH and rain (r ≈ 0.32 and 0.06) means it shouldn’t be used as a fit_met_bias_correction() reference for those variables.
Wind direction and shortwave timing check out. ERA5 reproduces the prevailing WSW–W flow (hourly mean absolute direction error ~39–50°) and the shortwave daily cycle (r = 0.91 against the new buoy and 0.95 against MetService), so ERA5-derived direction and radiation are defensible for the model.



Caveats

Buoy relative humidity is not a reliable reference, so ERA5 humidity is corrected against the MetService airport instead. The old buoy (2007–22) reads ~5–9.5 % below ERA5 and the MetService airport, and the new buoy’s offset drifts from +2–3 % in 2022–23 to +9.5 % (2024), +13 % (2025) and +48 % in 2026 (mean RH 47 %). era5_bias_correction therefore no longer corrects MET_humrel; era5_humrel_correction fits it to airport_met_aeme (1993–Jun 2023, so the fit covers 2011–Jun 2023 of ERA5), and the correction is applied before the buoy-based one. buoy_met_fit_ref keeps buoy RH only for 2022-01-01 to 2023-12-31 for the remaining buoy-referenced fits (niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction and, through it, era5_bias_correction_extended, which still corrects humidity against that lake-equivalent series). all_buoy_met_data and the comparisons above still include all buoy RH. The airport station is a land station, so any lake effect on humidity (the buoy is the only lake-surface sensor) is not captured; the airport fit assumes the same land–lake humidity relationship ERA5 already has.
Station pressure (MET_prsttn). The buoys log sensible station pressure (~98.3 kPa on both loggers; the MetService airport 98.2 kPa). ERA5 reads a near-constant 1.1 kPa lower (r = 0.997), a grid-cell elevation difference of order 100 m, not a units error; the NIWA airport reads ~3.3 kPa higher. All offsets are removed by the scale corrections (ERA5 RMSE falls to ~60 Pa), but raw ERA5 and NIWA pressures should not be used uncorrected.
era5_bias_correction_extended wind and shortwave rest on almost no data. Its cross-validation has only 28 wind and 10 shortwave paired hours (versus ~130,000 for temperature/humidity), so for MET_wndspd and MET_radswd prefer era5_bias_correction. The comment in _targets.R describing these as “uncorrected airport values” predates the old buoy being added to the reference and is worth revisiting.
Shortwave is validated on limited data. The old buoy has no shortwave, the NIWA airport has none that overlaps the buoy, and the MetService airport overlaps the new buoy only from Feb 2022 to Jun 2023 (~11,000 hours), so ERA5 shortwave rests on the new buoy (~30,000 hours) plus that MetService overlap.
Sub-daily timing. The buoy stamps are offset from ERA5/MetService hour-ending stamps by roughly 30–60 minutes (see the diurnal section). This matters for hourly radiation and temperature, not for daily results.
ERA5 rain is wet too often (41 % of hours vs 12–16 %) with weak hourly intensity; fine for totals, less so for event-scale extremes. The current scale rain correction does not address this; eqm followed by scale does (see “Fixing ERA5 rainfall”). era5_bias_correction_extended still uses plain scale for rain.
PC10 has no radiation or wind data, so pc10_climate_met is a partial forcing (temp/RH/rain only) — useful for comparison and historical context, not as a standalone forcing source.
Hour-stamp de-duplication. prep() in the hourly section drops a large number of duplicated hour stamps (first value kept); the old buoy’s 15-minute rows are reduced to the :00 record. This is harmless for the comparisons here but means sub-hourly information is not used.

title: Meteorological Data Sources & Forcing Comparison
section: Hourly comparison: buoys, MetService airport and ERA5
text:
Hourly comparison: buoys, MetService airport and ERA5
The daily comparison scores sources against a single combined buoy series. This section looks at hourly resolution and brings in four series: the old buoy (2007–22), the new buoy (2022–), ERA5, and the MetService airport record (1993–Jun 2023), which is the only independent, complete hourly station in the set and overlaps the old buoy for 16 years. It answers three questions the daily view cannot: (1) can the two buoy loggers be treated as one record?, (2) what are ERA5’s biases on matched hours, variable by variable, including shortwave, pressure and wind direction? and (3) is the buoy itself a trustworthy reference for each variable? The old and new buoys never overlap in time, so they are compared with each other through their distributions and indirectly through ERA5 and MetService.
All series are floored to the hour (the old buoy logs every 15 minutes, so the :00 record is kept) and duplicate hours are dropped, keeping the first value so wind direction is never averaged arithmetically. MetService rain, wind and radiation are hour-ending values (they describe the hour preceding the stamp); MetService wind is the hourly mean where recorded and the 10-minute mean otherwise.


Code
era5_hourly_met          <- tar_read(era5_hourly_met)
airport_met_aeme         <- tar_read(airport_met_aeme)
old_buoy_met_hr_aeme     <- tar_read(old_buoy_met_hr_aeme)
rotorua_buoy_met_aeme_hr <- tar_read(rotorua_buoy_met_aeme_hr)

dfs <- list(
  "Buoy (new, 2022-)"   = rotorua_buoy_met_aeme_hr,
  "Buoy (old, 2007-22)" = old_buoy_met_hr_aeme,
  "ERA5"                = era5_hourly_met,
  "MetService airport"  = airport_met_aeme
)

# Variables shared by at least two sources (missing ones are filled with NA)
vars <- c("MET_tmpair", "MET_prsttn", "MET_wndspd", "MET_humrel",
          "MET_radswd", "MET_pprain", "MET_wnddir")

var_labels <- c(
  MET_tmpair = "Air temperature (°C)",
  MET_prsttn = "Station pressure (Pa)",
  MET_wndspd = "Wind speed (m/s)",
  MET_humrel = "Relative humidity (%)",
  MET_radswd = "Shortwave radiation (W/m²)",
  MET_pprain = "Rain (check units!)",
  MET_wnddir = "Wind direction (°)"
)

cols <- c("Buoy (new, 2022-)"   = "#1b9e77",
          "Buoy (old, 2007-22)" = "#d95f02",
          "ERA5"                = "#7570b3",
          "MetService airport"  = "#e7298a")

prep <- function(df) {
  for (v in setdiff(vars, names(df))) df[[v]] <- NA_real_
  out <- df |>
    mutate(Date = lubridate::floor_date(Date, "hour")) |>
    select(Date, all_of(vars)) |>
    arrange(Date)
  distinct(out, Date, .keep_all = TRUE)
}

dfs_h <- purrr::map(dfs, prep)

met_all <- dfs_h |>
  bind_rows(.id = "source") |>
  mutate(source = factor(source, levels = names(dfs)))

met_long <- met_all |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(all_of(vars), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = vars, labels = var_labels[vars]))

lin_vars <- setdiff(vars, c("MET_wnddir", "MET_pprain"))  # linear, non-rain
lin_long <- met_long |> filter(variable %in% var_labels[lin_vars])

# Timezone of each series (ERA5 starting at 13:00 hints at a UTC vs NZ offset)

  source = names(dfs),
  tzone  = sapply(dfs, \(d) attr(d$Date, "tzone")),
  start  = do.call(c, lapply(dfs_h, \(d) min(d$Date))),
  end    = do.call(c, lapply(dfs_h, \(d) max(d$Date)))
) |>

The two buoy loggers are statistically interchangeable for temperature, wind and pressure. Mean air temperature (14.0 °C both), 10 m wind speed (5.45 vs 5.34 m/s) and pressure (98.34 kPa both) match to within about 2 %, so there is no sign of a step change at the 2022 handover, and ERA5’s matched-hour offsets for these variables are nearly identical against each logger (below). Relative humidity is the exception (see the annual-bias table). The land and reanalysis series differ from the buoys in consistent ways: ERA5 is ~1.5 °C cooler, more humid (mean 83 % vs 75 %; median 87 % vs 77 %), has a wider temperature range (SD 4.6 vs 4.0 °C) and a much lower mean wind (2.48 vs ~5.4 m/s). The MetService airport sits in between on wind (3.58 m/s), is cooler than the buoys (12.7 °C, with a much wider range of −5 to 30 °C), is more humid (81 %), and reads 98.20 kPa station pressure (the buoys 98.34 kPa). Shortwave means agree across the three sources that measure it (new buoy 165, ERA5 170, MetService 167 W/m²).


Is the buoy a stable reference? Annual bias by year
Because ERA5 and the MetService airport are independent of the buoy and of each other, year-by-year bias against them shows whether a buoy sensor has drifted. A real, physical offset (such as lake vs. land air temperature) should be steady; sensor drift should not.


Code
b_all <- bind_rows(dfs_h[["Buoy (old, 2007-22)"]], dfs_h[["Buoy (new, 2022-)"]])
era5_h <- dfs_h[["ERA5"]]
ms_h   <- dfs_h[["MetService airport"]]

yr_bias <- function(ref, test, v, lab) {
  inner_join(select(ref, Date, ref = all_of(v)),
             select(test, Date, test = all_of(v)), by = "Date") |>
    filter(!is.na(ref), !is.na(test)) |>
    mutate(yr = lubridate::year(Date)) |>
    group_by(yr) |>
    summarise(bias = mean(test - ref), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(comparison = lab, variable = v)
}

annual_bias <- bind_rows(
  yr_bias(b_all, era5_h, "MET_tmpair", "ERA5 - buoy"),
  yr_bias(b_all, era5_h, "MET_humrel", "ERA5 - buoy"),
  yr_bias(b_all, era5_h, "MET_wndspd", "ERA5 - buoy"),
  yr_bias(ms_h,  era5_h, "MET_tmpair", "ERA5 - MetService"),
  yr_bias(ms_h,  era5_h, "MET_humrel", "ERA5 - MetService"),
  yr_bias(ms_h,  era5_h, "MET_wndspd", "ERA5 - MetService")
) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = vars, labels = var_labels[vars]))

annual_bias |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = comparison, values_from = bias) |>
  arrange(variable, yr) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Annual mean hourly bias of ERA5 against the buoys and against the MetService airport.")

Code
ggplot(annual_bias, aes(yr, bias, colour = comparison)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("ERA5 - buoy" = "#1b9e77", "ERA5 - MetService" = "#e7298a")) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "Annual ERA5 bias vs. buoy and vs. MetService airport",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean bias (ERA5 - reference)", colour = NULL)









Temperature and wind offsets are steady; the RH offset is not. ERA5 − buoy temperature stays between −1.3 and −1.7 °C every year (and ERA5 − MetService between −0.3 and −0.7 °C), and ERA5 − buoy wind between −2.6 and −3.4 m/s, so those are stable properties of the sources. ERA5 − MetService RH is within about ±1–2 % in every year. Against the buoy, however, the RH bias wanders from +5 % to +9.5 % through 2011–2020, falls to +2–3 % in 2022–23, then rises to +9.5 % (2024), +13 % (2025) and +48 % in 2026, when the buoy reports a mean RH of only 47 %. That pattern points to calibration drift or a failing sensor rather than a lake effect, and it matters because era5_bias_correction currently fits MET_humrel against this buoy record.


Distributions
The ECDF is the most useful view for spotting shifts (a horizontal offset between curves is a bias) and differences in the tails (e.g. ERA5’s dampened wind extremes).

Rainfall
Rainfall is zero-inflated, so it is compared by wet-hour fraction and by the distribution of non-zero hours rather than by mean and SD alone.
All four series are now in the same unit (m/hour — the old buoy’s maximum is 0.046 m/hr and the MetService maximum 0.047 m/hr, in line with the others), so no rescaling is needed; rain_scale is kept at 1 as a hook in case that changes.


Code
rain_scale <- c("Buoy (new, 2022-)"   = 1,
                "Buoy (old, 2007-22)" = 1,
                "ERA5"                = 1,
                "MetService airport"  = 1)    # edit once units are confirmed

rain <- met_all |>
  filter(!is.na(MET_pprain)) |>
  mutate(rain = MET_pprain * rain_scale[as.character(source)])

rain |>
  group_by(source) |>
  summarise(
    n_obs        = n(),
    wet_fraction = mean(rain > 0),
    mean_all     = mean(rain),
    mean_wet     = mean(rain[rain > 0]),
    p95_wet      = quantile(rain[rain > 0], 0.95),
    max          = max(rain),

ERA5 gets the rain total right but not its character. Mean hourly rain is similar across sources (≈ 0.00014–0.00018 m/hr), but ERA5 is “wet” in 41 % of hours versus 12–16 % on both buoys and the MetService gauge, and its wet hours are weaker (mean 0.43 mm/hr vs 0.9–1.3 mm/hr; 95th percentile 2.1 vs 4.5–5.5 mm/hr; maximum 21 vs 28–47 mm/hr). The two buoys and the independent MetService gauge agree with each other, which is strong evidence that the buoy rain gauge is not the problem. For lake forcing this matters mostly for event-scale inflow and extremes; daily and longer totals are fine.

Matched-hour comparison: ERA5, MetService and the buoys
To remove sampling differences between periods, series are paired on hours where both have valid data: ERA5 against each buoy, ERA5 against the MetService airport, and MetService against each buoy. Bias is the second-named series minus the first-named reference, i.e. ERA5 − buoy, ERA5 − MetService, and MetService − buoy, so a negative wind bias means the first series reads low.


Code
paired <- function(ref, test, vars) {
  inner_join(
    ref  |> select(Date, all_of(vars)),
    test |> select(Date, all_of(vars)),
    by = "Date", suffix = c("_ref", "_test")
  ) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-Date, names_to = c("variable", "which"),
                        names_pattern = "(.*)_(ref|test)$", values_to = "value") |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = which, values_from = value) |>
    filter(!is.na(ref), !is.na(test))
}

All four Date columns carry the same fixed-offset timezone (Etc/GMT-12, NZST, no daylight saving), so this is not a timezone mismatch in the stored data. ERA5 and MetService values are hour-ending (they describe the preceding hour), whereas the buoy stamp is instantaneous or hour-centred, so the series are offset by roughly 30–60 minutes. The lag table below shows the effect on hourly skill is small, but it is worth knowing for sub-daily radiation work.


Code
lag_r <- function(ref, test, v, k) {
  t2 <- test
  t2$Date <- t2$Date - k * 3600
  d <- inner_join(select(ref, Date, a = all_of(v)), select(t2, Date, b = all_of(v)), by = "Date")
  d <- filter(d, !is.na(a), !is.na(b))
  cor(d$a, d$b)
}

title: Meteorological Data Sources & Forcing Comparison
section: A real bug this comparison caught
text:
A real bug this comparison caught
Running this comparison surfaced a unit mismatch that a single-source sanity check would have missed: ERA5-Land’s raw MET_pprain column is stored in mm/hour, while every other source in this pipeline (buoy, airport, PC10) is in m/hour/m-day, the AEME convention. Uncorrected, ERA5’s rainfall was reading roughly 1000x too high in the shared units (mean 0.18 vs. the buoy’s 0.0008 m/hr) — and because era5_bias_correction originally excluded MET_pprain from correction (rainfall was assumed to be a poor target due to buoy-gauge reliability, not a units problem), that inflated value would have flowed straight through era5_corrected_hourly into every scenario baseline.
Fixed in two places:

read_era5_hourly_met() now converts MET_pprain mm/hour → m/hour at read time, so the fix applies everywhere the ERA5 series is used, not just here.
MET_pprain is now included in both era5_bias_correction and era5_bias_correction_extended’s vars, using the same method = "scale" day-of-year correction as the other variables — see the comparison above for why this is reasonable (no evidence of a buoy under-catch, just noise), while still treating the buoy’s rain series with more caution than its temperature/RH/wind.

Note: the pipeline now quantile-maps rain before this fit (see “Fixing ERA5 rainfall”), so the raw rows for MET_pprain here and in the table below are the quantile-mapped series, and the skill shown is the second-stage monthly scale. With the units fixed, ERA5 rain now agrees with the buoys on mean totals (hourly r ≈ 0.52 overall). The scale correction leaves rain essentially unchanged — cross-validated KGE is marginally lower after correction (0.31 vs 0.34) — which is the expected outcome for a variable whose mismatch is in timing and intensity rather than in the mean. Rain correction is harmless but should not be credited with improving the forcing.

Wind is now the largest correction: bias −2.82 → 0.00 m/s, RMSE 3.52 → 2.06 m/s and KGE 0.19 → 0.72, with correlation unchanged (r ≈ 0.73) — a scale correction fixes the mean, not the hourly timing error visible in the matched-hour scatter.
Temperature and pressure improve a lot: temperature bias −1.48 → 0.00 °C and RMSE 2.00 → 1.33 °C; pressure bias −1,103 Pa → 0 and RMSE 1,104 → 59 Pa.
Humidity is now fit to the MetService airport (airport_met_aeme, 108,630 matched hours, 2011–Jun 2023) rather than the buoy, as a separate stage in front of era5_bias_correction (target era5_humrel_correction). Raw ERA5 already agrees closely with that station (bias +0.6 %, r 0.88), so the correction is small: cross-validated RMSE 7.15 → 7.08 %, KGE 0.828 → 0.837, and the mean bias goes to zero. It lowers ERA5’s mean RH only from 83.0 % to 82.4 %, whereas fitting to the buoy lowered it to 80–81 %. Against the buoys the corrected series still reads ~2 % above the 2022–23 new buoy and ~7 % above the 2011–2020 old buoy, which is the buoy offset described below, not an ERA5 error.
Shortwave: already close to unbiased (+9 W/m²); correction gives only a small gain, and it is fit on the new buoy alone (~30,000 hours).
Rain: no gain from scale (above). Quantile mapping followed by a monthly scale does fix wet-hour frequency and intensity — see the next subsection.


Fixing ERA5 rainfall: quantile mapping vs. scaling
The default method = "scale" rain correction is only a monthly multiplier on totals, so it cannot touch the drizzle problem found above. metscale::fit_met_bias_correction() also offers empirical quantile mapping ("eqm") and quantile delta mapping ("qdm"), which remap the whole ERA5 distribution — zeros included — onto the buoy distribution month by month. Four ERA5 rain variants are compared here, all fit against all_buoy_met_data:

raw — uncorrected ERA5.
scale — the current era5_bias_correction approach (monthly multiplier).
eqm — quantile mapping (100 quantiles), which also adjusts wet-hour frequency and intensity.
eqm+scale — eqm, then a second monthly scale fit on the eqm output to put the total back on the buoy’s.

qdm was also fitted and gives numbers identical to eqm on the historical period (it only differs when extrapolating a trend), so it is not shown separately.


Code
all_buoy_met_data <- tar_read(all_buoy_met_data)

fit_rain <- \(e, m) metscale::fit_met_bias_correction(
  e, all_buoy_met_data, vars = "MET_pprain", method = m,
  nquantiles = 100, verbose = FALSE)
apply_rain <- \(e, f) metscale::apply_met_bias_correction(e, f, verbose = FALSE)

f_scale <- fit_rain(era5_hourly_met, "scale")
f_eqm   <- fit_rain(era5_hourly_met, "eqm")
e_eqm   <- apply_rain(era5_hourly_met, f_eqm)
f_es    <- fit_rain(e_eqm, "scale")

rain_variants <- list(
  raw         = era5_hourly_met,
  scale       = apply_rain(era5_hourly_met, f_scale),
  eqm         = e_eqm,
  `eqm+scale` = apply_rain(e_eqm, f_es)
)

# Cross-validated (leave-one-year-out) skill. For eqm+scale this is the
# second-stage fit only (scored against the eqm output); the first-stage
# skill is in the "eqm" row.
bind_rows(
  raw         = f_scale$skill |> filter(stage == "cv_raw"),
  scale       = f_scale$skill |> filter(stage == "cv_corrected"),

Buoy: eqm+scale matches the buoy’s annual total (1,445 vs. 1,446 mm/yr), p95 (21.8 vs. 21.2 mm/day) and maximum (267 vs. 281 mm/day); raw ERA5 has 44 % wet days against the buoy’s 27 %, and the eqm-based variants 25 %. The upper tail is slightly over-stretched (p99 71 vs. 65 mm/day).
MetService airport (independent hourly gauge) is the strongest check, because it shares no instrument with the buoy: it reads 1,470 mm/yr on matched days, between the buoy (1,446) and PC10 (1,514). On matched hours its wet-hour fraction is 12.6 %, mean wet-hour rain 1.33 mm/hr and p95 5.0 mm/hr; eqm+scale gives 15.3 %, 1.09 and 5.4 mm/hr and a total of 1,461 mm/yr — within 1 % of the MetService total, whereas raw ERA5 is 8 % high (1,589) with 42 % wet hours and weak wet-hour intensity (0.43 mm/hr). At daily resolution eqm+scale reaches the MetService p95 (21.7 vs. 22.2 mm/day) but slightly under-counts wet days (24.9 % vs. 32.3 %) and over-stretches the extreme tail (p99 73 vs. 54 mm/day; maximum 244 vs. 157 mm/day), consistent with the buoy’s heavier tail.
PC10 (Whakarewarewa gauge) reads 1,514 mm/yr, so eqm+scale (1,451) is within 4 % of it. Its p95 (22.1 mm/day) is matched by eqm+scale (21.9). PC10’s wet-day fraction (35 %) is the highest of the gauges, but a once-daily reading probably smears wet days across two calendar days and inflates the count. Its daily correlation with ERA5 is very low in every case (r < 0.1), as in the source comparison above.
NIWA airport: this check is inconclusive. Its daily rainfall averages only 0.7 mm/day (~250 mm/yr) on days it is “valid”, roughly a fifth of every other gauge, so its rain series appears incomplete (many days probably contain only some of the 3-hourly observations) and cannot be used to judge totals or wet-day frequency. The MetService record now fills that role.
Daily skill: all eqm variants have somewhat higher daily RMSE than scale against the buoy (9.5 vs. 8.7 mm/day for eqm+scale) with similar r (0.77), consistent with the hourly double penalty.
