Recommendation (now implemented in the pipeline): use MET_pprain = "eqm" followed by a monthly scale for the historical ERA5 baseline. That fixes drizzle frequency, wet-hour intensity and the bulk of the tail, keeps the total on the buoy, and is consistent with the independent MetService total to within 1 % and PC10 to within ~4 %. Because the second stage is fit on the output of the first, it needs two chained calls rather than a single method = vector:
In _targets.R this is era5_rain_eqm_correction → era5_hourly_met_rainqm (stage 1), then era5_bias_correction fitted on era5_hourly_met_rainqm (stage 2, together with the other variables), with era5_corrected_hourly and era5_corrected_daily_baseline built from era5_hourly_met_rainqm. The equivalent standalone code is:


Code
# 1. quantile-map rain onto the buoy distribution
bc_rain_eqm <- metscale::fit_met_bias_correction(
  era5_hourly_met, all_buoy_met_data, vars = "MET_pprain",
  method = "eqm", nquantiles = 100, verbose = FALSE)
era5_eqm <- metscale::apply_met_bias_correction(era5_hourly_met, bc_rain_eqm)

# 2. restore the buoy's total with a monthly ratio
bc_rain_scale <- metscale::fit_met_bias_correction(
  era5_eqm, all_buoy_met_data, vars = "MET_pprain",
  method = "scale", by = "doy-loess", verbose = FALSE)
era5_rain_corrected <- metscale::apply_met_bias_correction(era5_eqm, bc_rain_scale)








Note



expand_met() rounding (fixed). metscale::expand_met() previously rounded every column to 3 decimals. Rain is in m/hr, so that quantised it to whole millimetres: in testing it cut the corrected wet-hour fraction from 15.2 % to 4.9 % and erased all the drizzle correction (and coarsened earlier era5_corrected_hourly rain). It now rounds to 6 decimals and the pipeline calls apply_met_bias_correction(expand = TRUE) directly. era5_corrected_daily_baseline rounds daily totals to 6 decimals too, so it is unaffected.


Caveats: hourly timing is unchanged (r stays ≈ 0.5) — this corrects the distribution, not when rain falls. The quantile map caps ERA5 extremes at the buoy’s observed maximum, and the extreme daily tail ends up somewhat heavier than the MetService gauge shows.

title: Meteorological Data Sources & Forcing Comparison
section: How this improves lake model forcing
text:
How this improves lake model forcing

The buoy reference is now ~19 years, not ~4.5. Adding the old buoy lets the day-of-year corrections in era5_bias_correction and niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction train on ~130,000 hourly pairs instead of ~40,000, and the hourly comparison shows the two loggers agree on temperature, wind and pressure.
Caught a forcing bug before it reached the model. The ERA5 rain unit error above would have meant every ERA5-driven scenario — including every future GCM projection, since deltas are applied to the ERA5 baseline — ran with rainfall roughly 3 orders of magnitude too high. A single-source pipeline has no way to notice this; comparing independent sources does.
Wind is the largest bias in the forcing, and it is now correctly sized. With the doubled unit conversion removed, ERA5 reads ~2.8 m/s (~52 %) below the buoy’s 10 m wind, not ~0.2 m/s. Wind drives mixing and surface heat flux directly, so era5_bias_correction’s MET_wndspd scale correction (cross-validated RMSE 3.52 → 2.06 m/s, KGE 0.19 → 0.72) is one of the most consequential steps in the pipeline. The land stations cannot substitute: the MetService airport also reads 1.7 m/s below the buoy, so the correction really is a land/reanalysis → lake transfer and depends on the buoy’s 2 m/1.5 m → 10 m extrapolation being right.
The buoy → airport extension helps temperature and humidity, less so wind. niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction trains on the full buoy overlap (2007–present) and cuts NIWA-airport-vs-buoy RMSE from 2.02 → 1.74 °C (temperature) while humidity, which uses the 2022–23 buoy only in this fit, shows no cross-validated gain (RMSE 5.7 → 6.6 %; in-sample 5.7 → 5.5 %); wind is corrected for bias (−2.3 → −0.1 m/s) but with only modest gains in RMSE (3.18 → 2.94 m/s) and weak correlation (r ≈ 0.63). era5_bias_correction_extended cuts ERA5 temperature RMSE from 2.08 → 1.45 °C and humidity from 7.3 → 7.0 %.
A second, independent hourly station is now available. The MetService airport record (1993–Jun 2023) has a real rain gauge, shortwave and wind, and agrees with ERA5 on temperature (−0.5 °C), humidity (+0.6 %) and shortwave (−2 W/m²). It validates the rain correction independently of the buoy, exposes the buoy RH drift, and is a candidate for extending reference records back before 2007 (for variables where it agrees well with the buoy: temperature, pressure, rain).
PC10’s 1901–present rainfall record is the longest available context for Rotorua rainfall, over 40 years longer than the airports’. That’s directly useful for summarise_climate_extremes.R / climate-extreme-events.qmd’s historical-extremes framing, and as a long-run independent check on whatever ERA5 rainfall climatology ends up driving the historical baseline and scenario deltas. Its weak daily correlation with the buoy for RH and rain (r ≈ 0.32 and 0.06) means it shouldn’t be used as a fit_met_bias_correction() reference for those variables.
Wind direction and shortwave timing check out. ERA5 reproduces the prevailing WSW–W flow (hourly mean absolute direction error ~39–50°) and the shortwave daily cycle (r = 0.91 against the new buoy and 0.95 against MetService), so ERA5-derived direction and radiation are defensible for the model.

title: Meteorological Data Sources & Forcing Comparison
text:
Caveats

Buoy relative humidity is not a reliable reference, so ERA5 humidity is corrected against the MetService airport instead. The old buoy (2007–22) reads ~5–9.5 % below ERA5 and the MetService airport, and the new buoy’s offset drifts from +2–3 % in 2022–23 to +9.5 % (2024), +13 % (2025) and +48 % in 2026 (mean RH 47 %). era5_bias_correction therefore no longer corrects MET_humrel; era5_humrel_correction fits it to airport_met_aeme (1993–Jun 2023, so the fit covers 2011–Jun 2023 of ERA5), and the correction is applied before the buoy-based one. buoy_met_fit_ref keeps buoy RH only for 2022-01-01 to 2023-12-31 for the remaining buoy-referenced fits (niwa_to_buoy_bias_correction and, through it, era5_bias_correction_extended, which still corrects humidity against that lake-equivalent series). all_buoy_met_data and the comparisons above still include all buoy RH. The airport station is a land station, so any lake effect on humidity (the buoy is the only lake-surface sensor) is not captured; the airport fit assumes the same land–lake humidity relationship ERA5 already has.
Station pressure (MET_prsttn). The buoys log sensible station pressure (~98.3 kPa on both loggers; the MetService airport 98.2 kPa). ERA5 reads a near-constant 1.1 kPa lower (r = 0.997), a grid-cell elevation difference of order 100 m, not a units error; the NIWA airport reads ~3.3 kPa higher. All offsets are removed by the scale corrections (ERA5 RMSE falls to ~60 Pa), but raw ERA5 and NIWA pressures should not be used uncorrected.
era5_bias_correction_extended wind and shortwave rest on almost no data. Its cross-validation has only 28 wind and 10 shortwave paired hours (versus ~130,000 for temperature/humidity), so for MET_wndspd and MET_radswd prefer era5_bias_correction. The comment in _targets.R describing these as “uncorrected airport values” predates the old buoy being added to the reference and is worth revisiting.
Shortwave is validated on limited data. The old buoy has no shortwave, the NIWA airport has none that overlaps the buoy, and the MetService airport overlaps the new buoy only from Feb 2022 to Jun 2023 (~11,000 hours), so ERA5 shortwave rests on the new buoy (~30,000 hours) plus that MetService overlap.
Sub-daily timing. The buoy stamps are offset from ERA5/MetService hour-ending stamps by roughly 30–60 minutes (see the diurnal section). This matters for hourly radiation and temperature, not for daily results.
ERA5 rain is wet too often (41 % of hours vs 12–16 %) with weak hourly intensity; fine for totals, less so for event-scale extremes. The current scale rain correction does not address this; eqm followed by scale does (see “Fixing ERA5 rainfall”). era5_bias_correction_extended still uses plain scale for rain.
PC10 has no radiation or wind data, so pc10_climate_met is a partial forcing (temp/RH/rain only) — useful for comparison and historical context, not as a standalone forcing source.
Hour-stamp de-duplication. prep() in the hourly section drops a large number of duplicated hour stamps (first value kept); the old buoy’s 15-minute rows are reduced to the :00 record. This is harmless for the comparisons here but means sub-hourly information is not used.

title: Rotorua Lake Modelling – PC10 Support
text:
The Rotorua Lake model will be updated to GLM-AED, an open-source hydrodynamic–ecological model that enables improved simulation of vertical mixing, nutrient cycling, and management interventions under variable climate conditions.
This upgrade will allow long-term scenario testing and a more flexible, modular architecture.

title: Rotorua Lake Modelling – PC10 Support
text:
🔍 Overview
Key enhancements over previous Lake Rotorua models will include:

Dynamic sediment–water feedback to better represent internal nutrient loading and delayed responses to external inputs.

Support for climate change scenarios, enabling projections of lake responses over decadal scales.

Mechanistic simulation of alum dosing, which is currently conducted in two inflows on a near-daily basis.

Active and ongoing development of model software and related tools.

title: Rotorua Lake Modelling – PC10 Support
text:
⚗️ Alum–Phosphorus Modelling
One important improvement will be incorporating a mechanistic representation of Al–P interactions.
Current models do not explicitly simulate alum chemistry or its interaction with phosphorus.
Model description here.
We are engaging with the University of Western Australia (UWA) to explore support for code modification within the AED structure.
The proposed model will simulate:

Hydrolysis of dosed alum and speciation of aluminium (e.g. Al³⁺, Al(OH)₃)

pH and temperature dependence of phosphate binding efficiency

Sediment-mediated sorption and variable effectiveness depending on depth, organic content, and redox state

Aging or decay of reactive Al over time to simulate persistence of alum effects

Dosing through inflow boundary conditions, allowing for flexible scenario testing


If this collaboration is not confirmed, alternate pathways for implementing alum dynamics will be explored to maintain model delivery timelines.

title: Rotorua Lake Modelling – PC10 Support
text:
🗓️ Timeline and Resources

The model upgrade and calibration will begin in September 2025, using existing University of Waikato resources.

Initial climate change scenarios will be prioritised and delivered by September 2026, with alum scenario testing dependent on code development.

This lake modelling work will proceed independently of catchment model scaling, ensuring continuity regardless of SWAT-MODFLOW outcomes.

title: Visualise CMIP6
text:
After processing the CMIP6 data for the Rotorua catchment, we can visualise the results.
We present both the spatial summary and time series summary for each GCM and scenario. This allows us to inspect how the different models and scenarios represent climate variables over the catchment area.

title: Visualise CMIP6
text:
CMIP6 Variable Plots

Air Temperature (2 m above ground level)
The annual mean 2 m air temperature anomalies show robust warming across all CMIP6 models and emissions scenarios, although the magnitude and rate of warming vary among models. Historical simulations indicate a modest warming of ~0.5–1 °C relative to the mid-20th-century baseline, with relatively small inter-model spread during this period.
From ~2020 onward, the scenarios diverge and uncertainties increase. Under SSP1-2.6, most models project warming that stabilises at around 1–1.5 °C above the historical mean by mid-century, with limited additional warming thereafter. The ensemble spread remains comparatively narrow in this scenario, reflecting greater model agreement under strong mitigation.
Under SSP2-4.5, temperatures continue to increase throughout the century, reaching approximately 2.5–3 °C by 2100. Inter-model variability broadens slightly over time, but the overall warming trajectory remains consistent across the ensemble.
The higher-emission scenarios show both stronger warming and greater uncertainty. SSP3-7.0 produces accelerated warming after 2050, with end-of-century anomalies near 4 °C, although individual model projections span a wider range. SSP5-8.5 exhibits the largest spread and steepest trend, with most models exceeding 5 °C by 2100, but with notable divergence in the upper tails of the ensemble.
Despite year-to-year variability and differences among models, all scenarios show statistically robust warming relative to the historical period. The increasing separation of scenario trajectories after ~2040 highlights both the importance of emissions pathway choice and the expanding uncertainty associated with long-term climate projections.



Timeseries of air temperature for scenarios and annual and seasonal projections

title: Climate-Scenario Meteorology Workflow
text:
cmip6-processing.qmd and cmip6-visualisation.qmd extract and plot the raw, absolute CMIP6/CCAM values at the lake point (gcm_point_data_df). Raw GCM output is not suitable for directly driving a sub-daily lake model: it carries its own absolute-level biases (mean offset, distorted seasonal cycle, wrong wind climatology) that would land straight in simulated stratification, ice and evaporation, and it is daily on a coarse grid with no sub-daily information.
This page instead builds the meteorological forcing the lake model actually uses, following the metscale package’s bias-correct → delta-change → disaggregate workflow (vignette("scenario-workflow", package = "metscale"), vignette("climate-extremes") for storm/heatwave-focused alternatives):
The corrected reanalysis carries real weather — genuine day-to-day persistence, event structure and a real diurnal cycle, all on actual calendar dates. Warping it with a model’s own future-vs-historical change (which is far more reliable than the model’s absolute output) keeps that physical realism while shifting its statistics onto each scenario. See the vignette for the full reasoning and the calendar-handling details (NorESM2-MM runs a 365_day calendar, NZESM a 360_day calendar – metscale::climate_point_monthly_climatology() decodes each correctly before averaging).
These steps are wired into _targets.R as era5_hourly_met → era5_bias_correction → era5_corrected_hourly / era5_corrected_daily_baseline → gcm_monthly_deltas_df → scenario_daily_met → scenario_hourly_met, added alongside (not replacing) the existing raw gcm_point_data* targets.

Air temperature, wind speed, shortwave radiation and relative humidity all improve out-of-sample after the monthly scale correction (day-of-year loess-smoothed offset). Station pressure (MET_prsttn) is a known data issue, not yet resolved: the raw bias between ERA5 (Pa) and the buoy’s PrBaro field is ~96 kPa, an order of magnitude larger than the ~3 kPa elevation-offset effect the metscale vignette describes for its own site – this looks like a unit mismatch in buoy_to_aeme_met() (PrBaro likely arrives in hPa, not Pa) rather than a real atmospheric difference, and should be checked before MET_prsttn from this workflow is trusted.
Update: rainfall (MET_pprain) is now included in this correction, having previously been left uncorrected on the assumption that the buoy gauge was an unreliable target. A multi-source comparison (buoy vs. airport vs. ERA5 vs. BOPRC/PC10 stations – see met-source-comparison.qmd) found no evidence the buoy under-reads rain relative to the land stations, but did surface a real unit bug: the raw ERA5-Land CSV stores MET_pprain in mm/hour, not the m/hour every other source in this pipeline uses, which was silently inflating ERA5 rainfall ~1000x wherever it passed uncorrected. That’s fixed at the source in read_era5_hourly_met(). The buoy’s rain record is still noisier than its other variables (weak correlation with the long land records), so treat the corrected MET_pprain here with more caution than temperature/humidity/wind – see the comparison page for the numbers.
Further update – found and fixed: comparing the raw buoy PpRain record against its own known climatology surfaced a systematic ~10x inflation from the start of the record (Feb 2022) through October 2023 – mean daily rain of ~47 mm/day (annualising to ~17,000 mm/yr, physically impossible for Rotorua) versus ~4 mm/day (~1,500 mm/yr, matching raw ERA5 and the 125-year Whakarewarewa gauge closely) from late October 2023 onward. The root cause is a recording-unit change at the buoy on 2023-10-23, not an instrument calibration drift: before that date PpRain was logged in mm/10min (not mm) and WndSpd in knots (not m/s). Both are now converted in rotorua_buoy_met_data (_targets.R) – PpRain / 10 and WndSpd * 0.514444 – for the pre-2023-10-23 rows before being combined with the already-correct-unit rows after it, so era5_bias_correction now fits against a consistently-unit’d buoy record across its full span. The plots below reflect whatever era5_bias_correction/era5_corrected_hourly build was current when last rendered – re-render this page after a fresh tar_make() to confirm the corrected distribution’s tail now tracks the buoy/long-record rainfall instead of overshooting it.

Bias-correction diagnostics: wind speed and rainfall
The skill table above summarises cross-validated numeric performance; the figures below show what the correction is actually doing to the daily time series and distribution, for the two variables most consequential downstream (wind drives the storm indices in climate-extreme-events.qmd, rainfall drives the heavy-rain indices there).


















Wind speed is expected to be the cleaner case: the corrected series should track the buoy’s day-to-day variability more closely than raw ERA5 does, and the corrected distribution should sit closer to the buoy’s than the raw distribution – check the two plots above confirm that once rendered from a build that includes the rotorua_buoy_met_data knots-to-m/s fix above.


















Rainfall is the variable to check most carefully here, given the buoy unit issue above: if these plots were last rendered from a build of era5_bias_correction/era5_corrected_hourly that predates the rotorua_buoy_met_data unit fix, expect the corrected distribution’s upper tail to sit well beyond both the raw ERA5 and the buoy’s own post-fix distribution, and the time series to show the correction pulling rainfall up hardest during the pre-October-2023 window. A rebuild after the fix should bring the corrected distribution back in line with raw ERA5 and the long-record rainfall data – re-render this page after tar_make() and check these two plots specifically before trusting MET_pprain downstream.

title: Climate-Scenario Meteorology Workflow
section: 3. CMIP6 monthly delta-change factors, and inter-GCM variability
text:
3. CMIP6 monthly delta-change factors, and inter-GCM variability
For each of the 7 downscaled GCMs (ACCESS-CM2, AWI-CM-1-1-MR, CNRM-CM6-1, EC-Earth3, GFDL-ESM4, NZESM, NorESM2-MM) and each SSP (ssp126/ssp245/ssp370/ssp585, NZESM has no ssp585 run), compute_gcm_monthly_deltas() reads that GCM’s own already-cropped netCDFs directly at the lake point and computes a monthly change factor – additive for temperature and shortwave, multiplicative (ratio) for the bounded/skewed fields (rainfall, wind, humidity) – for three future windows against a 1995-2014 historical reference.
The dominant source of uncertainty in this workflow, once the downscaling chain and delta-change method are fixed, is which GCM drives the projection. The figure below makes that spread explicit for the end-of-century window:



Inter-GCM spread in monthly delta-change factors, 2071-2100. Thin lines are individual GCMs, the shaded band spans the GCM min-max range, and the thick line is the GCM mean, for each SSP.


The spread is not uniform across variables. Annual-mean warming under ssp585 ranges from +2.8 °C (NorESM2-MM) to +4.6 °C (ACCESS-CM2) by 2071-2100 – a ~1.8 °C spread from GCM choice alone, on top of the ~3.5 °C spread already visible between the lowest (ssp126) and highest (ssp585) emissions pathway. Shortwave and rainfall change factors span, and in some months straddle, both sides of no-change (ratio = 1 / delta = 0) across the GCM ensemble, meaning some models project a drier or cloudier Rotorua in a given month under the same scenario that others project the opposite sign for. Wind and humidity changes are comparatively modest and more consistent in sign across GCMs. The mid-century window shows the same pattern at reduced magnitude:



Inter-GCM spread in monthly delta-change factors, 2041-2070.


Collapsing each GCM’s 12 monthly values into a single box per model makes the same GCM-consensus-vs-disagreement question easier to read at a glance, independent of the seasonal cycle:



GCM consensus in delta-change factors, 2071-2100. Each box summarises one GCM’s 12 monthly values; overlapping boxes indicate GCM consensus, separated boxes indicate disagreement between models.





GCM consensus in delta-change factors, 2041-2070.

title: Climate-Scenario Meteorology Workflow
text:
4. Delta-changed baseline and hourly disaggregation
scenario_daily_met applies each GCM/scenario/window’s monthly deltas to the corrected daily baseline (apply_gcm_delta_to_baseline()), and scenario_hourly_met disaggregates the result to hourly with metscale::disaggregate_met_to_hourly(), borrowing the within-day shape of era5_corrected_hourly (method of fragments) and reconstructing shortwave from clear-sky solar geometry – identical to steps 3-4 of vignette("scenario-workflow"), just run once per combination of scenario_delta_grid (7 GCM × 4 SSP × 3 windows, minus NZESM/ssp585 = 83 combinations).
That is enough runs (each disaggregating 20-30 years to hourly) that, like gcm_ts_summary and tutira_cmip6_files elsewhere in this pipeline, both targets are gated with cue = tar_cue(mode = "never") so a routine tar_make() does not trigger them. Build them explicitly with:
targets::tar_make(names = c("scenario_daily_met", "scenario_hourly_met"))
or invalidate just the combinations that changed with tar_invalidate() / tar_cue(mode = "always") per branch.

title: Climate-Scenario Meteorology Workflow
section: How this feeds into the lake model
text:
How this feeds into the lake model
scenario_hourly_met is the AEME MET_*-formatted hourly forcing GLM-AED needs for a climate-scenario simulation, one branch per GCM/scenario/window combination. The intended path from here into a model run is:

AEME::add_met(aeme, met = scenario_hourly_met[[i]]) for the branch of interest, in place of the placeholder gcm_point_data_std_df-based forcing in the commented-out aeme_sims target.
AEME::set_time() with the corresponding sim_periods$ssp window (10-year spin-up, matching the existing convention for historical runs).
AEME::build_aeme() / AEME::run_aeme() as for the calibration runs in aeme_glm4.

Because scenario_delta_grid already carries gcm, scenario and window as columns, the same pattern = map(scenario_delta_grid) branching used to build scenario_hourly_met extends directly to a per-combination AEME::run_aeme() target once the model-build step above is wired in – each of the 83 branches becomes one lake simulation, and the GCM-variability figure above is then the basis for interpreting how much of the simulated spread across those 83 runs is driven by meteorological forcing choice (GCM), scenario, or window, versus lake-model internal dynamics.

title: Climate-Scenario Meteorology Workflow
text:
Caveats
Both the bias-correction and the delta-change step assume stationarity – a transfer function fitted on the ERA5/buoy overlap period is asserted to hold under a future climate, and the scale method used here rescales the observed daily sequence rather than reshaping its day-to-day variability (see ?metscale::scenario_workflow). The buoy overlap (2022-2026) is short relative to the vignette’s recommendation of a long reanalysis record and 20-year climate windows; the ERA5-only record (2011-2026) is longer and used for the daily baseline and hourly donor, but the fit of the bias correction itself is necessarily anchored to the shorter buoy overlap. Treat the across-scenario spread as a lower bound on total uncertainty, and fix the MET_prsttn unit issue noted in step 1 before using corrected station pressure downstream.

title: Climate-Scenario Extreme & Storm-Event Analysis
text:
climate-scenario-workflow.qmd builds scenario_hourly_met – the AEME MET_*-formatted hourly forcing for every GCM x SSP x future-window combination (7 GCMs x 4 SSPs x 3 windows, minus NZESM/ssp585 = 81 branches), by applying each GCM/scenario’s monthly delta-change signal to the bias-corrected daily ERA5 baseline and disaggregating back to hourly against the bias-corrected hourly ERA5 record.
This page uses that same hourly forcing to ask a narrower question: how does the frequency and intensity of extreme/storm-scale events change, not just the monthly-mean climate? Sub-daily (hourly) data matters here because heavy-rain intensity, wind-storm duration and short heatwaves are sub-daily-to-daily phenomena that a monthly delta-change factor alone cannot resolve – they only show up once the delta has been re-expanded to hourly.
This is a rebuild of an earlier version of this page, incorporating two changes made since:

title: Climate-Scenario Extreme & Storm-Event Analysis
text:
Method
For every branch of scenario_hourly_met, and separately for the bias-corrected historical baseline (era5_corrected_hourly, 1995-2014), compute_annual_extreme_indices() (R/summarise_climate_extremes.R) computes one row per calendar year for:







Index
Definition




rx1day
Annual maximum daily rainfall (mm)


heavy_rain_days
Days/year with daily rainfall above the p95 (wet days only)


extreme_rain_days
Days/year above the p99


hot_days
Days/year with daily maximum air temperature above the historical p95


wsdi
Warm-spell duration index: days/year in spells of >=3 consecutive hot days


max_wind
Annual maximum hourly wind speed (m/s)


storm_wind_hours
Hours/year with hourly wind speed above the historical p95


severe_wind_hours
Hours/year above the historical p99


storm_events
Number of separate contiguous spells/year above the wind p95 threshold



Thresholds (compute_extreme_thresholds()) are fixed once and applied unchanged to every future branch, so “heavy rain” and “storm wind” mean the same absolute thing in every period – a change in frequency is then a genuine intensification/frequency signal, not an artefact of a moving definition. Wind and temperature thresholds still come from the bias-corrected ERA5 hourly baseline (1995-2014) – there’s no long-record alternative for those at this site. Rainfall thresholds now come from the 125-year Whakarewarewa daily rain-gauge record (compute_long_rain_thresholds(), on pc10_climate_met) rather than the 20-year ERA5 window: 20 years is thin for estimating a p95/p99 event, and the long, independently-measured record is unaffected by anything in the reanalysis/bias-correction/delta-change chain the scenarios themselves are built from.

title: Climate-Scenario Extreme & Storm-Event Analysis
text:
Discussion
Rainfall. heavy_rain_days and extreme_rain_days increase modestly and roughly monotonically with emissions scenario and window, consistent with a warmer atmosphere holding more moisture – but the ensemble range across GCMs is wide relative to the mean shift, and for rx1day several GCMs project little change or a slight decrease at some windows (the ratio-based delta-change method rescales the historical daily rainfall sequence rather than restructuring its day-to-day intermittency, so it cannot invent a heavier single-day extreme than proportional scaling of the historical record allows – see the stationarity caveat in climate-scenario-workflow.qmd). Anchoring the rainfall thresholds to the 125-year Whakarewarewa record instead of the 20-year ERA5 window matters here specifically because a 20-year sample gives a noisy p95/p99 estimate – with a long, independent record the “heavy”/“extreme” definitions themselves are far more stable, so a projected change in frequency is more trustworthy as an actual signal rather than partly an artefact of which 20 years happened to set the threshold.
Heat. hot_days and wsdi (warm-spell duration) show the clearest, most consistent scenario/window gradient of the three groups – both increase substantially and near-monotonically from ssp126 to ssp585 and from the near-term to the end-of-century window, with comparatively narrow GCM spread. This is the expected signature of a monotonic mean-warming delta applied to a fixed threshold: as the whole distribution shifts up, an increasing share of days cross a fixed, historical p95 threshold.
Wind storms. With the vector-disaggregation fix, wind speed is now shaped directly from the donor’s own hourly wind-speed pattern rather than being recomputed from reshaped u/v components, removing the disaggregation-side inflation flagged in the previous version of this page (disaggregated hourly wind no longer runs systematically higher than its own delta-adjusted daily target). The wind-storm indices above should now be read as a direct read on the GCM ensemble’s wind delta-change signal, which – per gcm_monthly_deltas_df – is close to 1 (little change) for most GCM/scenario combinations, with a modest number of outlier models/months driving any larger shifts. Wind remains the index group with the least physical basis for a strong climate-change signal at monthly delta-change resolution, since storm-scale wind events are a synoptic-scale phenomenon that a monthly mean factor is a weak proxy for.
Practical implication for lake modelling. Heavy-rain and warm-spell frequency both increase with scenario severity in a way that is directionally robust across the GCM ensemble, and both are levers on lake response that matter beyond the monthly-mean forcing already explored in climate-scenario-workflow.qmd: more frequent heavy-rain days translate to more frequent high-inflow/nutrient-loading pulses, and longer warm spells extend the window over which thermal stratification can strengthen and hypolimnetic anoxia can develop. The return-level table above gives a fixed, long-record reference point (e.g. a 1-in-50-year daily rainfall total) against which to judge whether a given scenario/window’s mean rx1day represents a meaningfully more frequent extreme, rather than reasoning from the 20-30 year scenario windows alone.

title: Climate-Scenario Extreme & Storm-Event Analysis
text:
Caveats
In addition to the caveats already noted in climate-scenario-workflow.qmd (stationarity of the bias-correction and delta-change transfer functions, the short buoy overlap period, and the known MET_prsttn unit issue) and met-source-comparison.qmd (PC10’s weak day-to-day correlation with the buoy for rainfall, r ~ 0.12 – a long-run climatology/threshold use like this is far less sensitive to that than a day-by-day bias-correction reference would be):

The Whakarewarewa gauge is a land station, not over the lake; its absolute rainfall total may differ from true over-lake rainfall even though its long-run climatology is the best available basis for a stable extreme-event threshold at this site.
The Gumbel method-of-moments fit is a simple, standard estimator but not the only reasonable choice (e.g. GEV with a shape parameter, or L-moments); treat the return-level table as indicative rather than a design-standard flood estimate.
Wind and temperature thresholds still come from only 20 years of ERA5 (1995-2014) – no equivalently long, independent wind/temperature record exists at this site the way it does for rainfall.
Extreme indices here are derived from the delta-changed reanalysis sequence, not from the GCM’s own extremes – by construction they inherit the historical record’s actual extreme events (dates, storm tracks, event structure), rescaled by a smooth monthly climate signal, so they cannot represent a genuinely new type of extreme event outside the historical envelope.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
NoteSummary



This document summarises a simple process representation of alum–phosphorus interactions for integration into GLM-AED. The formulation is intended to capture the main management-relevant processes in Lake Rotorua:

alum delivery from treated inflows,
SRP uptake in the water column,
settling of remaining reactive material,
continued uptake at the sediment–water interface,
a gradual loss of reactivity through ageing, and
a bell-shaped pH response included as a pragmatic modifier of binding efficiency.





The schematic below shows how the simplified module fits together. Treated inflows add effective reactive capacity to the pelagic pool, which removes SRP while suspended. Remaining capacity then settles to the bed, where it continues to suppress SRP in the bottom layer. Ageing reduces reactivity in both compartments.







Conceptual process diagram of the simplified alum–phosphorus module.







Reactive suspended alum capacity in the water column, \(C_w\) (mg P m−3), removes dissolved reactive phosphorus, SRP (mg P m−3). The uptake rate is controlled by a pelagic kinetic coefficient, \(k_w\) (d−1), the pH modifier, \(f_\text{pH}\) (−), and a saturating uptake term governed by \(K_P\) (mg P m−3). The saturating form ensures uptake increases with SRP but levels off as SRP becomes small relative to \(K_P\).

\[
\frac{dSRP}{dt} = -k_w f_{pH} C_w \frac{K_P \, SRP}{K_P + SRP}
\tag{1}\]




The pelagic reactive-capacity pool, \(C_w\) (mg P m−3), increases with alum input from the treated inflows, represented by \(J_\text{cap}\) (mg P d−1), and decreases through three pathways: SRP uptake, settling to the bed, and ageing. The volume term, \(V\) (m3), converts inflow capacity into a concentration-based state variable. \(J_\text{set}\) (mg P m−3 d−1) is the settling loss from the water column, while \(k_{\text{age},w}\) (d−1) controls the exponential decline in pelagic reactivity.
\[
\frac{dC_w}{dt} = \frac{J_\mathrm{cap}}{V} - k_w f_\mathrm{pH} C_w \frac{K_P\,\mathrm{SRP}}{K_P + \mathrm{SRP}} - J_\mathrm{set} - k_{\mathrm{age},w}\,C_w
\tag{2}\]



Once alum settles, the remaining reactive capacity at the bed, \(C_s\) (mg P m−2), continues to remove SRP from the bottom computational layer, \(\text{SRP}_b\) (mg P m−3). The benthic uptake rate is controlled by \(k_s\) (d−1), the same pH modifier, and the same saturating uptake term. The factor \(1/h_b\) converts an areal benthic sink into a concentration change in the bottom water layer of thickness \(h_b\) (m).
\[
\frac{d\mathrm{SRP}_b}{dt} = -\frac{1}{h_b}\,k_s f_\mathrm{pH} C_s \frac{K_P\,\mathrm{SRP}_b}{K_P + \mathrm{SRP}_b}
\tag{3}\]



The benthic reactive-capacity pool, \(C_s\) (mg P m−2), increases through settling input from the pelagic compartment, \(J_\text{set}^\text{area}\) (mg P m−2 d−1), and decreases through bottom-water uptake, ageing, and burial or permanent isolation from exchange. The terms \(k_{\text{age},s}\) (d−1) and \(k_\text{bur}\) (d−1) therefore represent two separate loss pathways: gradual deactivation of reactivity and physical removal from the active sediment–water interface, respectively.
\[
\frac{dC_s}{dt} = J_\mathrm{set}^\mathrm{area} - k_s f_\mathrm{pH} C_s \frac{K_P\,\mathrm{SRP}_b}{K_P + \mathrm{SRP}_b} - k_{\mathrm{age},s}\,C_s - k_\mathrm{bur}\,C_s
\tag{4}\]



The pH modifier, \(f_\text{pH}\) (−), is represented as a bell-shaped response centred on the optimal pH, \(\text{pH}_\text{opt}\) (−). The parameter \(\sigma_\text{pH}\) (−) controls the width of the response. This is not a full chemical equilibrium model; it is a practical way of reducing effective uptake when pH moves away from the range where alum is expected to bind phosphorus most efficiently.
\[
f_\mathrm{pH} = \exp\!\left[-\frac{(\mathrm{pH} - \mathrm{pH_{opt}})^2}{2\,\sigma_\mathrm{pH}^2}\right]
\tag{5}\]




Ageing is represented as a first-order exponential loss of reactivity. Here, \(A(t)\) denotes the remaining reactive fraction at time \(t\) and \(A_0\) is the initial reactive fraction. For the current implementation, the ageing parameter is chosen so that 95% of reactive uptake capacity is lost after 30 days. This gives \(k_\text{age} \approx 0.10\) d−1. In practice, this same logic is applied to the pelagic and benthic ageing terms, \(k_{\text{age},w}\) and \(k_{\text{age},s}\).
\[
A(t) = A_0\,e^{-k_\mathrm{age}\,t} \qquad k_\mathrm{age} = -\frac{\ln(0.05)}{30} \approx 0.10 \ \mathrm{d}^{-1}
\tag{6}\]




The table below lists the state variables, fluxes, and parameters used in the simplified model. All symbols referenced in the equations are included here so the document can be read either as a stand-alone concept note or as a guide for module implementation.

A practical first implementation in GLM-AED could introduce two new state variables: a pelagic reactive-capacity pool (\(C_w\)) and a benthic reactive-capacity pool (\(C_s\)). The main calibration priorities are likely to be the dose-to-capacity conversion (\(J_\text{cap}\)), the pelagic and benthic kinetic coefficients (\(k_w\) and \(k_s\)), the settling transfer, and the pH response parameters. For ageing, the intended behaviour is simple exponential loss of reactivity rather than a more complex multi-pool formulation.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
section: 2.1 Kinetic formulation, AED units and notation
text:
2.1 Kinetic formulation, AED units and notation
This document presents a simplified process representation of alum–phosphorus interactions for integration into GLM-AED as the module aed_alum. SRP uptake is represented as a kinetic rate process. Units, variable notation, and parameter conventions follow aed_phosphorus and the AED framework. A sediment resuspension term is included but disabled by default via a logical switch.
The module is intended to capture the main management-relevant processes for Lake Rotorua:

alum capacity delivery from treated inflows,
kinetic uptake of dissolved reactive phosphorus in the water column,
settling of remaining reactive material to the bed,
continued kinetic uptake at the sediment–water interface,
a gradual loss of reactivity through ageing,
optional resuspension of settled alum, and
a bell-shaped pH response as a pragmatic modifier of binding efficiency.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
2.2 Structural decisions and open questions
The formulation below resolves several structural issues identified while reviewing the original concept note against the AED framework and the aed_phosphorus, aed_silica, and aed_tracer modules. The items still requiring confirmation are listed first.

2.2.1 Open — still requiring a decision

Numerical behaviour of kinetic uptake. SRP uptake is represented as a kinetic rate (Equation 1). Alum P-binding is physically fast, so a realistic k_w may be large enough to introduce stiffness and overshoot in an explicit ODE step. This needs to be checked in testing; if it proves unstable, the alternative is an equilibrium partition computed in an equilibrate routine, as aed_phosphorus does for adsorption.
Does ageing release or trap bound phosphorus? Ageing reduces binding capacity, but whether it also releases already-bound P depends on the physical interpretation — occlusion (P trapped) versus floc dissolution (P returned to frp). The “trapped” interpretation is adopted here (no ageing term on the bound pools), but should be confirmed against data from Lake Rotorua.
Alum delivery mechanism. Delivering alum capacity by dividing an inflow load by a fixed receiving-layer volume is fragile, because GLM places inflows by density and the receiving layer changes over time. The recommended approach is to deliver alum as an inflow water-quality concentration and let GLM distribute it, retaining the explicit S_ala term only for direct dosing. This needs to be confirmed against how GLM-AED handles inflow WQ variables.



2.2.2 Resolved in this formulation

Phosphorus mass closure. Phosphorus removed from frp is tracked in explicit bound-P pools (alp, ben_alp) rather than disappearing from the budget.
Settling as one coupled flux. Settling is handled by the mobility routine and AED transport, not as separate hand-coded volumetric and areal terms.
Benthic pools as sheet variables. ben_ala and ben_alp are registered with aed_define_sheet_variable. This deliberately extends beyond the aed_phosphorus template, which carries no benthic adsorbed-P state variable.
pH dependency. pH is sourced from aed_carbon (CAR_pH), with a configurable variable name and an f_pH = 1 fallback when unavailable.
Units and rate conventions. Phosphorus is in mmol P m⁻³ / m⁻², matching frp; namelist rates are per-day and converted to per-second on read.
Bottom-water SRP. Bottom-water SRP is frp evaluated in the bottom layer, not a separate state variable.
Resuspension. An optional, switch-gated resuspension term is included (Equation 7), disabled by default.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
2.3 Notation and unit conventions

Phosphorus concentrations are in mmol P m⁻³ (pelagic) or mmol P m⁻² (benthic), consistent with aed_phosphorus. Where alum delivery is quoted as a mass dose, convert using a molar mass of P of 30.97 g mol⁻¹.
All rate parameters are supplied in the namelist per day and converted to per second on read in aed_define_alum (division by secs_per_day), following the AED convention.
Settling velocity w_ala is supplied in m day⁻¹ and converted to m s⁻¹ on read.
Fluxes applied to frp are in mmol P m⁻³ s⁻¹ (pelagic) or mmol P m⁻² s⁻¹ (benthic).
The equations below are written with rates in per-day units for readability; the implementation uses the per-second equivalents.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
2.5 Core equations

2.5.1 Equation 1. Water-column SRP uptake
Reactive suspended alum capacity ala removes dissolved reactive phosphorus frp. The uptake rate U_w is controlled by the pelagic kinetic coefficient k_w, the pH modifier f_pH, and a Michaelis–Menten saturation term governed by the half-saturation constant K_P.
\[
\frac{d\,\mathrm{frp}}{dt} = -\,U_w
\]
\[
U_w = k_w\, f_\mathrm{pH}\, \mathrm{ala}\;\frac{\mathrm{frp}}{K_P + \mathrm{frp}}
\]
U_w has units of (d⁻¹)(−)(mmol P m⁻³)(−) = mmol P m⁻³ d⁻¹. The saturation term is linear at low frp and saturates at 1 at high frp. Uptake is linear in ala, so there is no saturation in available binding capacity.


2.5.2 Equation 2. Suspended alum capacity
ala is replenished by alum input S_ala, consumed one-to-one as it binds phosphorus, and lost through ageing. Settling is handled by transport via the mobility routine and does not appear as an explicit term.
\[
\frac{d\,\mathrm{ala}}{dt} = S_\mathrm{ala} - U_w - k_{age,w}\,\mathrm{ala}
\]
S_ala (mmol P m⁻³ d⁻¹) is the alum capacity input. It is best delivered as an inflow water-quality concentration so GLM distributes it by density; an explicit S_ala term is only needed for direct (non-inflow) dosing into a named layer.


2.5.3 Equation 3. Suspended alum-bound phosphorus
Phosphorus removed from frp enters the bound pool alp, preserving the phosphorus mass balance. alp settles with the same velocity w_ala as ala.
\[
\frac{d\,\mathrm{alp}}{dt} = U_w
\]
No ageing term is applied to alp: under the “trapped phosphorus” interpretation, ageing occludes binding sites but does not release already-bound phosphorus. If ageing were instead taken to represent floc dissolution, a term returning phosphorus to frp would be required. The trapped interpretation is the more conservative management assumption and is adopted here.


2.5.4 Equation 4. Bottom-water SRP uptake
Settled alum capacity ben_ala continues to remove frp from the bottom computational layer. The benthic uptake rate U_s is areal because ben_ala is areal; the factor 1/h_b converts it to a concentration change in the bottom layer of thickness h_b.
\[
\frac{d\,\mathrm{frp}_b}{dt} = -\frac{U_s}{h_b}
\]
\[
U_s = k_s\, f_\mathrm{pH}\, \mathrm{ben\_ala}\;\frac{\mathrm{frp}_b}{K_P + \mathrm{frp}_b}
\]
U_s has units of mmol P m⁻² d⁻¹; 1/h_b (m⁻¹) converts it to mmol P m⁻³ d⁻¹. frp_b is frp in the bottom layer, not a separate state variable.


2.5.5 Equation 5. Settled alum capacity
ben_ala gains the settling flux F_ala of ala arriving at the bed, and loses capacity through bottom-water uptake, ageing, burial, and optional resuspension.
\[
\frac{d\,\mathrm{ben\_ala}}{dt} = F_\mathrm{ala} - U_s - k_{age,s}\,\mathrm{ben\_ala} - k_\mathrm{bur}\,\mathrm{ben\_ala} - R_\mathrm{ala}
\]
F_ala (mmol P m⁻² d⁻¹) is supplied by AED’s vertical transport, not hand-coded. R_ala is the resuspension loss defined in Equation 7.


2.5.6 Equation 6. Settled alum-bound phosphorus
ben_alp gains the settling flux F_alp of alp, gains phosphorus bound at the bed (U_s), and loses mass through burial and optional resuspension.
\[
\frac{d\,\mathrm{ben\_alp}}{dt} = F_\mathrm{alp} + U_s - k_\mathrm{bur}\,\mathrm{ben\_alp} - R_\mathrm{alp}
\]
No ageing term is applied to ben_alp, consistent with the trapped-phosphorus interpretation in Equation 3.


2.5.7 Equation 7. Resuspension of settled alum (optional)
When simResuspension is enabled, a fraction of settled alum is returned to the water column. The resuspension fluxes R_ala and R_alp (mmol P m⁻² d⁻¹) are controlled by a resuspension coefficient k_res:
\[
R_\mathrm{ala} = \delta_\mathrm{res}\;k_\mathrm{res}\,\mathrm{ben\_ala},
\qquad
R_\mathrm{alp} = \delta_\mathrm{res}\;k_\mathrm{res}\,\mathrm{ben\_alp}
\]
where δ_res is 1 when simResuspension = .true. and 0 otherwise. The resuspended capacity and bound phosphorus are added back to the pelagic pools ala and alp in the bottom layer (divided by h_b to convert the areal flux to a concentration change). By default simResuspension = .false., so R_ala = R_alp = 0 and Equations 5 and 6 reduce to their non-resuspension form.
A more physically based option is to scale k_res by bottom shear stress relative to a critical threshold (as in aed_tracer), or to link to an external sediment-resuspension diagnostic (as the resus_link mechanism does in aed_phosphorus). The constant-coefficient form above is the minimal default; either extension can replace k_res later without changing the equation structure.


2.5.8 Equation 8. Bell-shaped pH modifier
The pH modifier f_pH is a bell-shaped response centred on the optimal pH, pH_opt, with width controlled by sigma_pH. It is a pragmatic efficiency modifier, not a chemical equilibrium model.
\[
f_\mathrm{pH} = \exp\!\left[-\frac{(\mathrm{pH} - \mathrm{pH_{opt}})^2}{2\,\sigma_\mathrm{pH}^2}\right]
\]
pH is obtained from the AED carbon-chemistry module, by default the variable CAR_pH, located with aed_locate_variable. The variable name is configurable via the namelist (pH_variable).


2.5.9 Equation 9. Ageing coefficient
Ageing is a first-order exponential loss of reactive capacity. Choosing the coefficient so that 95% of capacity is lost after 30 days gives:
\[
A(t) = A_0\, e^{-k_\mathrm{age}\, t},
\qquad
k_\mathrm{age} = -\frac{\ln(0.05)}{30} \approx 0.0998 \ \mathrm{d}^{-1}
\]
The same logic applies to the pelagic and benthic ageing coefficients k_age_w and k_age_s. The value 0.0998 d⁻¹ is the namelist value; internally it is converted to ≈ 1.16 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
2.6 Phosphorus mass balance
With the trapped-phosphorus interpretation, total phosphorus is conserved. Every term leaving frp enters a bound pool (alp or ben_alp); settling transfers ala and alp to ben_ala and ben_alp; resuspension transfers them back; and only burial (k_bur) permanently removes phosphorus from the modelled system. Retaining an ageing term on a bound pool without a compensating release term would introduce a silent phosphorus sink and should be avoided.

title: Proposed Alum Model for AED
text:
2.9 Calibration priorities
The main calibration targets are likely to be the dose-to-capacity conversion feeding S_ala (or the inflow alum concentration), the pelagic and benthic kinetic coefficients k_w and k_s, the settling velocity w_ala, and — if the pH modifier is enabled — pH_opt and sigma_pH. Ageing is intended as a simple first-order loss rather than a multi-pool formulation, and k_age_w and k_age_s can reasonably be fixed at the 30-day value unless data suggest otherwise. Resuspension is off by default; if enabled, k_res becomes an additional calibration parameter.

title: GLM-AED Sensitivity Analysis and Calibration Plan
text:
3 How SA and calibration relate

Screening SA (e.g. Morris / elementary effects). Run over the full parameter union below with wide ranges. Fix stoichiometry and most Arrhenius (theta_*) terms. Goal: discard parameters with negligible influence on the four targets.
Variance-based SA (e.g. Sobol) — optional. Run on the ~10–15 survivors with ranges tightened to roughly ±25–50 % of the expected value. Goal: rank interactions and first-order effects per target metric.
Calibration. Tune only the high-ranking, poorly-constrained, identifiable subset (Section 5). Typically 12–18 parameters.

Order matters. Get temperature/stratification and DO right first: the redox switches controlling NH4 and FRP sediment release (ksed_amm, ksed_frp) are gated on the simulated O2 field, so calibrating them before DO is closed will bias them.

Confirm switches (Section 6) match the intended process representation.

title: Simplified Alum–Phosphorus Module for GLM-AED
text:
To maintain mechanistic defensibility while keeping the implementation simple, we propose a minimal two-state kinetic model representing alum–phosphorus (Al–P) interactions in the water column.
The model captures:

pH-dependent aluminium hydrolysis and reactivity

Phosphate sorption onto amorphous Al(OH)₃ flocs

Temperature effects on reaction kinetics

Rapid settling of aluminium flocs (~10 m d⁻¹)

Optional slow aging (loss of reactivity)

This structure is designed for scenario testing of alum dosing strategies.

title: Simplified Alum–Phosphorus Module for GLM-AED
text:
Water Column

\(Al_r\) — Reactive aluminium floc (g Al m\(^{-3}\))

\(P_{Al}\) — Phosphorus bound to aluminium floc (g P m\(^{-3}\))

Coupled to existing AED variable:

\(PO_4\) — Dissolved reactive phosphorus (FRP)

title: Simplified Alum–Phosphorus Module for GLM-AED
text:
1. Reactive Aluminium
Alum added via inflows is assumed to rapidly hydrolyse to reactive floc.
\[
\frac{d Al_r}{dt} =
L_{Al,in}
- k_{age} Al_r
- R_{bind}
- settling
\]
Where:

\(L_{Al,in}\) = alum loading from inflow forcing

\(k_{age}\) = first-order aging constant (loss of reactivity)

\(R_{bind}\) = phosphate binding rate

title: Simplified Alum–Phosphorus Module for GLM-AED
text:
2. Phosphate (FRP)
\[
\frac{d PO_4}{dt} = - R_{bind}
\]

title: Simplified Alum–Phosphorus Module for GLM-AED
text:
3. Aluminium-Bound Phosphorus
\[
\frac{d P_{Al}}{dt} =
+ R_{bind}
- settling
\]

title: Alum Dosing in Lake Rotorua
text:
Source: Sanila, S. (2026). Evaluation of Aluminium–Phosphorus Binding and pH Responses to Alum Dosing of Three New Zealand Lakes. MSc thesis, University of Waikato.



This thesis evaluates the effectiveness of alum (aluminium sulphate, Al₂(SO₄)₃) as a tool for reducing dissolved reactive phosphorus (DRP) across five New Zealand waters: Lake Rotorua, the Utuhina and Puarenga Streams, Lake Ōkaro, and Lake Moawhitu. The study was motivated by a recognised gap in site-specific, controlled evidence for Al:P binding behaviour across the Rotorua catchment lakes, despite many years of operational dosing.
The methodology centred on standardised 3-hour jar tests, with acid titrations used to quantify buffering capacity at each site. For Lake Rotorua specifically, video-based settling measurements and stereomicroscopy were used to characterise the physical properties of alum floc — providing the most detailed floc data available for this lake.
Across all sites, alum reduced DRP, but the magnitude of removal and pH response varied considerably. Al:P molar ratios ranged from 0.7:1 to 15.1:1 depending on site chemistry, and pH behaviour was governed primarily by alkalinity rather than dose rate. Lake Rotorua and the Puarenga Stream had the lowest alkalinity (~19 mg CaCO₃ L⁻¹) and showed the weakest pH recovery after dosing. Lake Moawhitu, with the highest alkalinity (~67 mg CaCO₃ L⁻¹), recovered most strongly.




The following sections draw directly on thesis findings to inform parameterisation of the &aed_alum module for Lake Rotorua. Parameters are addressed in thematic groups.



The jar-test Al:P molar ratio for Lake Rotorua was 0.7:1 (mass ratio 0.6:1), based on a dose of 1.0 mg Al L⁻¹ and a measured DRP removal of 1.60 ± 0.008 mg L⁻¹ from a pre-treatment spiked concentration of 1.62 mg L⁻¹. This near 1:1 molar performance is consistent with the lake’s characteristically low dissolved organic carbon (~2 mg L⁻¹), which reduces competition for Al(OH)₃ surface sites and allows a high proportion of added aluminium to remain available for phosphate binding.
It is important to note that this represents a best-case, laboratory-derived estimate. Operational field dosing on the Utuhina and Puarenga inflows has historically required substantially higher effective ratios (~7:1 Al:P; McDowell & Hawke, 2006), reflecting the effects of turbulence, short flocculation contact times, and hydrodynamic losses in the stream environment.
Regarding binding kinetics, DRP removal appeared rapid under jar-test conditions — pH dropped within the first five minutes of dosing, and most removal was complete within the first 20 minutes of the 3-hour experiment. This is qualitatively consistent with a fast water-column binding rate (k_w), though no explicit first-order rate constant was fitted in the thesis. The near-complete removal of 1.62 mg P L⁻¹ (~52 mmol P m⁻³) at a 1 mg Al L⁻¹ dose suggests binding was not substrate-limited at that concentration, which is consistent with a relatively low half-saturation constant (K_P). The default value of 0.3 mmol P m⁻³ is not contradicted by the data, though it cannot be independently confirmed from this study.




The thesis provides the most quantitatively useful constraints for this parameter. Settling velocities were measured for 89 individually tracked flocs under low-turbulence conditions:



Floc size class
Typical settling velocity




< 1,000 µm
< 40 m day⁻¹


1,500–2,500 µm
50–80 m day⁻¹


> 3,000 µm
~100 m day⁻¹



The fitted linear regression across all flocs was: velocity (m day⁻¹) = 0.0324 × diameter (µm) − 0.94, with R² = 0.69. The median Martin diameter was 1,290 µm and the mean was 1,442 µm. Applying the fitted relationship to Lake Rotorua’s bathymetry, settling through the mean depth (10.8 m) is estimated at 0.2–0.7 days (5–17 hours), and through the maximum depth (45 m) at 0.9–3.0 days under quiescent conditions.
The bulk of the floc population clustered in the 20–60 m day⁻¹ range. A representative central estimate for w_ala of ~0.5 m day⁻¹ (the current default) is physically defensible and consistent with median floc behaviour. A range of 0.3–1.5 m day⁻¹ could be justified depending on whether conservative or mean settling is targeted. These estimates should be treated as upper bounds, as wind-driven mixing in the lake is expected to interrupt settling and prolong suspension.




Microscopic image analysis of 1,094 fine floc particles revealed:

Equivalent diameters ranged from 25 to 240 µm
87% of particles were below 120 µm; only 13% exceeded this
Mean equivalent diameter: 77.5 µm; median: 69.3 µm
Distribution was right-skewed (skewness = 0.95), dominated by small aggregates

The larger settling aggregates tracked in video (median ~1,290 µm) are composite structures built from these fine sub-units. The thesis notes that alum flocs are inherently fragile and can release stable fine particles under gentle shear — a characteristic relevant to resuspension behaviour under wave action in the lake.




The thesis provides strong qualitative support for enabling resuspension in Lake Rotorua models. Sediment surveys (Tempero & Hamilton, 2016; Tempero, 2019) consistently show that amorphous Al(OH)₃ is concentrated in near-shore areas close to the Utuhina and Puarenga discharge zones, with limited accumulation in the deeper basin sediments. The thesis interprets this pattern as a consequence of fast near-shore settling (consistent with the 0.2–0.7 day estimate to mean depth) combined with subsequent wind-driven resuspension that prevents widespread offshore redistribution.
On this basis, simResuspension = .true. is recommended for Lake Rotorua, particularly in models that resolve spatial differences between near-shore and offshore zones. No quantitative value for k_res is derivable from the thesis; the authors recommend future wave-flume experiments to constrain this parameter.




The thesis provides directly relevant pH observations for Lake Rotorua:

Pre-treatment pH ranged from 6.9 to 7.9 across sites, with Lake Rotorua at the lower end
Following alum addition, pH dropped by up to 2.11 units within 10–20 minutes, then stabilised with minimal recovery (< 0.1 units over 3 hours)
Post-treatment pH in jar tests therefore sat persistently in the ~5–6 range
Alkalinity was the lowest of all sites at 19.20 mg CaCO₃ L⁻¹, providing very limited buffering against acidification
Al(OH)₃ is most stable and P-binding most effective in the pH 6–8 window; efficiency declines below pH 6 and Al³⁺ toxicity becomes a concern below pH 4.5

Since operational dosing is applied via the Utuhina and Puarenga inflows rather than directly to the open lake, pH in the lake body should remain close to ambient (~7–8) rather than dropping to the jar-test minimum. Under open-lake conditions, the pH efficiency modifier is therefore less critical than it would be for a direct-dosing scenario.
If ads_use_pH is activated, a pH_opt of 7.0 would better represent open-lake conditions than the default of 6.0. A sigma_pH of 1.0 is consistent with the observed ±1–2 unit swings recorded during dosing events.




Operational alum dosing has been applied continuously to the Utuhina Stream since 2006 and the Puarenga Stream since 2010, at a target rate of approximately 1 mg Al L⁻¹, adjusted automatically to stream flow. Cumulative aluminium applied reached 1,071 tonnes by end of 2024, at a long-term mean rate of 158.1 kg Al day⁻¹. Peak application occurred during 2011–2012 when more than 2,000 tonnes per year were applied.
Converting the mean operational rate to a whole-lake surface dose: 158.1 kg Al day⁻¹ ÷ 26.98 g mol⁻¹ = ~5,860 mol Al day⁻¹. At the observed 0.7:1 Al:P molar ratio, this binds approximately 8,370 mol P day⁻¹, or ~8.37 × 10⁶ mmol P day⁻¹. Distributed over Lake Rotorua’s surface area (80.6 km² = 80.6 × 10⁶ m²), this gives an indicative whole-lake mean of:

S_ala ≈ 0.10 mmol P m⁻² day⁻¹

Peak dosing years would yield approximately double this value. Note that this is a spatially averaged estimate; in practice, alum enters via discrete inflow points and is not uniformly distributed across the lake surface.




The thesis does not report explicit rate constants for the loss of binding capacity or burial of settled floc. It does confirm that sediment aluminium persists in near-shore zones over multi-year timescales, implying some long-term retention, but quantitative ageing or burial rates are not derivable from this study. The default values (k_age ~0.0998 day⁻¹, k_bur = 0.01 day⁻¹) cannot be validated or refuted from the available data and should be drawn from the broader literature or calibrated against monitoring data.

The jar-test Al:P ratios are best treated as site-specific indicators of performance under idealised, controlled conditions, not as fixed stoichiometric targets for field dosing. Operational experience consistently shows higher effective Al:P requirements in flowing systems due to turbulence and incomplete flocculation. Settling velocity estimates are similarly best-case figures derived under low-turbulence laboratory conditions; wind-driven mixing in Lake Rotorua will extend effective settling times and promote near-shore deposition over basin-wide distribution. Periodic re-evaluation of jar-test response and alkalinity is recommended, as water chemistry can shift over time and alter both treatment performance and operational risk.

title: Alum Dosing in Lake Rotorua
text:
This thesis evaluates the effectiveness of alum (aluminium sulphate, Al₂(SO₄)₃) as a tool for reducing dissolved reactive phosphorus (DRP) across five New Zealand waters: Lake Rotorua, the Utuhina and Puarenga Streams, Lake Ōkaro, and Lake Moawhitu. The study was motivated by a recognised gap in site-specific, controlled evidence for Al:P binding behaviour across the Rotorua catchment lakes, despite many years of operational dosing.
The methodology centred on standardised 3-hour jar tests, with acid titrations used to quantify buffering capacity at each site. For Lake Rotorua specifically, video-based settling measurements and stereomicroscopy were used to characterise the physical properties of alum floc — providing the most detailed floc data available for this lake.
Across all sites, alum reduced DRP, but the magnitude of removal and pH response varied considerably. Al:P molar ratios ranged from 0.7:1 to 15.1:1 depending on site chemistry, and pH behaviour was governed primarily by alkalinity rather than dose rate. Lake Rotorua and the Puarenga Stream had the lowest alkalinity (~19 mg CaCO₃ L⁻¹) and showed the weakest pH recovery after dosing. Lake Moawhitu, with the highest alkalinity (~67 mg CaCO₃ L⁻¹), recovered most strongly.

title: Calibration Step 1: Physics and Oxygen
text: This is the first step of the staged plan that follows the sensitivity analysis: calibrate the physics and the oxygen dynamics together, using the process signatures of the CSPS framework as well as state errors, with the alum module off, because alum does not change physics or oxygen. The target behaviour is a polymictic lake that stratifies for days at a time, mixes again, and develops short bottom-water anoxia.

title: Calibration Step 1: Physics and Oxygen
text: This is the first step of the staged plan that follows the sensitivity analysis: calibrate the physics and the oxygen dynamics together, using the process signatures of the CSPS framework as well as state errors, with the alum module off, because alum does not change physics or oxygen. The target behaviour is a polymictic lake that stratifies for days at a time, mixes again, and develops short bottom-water anoxia.

title: Calibration Step 1: Physics and Oxygen
text:
2 Set-up

Forcing: the hourly bias-corrected ERA5 series. The sensitivity analysis showed that daily forcing has less mixing energy, so mixing parameters fitted on it would not transfer.
Wind is not scaled. The wind is measured on the lake, so the wind scaling factor is fixed at 1 (earlier calibrations settled on 1.64, which was compensating for other errors). Heat and mixing errors are absorbed by the heat-flux coefficients and mixing coefficients instead.
Alum off: the dosed inflow concentration is set to zero. Phytoplankton and the other biogeochemical parameters are held at the earlier calibrated values (the phytoplankton parameters are calibrated in the next step).
Period: 2012-07 to 2022-06, the span with both hourly forcing and the inflow series, plus a 540-day spin-up. Calibration window 2012-07 to 2018-12; the years 2019-01 to 2022-06 are held out and are only used to check the result.
Free parameters (27): the radiation, air-temperature and humidity scalings; the heat-flux coefficients ce, ch, cd; the light extinction Kw; five mixing coefficients (coef_mix_shear is inert and fixed); the sediment oxygen demand in four zones with ksed_oxy and theta_sed_oxy; and eight organic-matter parameters (mineralisation and hydrolysis rates, their temperature coefficients and half-saturations, f_an, particle settling w_pom).
What is fitted (28 residuals, each in units of the lake’s tolerance or a fixed scale, so every metric counts equally):

16 process signatures: stratified fraction (all year, summer, winter), temperature difference statistics, spells per year, spell length, bottom temperature, anoxic fraction (below 2 and 1 mg/L), bottom oxygen statistics, the share of years with anoxia, and the oxygen decline rate in stratified spells.
Bias and RMSE of temperature and oxygen in the surface, middle and bottom layers.

Method: an ensemble smoother with multiple data assimilation (ES-MDA), 80 members, 6 assimilation steps, run in parallel (560 model runs). It gives an ensemble rather than one parameter set.

Anoxia: the anoxic fraction, bottom-oxygen mean and 10th percentile, and the oxygen decline rate in stratified spells are all within about half a tolerance. The model now produces short anoxic spells in the observed years (Figure 1, end of 2018 and the start of 2021).
Not fixed: summer stratification is still somewhat too strong in the calibration years (1.3 tolerances over, 0.4 in the held-out years), stratified spells are still too frequent and short (about 1.5 tolerances too many spells per year), and the share of years with anoxia is under-predicted (the model has anoxia in fewer years than the lake). Surface oxygen is about 0.65 mg/L too low in both windows, which this step did not target: surface oxygen is set by air-water exchange and phytoplankton production, and will be revisited with the phytoplankton step.

Well constrained: the deepest-zone oxygen demand (fsed_oxy zone 1; posterior spread 0.45 of the prior), the long-wave radiation scaling, the hypolimnetic mixing coefficient and the drag coefficient cd. These are the parameters the sensitivity analysis picked out as controlling the targets.
Not constrained: most of the organic-matter parameters and the shallower-zone oxygen demands keep a posterior spread close to their prior, as the sensitivity analysis predicted.
Wind is fixed at 1, and the calibrated model still reproduces the observed temperature structure and anoxia, which is consistent with the wind scaling of 1.64 in the earlier calibration having compensated for other errors.

title: Calibration Step 1: Physics and Oxygen
text:
5 Second pass with wider bounds
To check whether those limits were holding the fit back, I ran a second pass of 4 assimilation steps starting from half of the first posterior, with coef_mix_hyp up to 5, cd and ch up to 0.003, ce down to 0.0004, coef_mix_KH down to 0.02, and wider organic-matter ranges.



Best member of each pass.


Pass
Calibration phi (best)
Held-out phi (best)




1: original bounds
0.64
0.5


2: widened bounds
0.63
0.6






No improvement in the fit (0.63 against 0.64 on the calibration years) and a worse score on the held-out years (0.60 against 0.50), so widening the bounds is not worthwhile and pass 1 is kept as the step 1 result. The pinned parameters are not what limits the stratification.
The oxygen and organic-matter parameters are not unique. The second pass reached the same fit with very different values: for example rdom_minerl went from 0.045 to 0.006, kpom_hydrol from 6 to 95, w_pom from -0.40 to -0.02, the zone-4 oxygen demand from -134 to -38 and ksed_oxy from 97 to 35. The data constrain a combination of these (the total oxygen demand reaching the bottom water), not each one. The physics parameters were more stable (coef_wind_stir 0.56 in both passes, cd about 0.002, coef_mix_hyp 1.7 to 2). The next steps should treat these as an ensemble, not a single set.

title: Calibration Step 1: Physics and Oxygen
text:
6 Limitations

The residual stratification excess (summer fraction, spell frequency) is not removed by any of the bounded parameters, so it is probably structural (for example the missing deep pit). This was not tested here.
Surface oxygen is biased low; this is an air-water exchange and production issue.
Phytoplankton, nitrogen and phosphorus parameters were held at their earlier values, so the oxygen parameters may be compensating for phytoplankton oxygen production and respiration. They should be re-checked after the phytoplankton step.
Three and a half years are held out, which is short for the signatures that depend on rare events (anoxic years).

title: Calibration Step 1: Physics and Oxygen
text:
7 Next

The parameter set (calibration/checkpoints/step1_final_params.csv) becomes the physics and oxygen baseline for the next step.
Calibrate the sediment and phytoplankton parameters on the 1990 to 2006 nutrient and chlorophyll record with the alum module off. This needs the hourly forcing back to 1987.
Calibrate the alum parameters on the dosed years with everything else fixed.

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text: Status: draft strategy. It builds on components that already exist in this project and lists what still has to be done before the projections can be trusted. Numbers marked estimate are my planning figures, not measurements.

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text:
1 Purpose and questions
The aim is to estimate how climate change alters nutrient dynamics and the trophic state of Lake Rotorua, and how much alum dosing could offset it. Three questions drive the design:

Climate effect. With catchment loads and alum dosing held as they are now, how do water temperature, stratification, bottom-water oxygen, internal P release, chlorophyll-a and LKE_tli4 change by mid and late century, and how large is that change compared with year-to-year variability?
Management response. How does the effect of alum dosing (present operations, more, less, none) change under each climate? Put another way, how much more or less alum is needed to hold LKE_tli4 at a chosen target?
Uncertainty. How much of the spread comes from the GCM, the emissions pathway, the catchment response, the alum behaviour, and the model parameters?
