title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text:
4 Design

4.1 Overview





flowchart LR
  A[ERA5 baseline<br/>bias-corrected] --> C[Scenario forcing<br/>GCM x SSP x window]
  B[CMIP6 monthly deltas] --> C
  D[Historical inflows<br/>1959-2022] --> E[Inflow adaptation<br/>flow, load, temperature]
  C --> E
  C --> F[GLM-AED runs]
  E --> F
  G[Alum scenarios] --> F
  H[Parameter ensemble<br/>from calibration] --> F
  F --> I[Daily output<br/>nutrients, DO, TLI4]
  I --> J[Annual and seasonal metrics<br/>variance partitioning]








4.2 Climate forcing

Use the existing delta-change forcing (scenario_hourly_met). It keeps real weather sequences and shifts their statistics, which suits a model that needs realistic storms and calm spells.
Use 30-year time slices, not 10 or 15 years (see the next subsection for why and for the cost). The weather baseline for a slice is the 1991 to 2020 ERA5 climate normal (taken from the 1988 to 2024 record), with each GCM/SSP/window delta applied to it.
How the ERA5 record maps to the climate windows. The window (2015–2040, 2041–2070, 2071–2100) only selects which monthly delta is applied; it does not select ERA5 years. Every window uses the same 30 ERA5 weather years (1991–2020), so differences between windows are purely the climate signal. The deltas are relative to the CMIP6 1995–2014 reference (scenario_ref_years), which sits at the same centre (about 2005) as the 1991–2020 baseline, so the two are consistent. Keep the original ERA5 dates (1991–2020) in the model and label the run by window; relabelling the years to 2041–2070 gains nothing and causes leap-year problems (for example 2100 is not a leap year).
The remaining ERA5 years are not wasted: 1988–1990 can serve as spin-up weather, and 2021–2024 can be used for hindcast checks. Optionally run the full 37 years once as a robustness test of the baseline choice.
NZESM (360-day calendar). No long transient run is needed. Delta-change uses only 12 monthly factors per variable, and these are applied to the Gregorian ERA5 days, so the GCM calendar never enters the model. The one thing to verify is that metscale::climate_point_monthly_climatology() assigns NZESM days to calendar months correctly (the repository already handles 360-day time in R/summarise_gcm_ts.R and R/standardise_to_gregorian.R). NZESM contributes monthly means only; its daily variability is not used, as for the other GCMs.
Keep hindcast (no delta) as the reference, and compare future windows with it, not with observations.
Use all 7 GCMs for the main set, because GCM spread dominates (annual warming for SSP585 by 2071 to 2100 ranges from +2.8 to +4.6 °C). Do not rely on NorESM2-MM alone, which is at the low end.
Assumption to state clearly: delta-change keeps present variability and sequences, so it will not capture changes in the frequency of persistent calm spells beyond what the monthly means imply. The extreme-event indices are used to check this.



4.3 Simulation length
A 10-year run is too short for climate statements, and the 15 years of bias-corrected hourly ERA5-Land (2011 to 2026) that the pipeline uses today is also short. The reasons:

Variability. Rainfall, inflow and bloom years in the Rotorua catchment swing with ENSO and decadal climate. A single decade can sit in one phase, so a 10-year difference between scenarios can reflect the weather sequence, not the climate signal. Thirty years is the standard averaging period and gives a much smaller sampling error on annual metrics such as TLI4 (about 40% smaller than for 10 years, as the error falls with the square root of the number of years).
Rare events. Storms, heatwaves, calm spells and the blooms and anoxic periods that follow them need long samples to estimate how often they occur.
Slow state variables. Sediment P pools, benthic alum pools and the legacy effect of stopping or changing dosing evolve over 10 to 30 years, so they need a spin-up of 5 to 10 years and, for the alum questions, runs long enough to see the response.

What is needed to get 30 years:








Item
Status
Action




Weather baseline 1991 to 2020
The corrected daily series covers only 2011 to 2026; ERA5 for 1988 to 2024 is now available but not bias-corrected
Apply the same daily bias correction (fitted on the buoy overlap, assumed stationary) to the 1988 to 2024 record, then disaggregate to hourly using the 2011 to 2025 hourly donor. Fix the rainfall units first (gap 5)


Inflows
The historical inflow series covers 1959 to 2022, so 1991 to 2020 is available
None, but check the inflow record is consistent through the period


Alum dosing in the baseline
Dosing history starts in 2006 and 2010
Use a constant present-day dose for the slices (scenario A1) rather than the history



Time slices or transient runs. Use 30-year time slices (a stationary climate per window, 5 to 10 years of spin-up) as the main design. Add a small number of transient runs for the alum questions that depend on timing and legacy: for example 2 to 3 GCMs under SSP245 and SSP585, run continuously from 2015 to 2100 with the monthly deltas interpolated between windows. A slice cannot show how long P from a stopped dose lingers or how fast the benthic alum pool builds.
Cost. Thirty years roughly doubles the 15-year cost per run, so the full design below needs about 20 hours rather than about 11. A tiered plan keeps it manageable: 30-year slices for the core scenarios and the hindcast, and 15-year slices (the 2011 to 2025 weather) for the large sweeps over alum parameters and inflow tiers. Check the two give the same signal on the pilot set before relying on the shorter runs.
Do we need 1970 to 2100 runs? No, not for the main questions. With delta-change, a continuous run to 2100 would need a trend in the forcing that the monthly-window deltas do not provide, and the slices already answer “what is the lake like under climate X”. Transient runs are only justified for timing and legacy questions (A4 below), and are optional for now.


4.4 Spin-up and equilibrium
How long a run must be depends on which state variable carries memory:








Component
Memory
Consequence




Water column nutrients, chlorophyll-a, temperature
Months to about 1 to 2 years (residence time; check against modelled outflow)
A 2 to 3 year spin-up is enough


Sediment P pools, benthic alum pools
Many years
5 to 10 years of spin-up, and this is what matters for alum



For the alum on/off comparison the question decides the design:

Equilibrium contrast (A0 versus A1, each in its own steady state): spin each case up under its own dosing, then run the 30 years. This is the default for the slices, and it needs the full 5 to 10 year spin-up because the sediment and alum pools differ between the cases. Spin up by looping the first 5 to 10 years of the baseline weather (or using 1988 to 1990 plus a loop).
Transient response (what happens after dosing stops from today’s state): needs a continuous run from the present state and a long enough record to see the legacy P decline. Keep this as the small optional set (A4).

Check that the spin-up is adequate empirically, once, on the pilot: run a slice twice back to back and compare the first and last 10 years of annual LKE_tli4, sediment P and benthic alum pools. If the drift is small relative to the climate signal and to the A0–A1 difference, the spin-up is sufficient.


4.5 Inflows (three tiers)
Initial phase. Climate-adjusted inflows do not exist yet, so the first runs use T1 only (historical 1991 to 2020 inflows, which are coherent with the ERA5 weather years) with two alum cases: A0 (none) and A1 (present flow-paced dose). Optionally shift stream temperature with the air-temperature delta (T1+, a cheap and defensible adjustment). State plainly that flow and load are unchanged while rainfall changes, so results are a lower bound on the catchment-driven change. T2 and T3 and alum cases A2 to A5 are later phases.
Climate also changes what enters the lake, and this is likely to matter as much as in-lake warming for nutrients.








Tier
Inflow treatment
Purpose




T1
Historical inflows unchanged
Isolates the direct lake response to weather and temperature


T2
Scale flow with the rainfall delta (with a runoff elasticity) and the evapotranspiration implied by the temperature delta; scale loads with flow through a load–discharge exponent; shift stream temperature with air temperature
Plausible catchment response without a catchment model


T3
Drive a catchment model with the scenario forcing (if the catchment model used to make the 1959 to 2022 inflow series can be run)
Best available, and the way to test T2



Run T1 and T2 for the full ensemble and T3 for a subset if available. The alum dose is proportional to flow in the dosed streams, so T2 also changes the alum delivered, which is a real climate–management interaction and is kept.


4.6 Alum scenarios
Built on scale_alum_inflows(); efficiency uses the factor already defined as ratio_al_p.








Code
Dosing
Rationale




A0
None
Counterfactual


A1
Present operations (Utuhina and Puarenga, flow-paced at about 1 mg Al/L)
Business as usual


A2
A1 with doubled dose
Management response


A3
A1 with half dose
Reduced effort


A4
Dosing stops at a set date
Legacy P release from sediment


A5
Adaptive dose: increases when modelled lake TLI4 or FRP is above a target
Inverse question: dose needed to hold the target



Alum behaviour is treated as an uncertainty dimension, using the thesis-based ranges in the thesis notes and the calibration page: floc settling 0.3 to 1.5 m/d, binding efficiency (Al:P) from 0.15 (field, about 7:1) to 1.4 (jar test, 0.7:1), resuspension on or off. The stage 4 sensitivity check showed that, in the calibrated model, the FRP fit is nearly insensitive to the alum parameters within their ranges and that removing the dose raises mean FRP by only about 30%. The alum response in the projections is therefore uncertain and should be explored through these ranges, not taken from a single fitted value.


4.7 Parameter and structural uncertainty

Use a small parameter ensemble from the calibration posterior (about 5 members from the final pestpp-ies ensemble), plus the alum efficiency and settling range above.
Add structural checks: switch temperature dependence of sediment P release and mineralisation (theta_*) between default and a stronger response; test phytoplankton T_opt shifts, since adaptation is unknown.
Do not tune the model to future conditions. Parameters stay fixed at their calibrated values.



4.8 Metrics








Group
Variables
Reported as




Trophic state
LKE_tli4, LKE_tlic, LKE_tlin, LKE_tlip, LKE_tlise
Annual mean, change from hindcast, probability of exceeding the management target (BOPRC’s target for Lake Rotorua is 4.2; verify)


Nutrients
TP, TN, FRP, ammonium, nitrate (epilimnion and bottom)
Annual and seasonal means; TN:TP


Phytoplankton
Chlorophyll-a, cyanobacteria
Annual mean, days above bloom threshold, bloom timing


Oxygen and stratification
Bottom-water oxygen, CHM_oxynal (anoxic layers), days anoxic, stratified days, Schmidt stability
Days per year, onset and duration


Internal loading
Benthic FRP and P fluxes, alum pools (ALU_ben_*), P mass balance
Tonnes P per year, internal vs external share


Hydrology
Water level, outflow, evaporation, residence time
Annual means, extremes



TLI uses annual means in regulatory practice. Keep the daily series, but report the annual metric as the headline and show the seasonal cycle separately.

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text:
5 Experimental design and compute budget
Initial phase (current scope): 83 GCM × SSP × window combinations × 2 alum cases (A0, A1) × T1 inflows = 166 runs, plus the hindcast. At 5 to 6 minutes per 30 + 5 year run and about 2 runs per minute on six workers this is roughly 3 to 4 hours of wall time; pilot with 3 GCMs first (about 36 runs). The phases below are the fuller design for when inflow scenarios exist.
Estimate: a 15 + 3 year run takes about 1 minute of GLM time plus 1 to 2 minutes to read the output when only the needed variables are requested, so about 3 minutes per run, and a 30 + 5 year run about 5 to 6 minutes. Six workers give about 2 runs per minute for 15-year runs. The table below uses 15-year runs for the sweeps; the core scenarios and the hindcast use 30-year slices (see Simulation length).








Phase
Runs
Estimated time




P1 Hindcast and validation
5 parameter members × 2 alum cases
under 1 hour


P2 Pilot (T1 inflows)
3 GCMs × 2 SSPs × 2 windows × 3 alum (A0, A1, A2) = 36
about 20 minutes


P3 Main climate ensemble (T1 and T2)
27 GCM–SSP combinations × 2 windows (2041–2070, 2071–2100) × 2 inflow tiers × 3 alum (A0, A1, A2) = 324
about 3 hours


P4 Alum scenarios (full set A0 to A5)
27 × 2 × 6 × 2 tiers = 648
about 5.5 hours


P5 Parameter ensemble (reduced)
5 members × SSP245 and SSP585 × 7 GCMs × late window × A1 = 70
about 40 minutes


P6 Structural checks and T3 subset
about 100
about 1 hour



About 1,200 runs. With 15-year runs that is about 11 hours; with all of them at 30 years it would be about 20 hours, which is why the design is tiered. Run it as a targets pipeline, not a PEST script: these are deterministic, independent and benefit from caching, unlike the calibration. Use a crew controller with a worker count below the physical core count.

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text:
6 Analysis plan

Hindcast check. Compare the 2011 to 2022 hindcast (the period with water-quality observations) annual TLI4 and components with observed, per year. State the skill and bias explicitly and carry them into the interpretation.
Climate signal. For each metric, compute future minus hindcast per run. Report the ensemble median, the GCM range, and the fraction of runs agreeing in sign.
Signal against variability. Compare the climate change with the spread of annual values within the hindcast (internal variability). A change smaller than that is reported as such.
Variance partitioning. Decompose the spread into GCM, SSP, window, inflow tier, alum scenario and parameter member (ANOVA or mixed model). This answers question 3.
Alum response curves. For each climate, plot TLI4 and FRP against alum dose multiplier and efficiency, and read off the dose that holds the target. Report the extra dose required by climate.
Process attribution. Compare T1 and T2 inflows and A0 and A1 alum to separate in-lake warming, catchment input and alum effects. Use simple factorial contrasts.
Event view. Link the extreme-event indices (storms, heatwaves) to bloom and anoxia days in the runs where those change most.

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text:
7 Deliverables and layout

scenarios/ with scripts 10_build_scenario_aeme.R (forcing, inflows, alum, parameter set → Aeme object), 11_run_scenarios.R (targets-based, one branch per run, daily lake-mean and epilimnion/hypolimnion series only), 12_metrics.R (annual and seasonal metrics, TLI), and 13_analysis.R.
Summary tables as CSV in data/processed/scenarios/ so the website pages do not re-run models.
Quarto pages: results by metric, alum response curves, uncertainty partitioning, and a short non-technical summary.

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
section: 8 Risks and how they are handled
text:
8 Risks and how they are handled







Risk
Handling




Calibration still weak for chl-a, TP, TN
Gap list above; present results as change from the model’s own hindcast, and state hindcast skill


Catchment response unknown
Tiers T1 to T3; report T1 as a lower bound on change


Alum behaviour poorly constrained by data
Scenario dimension with thesis ranges; do not report a single efficiency


Delta-change misses changes in variability and extremes
Check against extreme-event indices; state the limitation


Compute
Tiered design; run the pilot first and re-estimate time per run before committing


Pipeline fragility (long runs, large netCDF)
Request only the variables needed; store small summaries, not netCDF; cache by branch


Rainfall unit issue in the forcing
Fix at source and add a unit and annual-total check to the pipeline

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text:
9 Sequence

Close the open calibration gaps (TP, TN and Secchi targets, ammonium, stage 3 with alum on) and fix the rainfall units and the aemetools unit bug at source.
Hindcast and TLI4 validation (P1). Go or no-go on skill before continuing.
Pilot (P2); re-time the run and refine the design.
Main ensemble and alum scenarios (P3, P4), then parameter and structural checks (P5, P6).
Analysis and reporting.

title: Climate-Change Impact Strategy for Lake Rotorua
text:
10 Open questions

Which TLI4 target or threshold should be used for management (for example BOPRC’s 4.2), and is annual mean TLI4 the right headline metric?
Is a catchment model available that can be driven with the scenario forcing (T3), and who owns the 1959 to 2022 inflow series?
Are there planned changes in dosing locations, dose rates or the Ōhau weir operation that should be scenarios in their own right?
For alum on/off, is the equilibrium contrast (each case spun up under its own dosing) the question of interest, or the transient response after stopping from today’s state?
Should land-use or point-source changes (WWTP, geothermal) be included, or is the question climate only?

title: CMIP 6 Processing
text:
Currently the CMIP6 data we have is in NetCDF format, which is not directly compatible with our model input requirements. Therefore, we need to preprocess this data to extract the relevant variables and reformat them appropriately.
Also there are >4 TB of data for all of New Zealand on a daily timestep, at a 5x5 km resolution. This is too large to process directly, so we will need to subset the data spatially and temporally.

title: CMIP 6 Processing
text:
Metadata
We have gathered metadata for the CMIP6 datasets available on the shared drive, including information on the variables, scenarios, models, and bias correction methods used.
Further details can be found here.

title: CMIP 6 Processing
text:
File access
The CMIP6 data is stored on a shared drive (Z: drive) accessible within our institutional network. The files are organized by variable, scenario, model, region, timestep, spatial resolution, and bias correction method e.g “hurs_historical_ACCESS-CM2_CCAM_daily_NZ5km_raw.nc”. This corresponds to relative humidity (hurs) for the historical scenario from the ACCESS-CM2 GCM, downscaled using the CCAM model over New Zealand at a daily timestep and 5 km spatial resolution, without bias correction.
Loading and reading data from these NetCDF files can be done using the ncdf4 package in R. However, reading large datasets can be time-consuming, so we have implemented a function which uses a grid reference system to efficiently extract only the required data points.
This provided as the VCSN agent data. This contains a grid of points at 5 km resolution covering New Zealand, with each point having a unique coordinate index. We use this grid to identify which points fall within our area of interest, and then extract only those points from the NetCDF files.

title: CMIP 6 Processing
text:
Create an area of interest
If you do not have a shapefile of your area of interest (AOI), you can easily generate one with the mapedit package.


Code
x <- mapedit::drawFeatures()


Save the drawn features for future use:


Code
saveRDS(x, here::here("data", "processed", "rotorua_area.rds"))

title: CMIP 6 Processing
text:
Processing function
The process_cmip6 function takes in a spatial polygon (defining the area of interest), the VCSN grid points, the path to a NetCDF file, and an output file path. It extracts the relevant data points from the NetCDF file based on the area of interest, and saves the processed data to a new NetCDF file.



Function Parameters for process_cmip6()


Parameter
Description




x
sf polygon


vcsn_grid_points
sf points of VCSN grid


file
path to input netCDF file


outfile
path to output netCDF file







Code
source(here::here("R", "process_cmip6.R"))
process_cmip6(x = x, vcsn_grid_points = vcsn_grid_points,
              file = file, outfile = outfile)

title: CSPS Evaluation Framework for Lake Rotorua
text:
The calibration so far scores the model on state variables (temperature, oxygen, nutrients, chlorophyll-a). A model can match those concentrations for the wrong reasons, particularly in a shallow lake where one parameter such as wind scaling can compensate for several errors (see the mixing section of the staged calibration). This page defines a metrics system based on the CSPS framework (Concept, State, Process, System; Hipsey et al. 2020), built from what the observations can actually support, and aimed at four things the model must get right:

Polymixis: a lake that stratifies for days to weeks and mixes again, many times a year.
Bottom-water anoxia: short, episodic and variable between years.
Internal loading: nutrient release from the sediment into stratified bottom water.
Seasonal phytoplankton dynamics: the magnitude, variability and timing of chlorophyll-a.

The code is in calibration/csps_metrics.R. calibration/csps_build_targets.R writes the observed targets to calibration/csps_targets.csv.

title: CSPS Evaluation Framework for Lake Rotorua
text:
The calibration so far scores the model on state variables (temperature, oxygen, nutrients, chlorophyll-a). A model can match those concentrations for the wrong reasons, particularly in a shallow lake where one parameter such as wind scaling can compensate for several errors (see the mixing section of the staged calibration). This page defines a metrics system based on the CSPS framework (Concept, State, Process, System; Hipsey et al. 2020), built from what the observations can actually support, and aimed at four things the model must get right:

Polymixis: a lake that stratifies for days to weeks and mixes again, many times a year.
Bottom-water anoxia: short, episodic and variable between years.
Internal loading: nutrient release from the sediment into stratified bottom water.
Seasonal phytoplankton dynamics: the magnitude, variability and timing of chlorophyll-a.

The code is in calibration/csps_metrics.R. calibration/csps_build_targets.R writes the observed targets to calibration/csps_targets.csv.

title: CSPS Evaluation Framework for Lake Rotorua

Lessons from the data that shape the targets:

The lake is polymictic. Surface minus bottom temperature (17 m and deeper) exceeds 1 °C on about 22% of days (35% from December to April, almost never in winter). Spells last a median of 2 days, with a 90th percentile of 17 days and about 9 spells a year. The model must produce frequent short stratification and mixing, not a seasonal thermocline.
Anoxia is episodic and uneven between years. Bottom oxygen is below 2 mg/L on about 11% of December to April days, but from 0% (2014, 2022, 2023) to 33% (2010) of days between years, and 83% of years have at least one event.
Internal loading shows as a bottom to surface contrast in the stratified season. Bottom ammonium is a median 7 times the surface value, FRP 2.6 times and TP 1.4 times. It is only measured at depth to 2020.
Chlorophyll-a has weak seasonality. The median is about 9 mg m-3, the summer to winter ratio is close to 1, and the signal is irregular blooms (the 90th percentile is about 20) rather than a regular spring peak. Matching a seasonal cycle would reward the wrong behaviour, so the targets use the distribution, bloom frequency and the annual peak.

title: CSPS Evaluation Framework for Lake Rotorua
text:
3 The framework





Level
Question
How it is assessed




0 Concept
Is the model structure appropriate for these questions?
Checklist (table below), reviewed before each scenario use


1 State
Do simulated concentrations match observations?
Bias, MAE, RMSE, correlation and KGE by variable and layer (log scale for chlorophyll and nutrients), plus seasonal correlation


2 Process
Is the model producing the observed behaviour through the right processes?
Signatures of mixing, oxygen demand and nutrient gradients, with tolerances from the interannual spread


3 System
Does the whole lake respond as observed?
Trophic state (TLI3), chlorophyll to TP relation, response to alum dosing and to wet and dry years






3.1 Level 0: concept checklist







Question
Status




Does the hydrodynamic model resolve rapid mixing and stratification cycles (hourly forcing, wind-driven mixing)?
Yes with hourly forcing; the daily-forced base is a coarser test


Is sediment oxygen demand and nutrient release linked to bottom-water oxygen?
Sediment release and oxygen demand are parameterised by zone (fsed_*, ksed_*); the oxygen dependence needs checking in the AED sediment settings


Are the 21.5 m basin and the deeper pit (to 27 m) represented?
No. The model uses hyps_no_hole. Observed ammonium is highest at 21 to 25 m, so this is a known structural gap


Is phytoplankton resolved by group (cyanobacteria, diatoms, green algae)?
Yes, but only total chlorophyll-a is observed


Are alum dosing and its effect on phosphorus represented?
Yes (aed_alum, stage 4), with dose and efficiency uncertain


Is rainfall, river inflow and nutrient loading consistent with the lake budget?
Water balance calibrated; nutrient loads and the organic share are assumptions


Does the forcing carry the climate-scenario signal at the time scale the lake responds to (days)?
Delta-change on hourly corrected ERA5; daily weather variability is preserved





3.2 Level 1: state metrics
For each variable and layer (surface 0 to 2 m, middle, bottom 17 m and deeper, and bottom from December to April) the scorecard reports bias, MAE, RMSE, correlation, KGE and the correlation of the monthly climatology. Chlorophyll-a and nutrients are compared on the log scale. These replace a single pooled error score: a model that gets the surface right and the bottom wrong is visible.


3.3 Level 2 and 3: signatures
Every signature is computed by one function on the observations and on the model, using only days on which an observation exists. This removes the effect of sampling. The tolerance for each signature is the standard deviation of that signature between observed years (at least 10% of the value; 50% for signatures with fewer than five usable years). A model is inside tolerance when it lands within one standard deviation of the observed value, and the score falls from 1 to 0 between one and three standard deviations.

Level 3 also includes checks that need model runs rather than signatures, which are not yet computed. They will come from the long (1992 to 2022) daily-forced run:

Year-to-year agreement: does the model have anoxia in the same years that the lake does (rank correlation of the annual anoxic fraction, 2008 to 2022)?
Trophic state over time: simulated against observed annual TLI3, in the 1990s before alum and after.
Response to alum: the change in summer bottom FRP and ammonium and in chlorophyll-a before and after dosing began.
Wet and dry years: bloom frequency and anoxic fraction in the top and bottom quartile of annual inflow.

text:
4 Observed year-to-year range
The tolerances come from how much the lake itself varies between years:

title: CSPS Evaluation Framework for Lake Rotorua
text:
5 Calibration, validation and scoring

Calibration window. The current PEST windows (2 to 3 years inside 2017 to 2020) fit states. They are not long enough to score signatures that depend on rare events (spells, years with anoxia).
Validation. Score the calibrated model on all other years that have daily temperature and oxygen (2007 to 2016, 2021 to 2025) and on the 1992 to 2006 nutrient record from the daily-forced run. The signatures are the validation targets; a model that passes state metrics but fails signatures is not accepted for scenarios.
Ensembles. Run the signature scorecard on each realisation of the final PEST ensemble, and report the range, not only the best run.
Using signatures inside PEST. The signatures can be added as observation groups in the next calibration round. The first candidates are mix_f_strat_summer and mix_spell_median_d in stage 2 (they separate wind scaling from mixing coefficients), and anox_f_lt2_summer, anox_do_decline_strat and the load_*_ratio set in stage 3. They have to be computed over windows long enough to hold several spells, so the calibration window would need to extend to about one full year.

title: CSPS Evaluation Framework for Lake Rotorua
text:
6 Gaps in the data

Process rates (sediment fluxes, productivity, denitrification) are measured only as the zone sediment fluxes in meas_param, with unconfirmed units, so the process level for internal loading relies on concentration gradients, not fluxes.
Nutrients are not measured at depth after 2020, so internal loading signatures are scored on 11 to 14 years.
TLI4 needs a simulated Secchi depth, which GLM-AED does not output; TLI3 is used instead.
Cyanobacteria and phytoplankton group data would test whether the right groups bloom in the right season; only total chlorophyll-a is available.
The deep pit (to 27 m) is outside the model.

9. Inflow Tests
Section 9 introduces a continuous FRP inflow to the lake, which is more realistic than a closed system and directly mirrors the Rotorua setup where streams (Utuhina, Puarenga) supply FRP continuously. title: Rotorua Light
text:
Lake Rotorua’s GLM-AED setup needs a light extinction (Kw) parameterisation. The options considered were:

A single static Kw (one value for the whole run).
A monthly Kw climatology (12 calendar-month values, time-varying).
A fully dated time-varying Kw built from the observed record.
A decomposed background Kw (observed Kw minus the fraction attributable to phytoplankton/turbidity), for use when AED’s own biology should generate the biotic part of light extinction dynamically.

This document works through the diagnostics behind that decision for the Rotorua PAR/Kd record, and lands on a recommendation for the climate scenario runs specifically (as opposed to a historical hindcast).
The helper functions used throughout live in R/recommend_light_parameterisation.R.

title: Rotorua Light
text:
Lake Rotorua’s GLM-AED setup needs a light extinction (Kw) parameterisation. The options considered were:

A single static Kw (one value for the whole run).
A monthly Kw climatology (12 calendar-month values, time-varying).
A fully dated time-varying Kw built from the observed record.
A decomposed background Kw (observed Kw minus the fraction attributable to phytoplankton/turbidity), for use when AED’s own biology should generate the biotic part of light extinction dynamically.

This document works through the diagnostics behind that decision for the Rotorua PAR/Kd record, and lands on a recommendation for the climate scenario runs specifically (as opposed to a historical hindcast).
The helper functions used throughout live in R/recommend_light_parameterisation.R.

title: Rotorua Light
section: Static vs. time-varying Kw: the trade-offs
text:
Static vs. time-varying Kw: the trade-offs
Time-varying Kw (monthly or dated) can capture real seasonal drivers of light attenuation — spring runoff/turbidity pulses, algal self-shading, CDOM inputs, ice-off resuspension — that a single Kw cannot. Where good profile data exist, throwing that signal away by collapsing to one number misrepresents both the clear and the turbid periods.
The trade-offs:

More data wrangling and another forcing file to QC.
Monthly resolution still misses short-lived bloom/storm spikes.
If Kw has been used as a tuning knob to compensate for other model deficiencies (mixing scheme, inflow temperatures), imposing an independently-derived time-varying Kw removes that degree of freedom and can expose calibration problems elsewhere.
A poorly-constrained time-varying curve (built on noisy or sparse data) is worse than a well-chosen static value.

Static Kw is defensible when extinction is dominated by relatively stable factors, when supporting data are too sparse/noisy to justify more resolution, or — as turns out to matter most here — when there is no calendar correspondence between the simulated period and the observed record, which is exactly the case for a forward climate scenario.

title: Rotorua Light
text:
GLM-AED’s own light feedback
When AED is coupled to GLM with bioshade_feedback = .true., light extinction is not just the prescribed Kw — GLM adds AED’s own simulated biotic/particulate extinction on top, additively (glm_aed.F90, update_light):
par(i) = par(i+1) * EXP( -(Kw + localext_up) * dz(i+1) )
IF (bioshade_feedback) extc(i) = Kw + localext
localext is the sum of whatever AED modules contribute a light-extinction diagnostic — in this setup that includes:

aed_phytoplankton — self-shading from simulated chlorophyll.
aed_noncohesive — extinction from simulated suspended sediment, Ke_ss(i) * SS_conc(i) summed across size classes. The active configuration:

&aed_noncohesive
   num_ss = 2
   ss_initial = 3, 1
   Ke_ss = 0.06, 0.06
   settling = 1
   w_ss = 0.5, 0.03
   rho_ss = 1800, 1200
   d_ss = 2e-05, 4e-06
   resuspension = 1
   epsilon = 0.02
   tau_0 = 0.04, 0.03
   tau_r = 1
   fs = 1, 1
   Fsed = 0, 0
   decay = 0, 0
   simSedimentMass = .false.
   sed_porosity = 0.3
   diag_level = 10
/
Practical consequence: the prescribed Kw/Kw_file should represent only the background (non-biotic, non-suspended-sediment) extinction — water + CDOM + anything not reproduced by AED’s own state. If a Kw derived from field-measured Kd (which already contains the biotic + SS signal at the time of sampling) is combined with bioshade_feedback and an active aed_noncohesive, the biotic/SS contribution is double-counted, over-attenuating light and biasing production, DO, and thermal structure.

title: Rotorua Light
section: Configuring GLM to use a time-varying Kw
text:
Configuring GLM to use a time-varying Kw
For reference, if a time-varying background is used, the &light namelist and Kw_file CSV are:
&light
   light_mode       = 0        ! single-Kw Beer-Lambert; required for Kw_file
   Kw               = 0.37     ! fallback/initial value
   Kw_file          = 'kw.csv' ! time-varying background Kw forcing
   n_bands          = 2
   light_extc       = 1.0, 0.5
   energy_frac      = 0.5, 0.5
   Benthic_Imin     = 10
   albedo_mode      = 1
   albedo_mean      = 0.08
   albedo_amplitude = 0.02
/
time,Kd
2015-01-01,0.62
2015-02-01,0.58
2015-03-01,0.51

The time column must use the same time_fmt/timezone as the &meteorology block.
GLM performs a daily lookup (holds the most recent row’s value), not sub-daily interpolation — the file needs one row per day you want a distinct value for.
Kw_file only drives the single scalar ExtcCoefSW, so it requires light_mode = 0; it has no effect on the per-band light_extc array used by light_mode = 1.

print(kd_recommendation)


Light extinction parameterisation recommendation
--------------------------------------------------
Input:              kw (n = 147, 0 dropped for NA/ordering)
Date range:         2003-08-20 to 2025-08-20 (23 distinct year(s))
Median sample gap:  35 days (max 426 days)
Kw:                 mean 0.714, median 0.601, sd 0.373, CV 0.52 (m^-1)
Interannual R^2:    47% of variance explained by year
Seasonal ratio:     1.62x (max:min monthly mean, detrended by year)

Recommendation: DATED TIME-VARYING Kw (use observed time series directly)

Year explains 47% of total variance in Kw, more than the seasonal cycle does
(interannual regime shifts / trends dominate over any recurring monthly
pattern, detrended seasonal ratio = 1.62x). A generic monthly climatology
would blend these regimes together and misrepresent most individual years.
Recommend driving GLM with the actual dated observations (interpolated/held
constant between sampling dates) for the specific years being simulated,
rather than a synthetic 'typical year' climatology. If a single
representative value is still needed (e.g. for scenario runs outside the
observed period), use the static mean/median (0.714 / 0.601 m^-1) with the
caveat that it will still miss whichever regime the simulated period actually
falls into.




Code
plot(kd_recommendation)










Key finding: interannual variability dominates over seasonality

Kd mean 0.71 m⁻¹, CV 0.52, range 0.25–1.92 m⁻¹.
Year explains ~47% of total variance — more than the seasonal cycle does. Annual means step from ~0.35–0.43 m⁻¹ (2003–2008) to a noisy 0.32–1.4 m⁻¹ regime from 2009 onward.
After removing each year’s own mean, the detrended seasonal ratio is only ~1.6–1.85x, and mostly driven by a handful of bloom/turbidity events rather than a robust recurring monthly pattern.
A pooled multi-year monthly climatology would blend a real interannual regime shift with a weak seasonal signal, misrepresenting most individual years — hence the function’s recommendation of a dated time-varying series over a monthly climatology for a hindcast.

title: Rotorua Light
section: Decomposing observed Kd into background vs. biotic components
text:
Decomposing observed Kd into background vs. biotic components
Available overlapping chemistry: CHLA (mg/m^3) and Turbidity (NTU) are the two usable predictors of the biotic/particulate extinction component (Secchi is itself just another optical measurement of the same quantity, so it is not used as a predictor).


Code
# `chem` should be one row per Kd date (aggregate multiple depths/stations to
# a single near-surface value per date *before* this step — the first attempt
# at this joined on Date without deduplicating, inflating n from 147 to 841
# rows and producing an unreliable, pseudo-replicated fit).
kw_decomp <- decompose_kw_biotic(
  date      = light_data$Date,
  kw        = light_data$Kd,
  chla      = light_data$chla,
  turbidity = light_data$turbidity
)




Code
print(kw_decomp)


Kw decomposition: background vs. biotic extinction
--------------------------------------------------
Model:              kw ~ chla + turbidity
n used:             142 (5 dropped for missing values)
R^2 / adj R^2:      0.067 / 0.054

Coefficients (p-value):
  (Intercept)     0.36815   (p = 0.0013)
  chla            0.00705   (p = 0.1669)
  turbidity       0.12692   (p = 0.0165)

Mean total Kw:      0.707 m^-1
Mean biotic Kw:     0.339 m^-1 (48% of total)
Mean background Kw: 0.382 m^-1 (intercept = 0.368)

NOTE: 26 of 142 background estimates were below the 0.020 m^-1 floor and
were clipped (see `$data$background_kw_raw` for the unclipped values) — this can
indicate the regression is over-attributing extinction to the biotic term on
some dates (e.g. collinearity, or a bloom event outside the fitted range).

Use `$data$background_kw` (dated) as the GLM `Kw_file` forcing when running with
AED's bioshade_feedback on. To check whether it should be static, monthly, or
fully dated, pass it on to:
  recommend_light_parameterisation(date = x$data$date, kw = x$data$background_kw)


Two fits were run against the real data as the join was corrected:


Code
plot(kw_decomp)











Code
print(kw_decomp)


Kw decomposition: background vs. biotic extinction
--------------------------------------------------
Model:              kw ~ chla + turbidity
n used:             142 (5 dropped for missing values)
R^2 / adj R^2:      0.067 / 0.054

Coefficients (p-value):
  (Intercept)     0.36815   (p = 0.0013)
  chla            0.00705   (p = 0.1669)
  turbidity       0.12692   (p = 0.0165)

Mean total Kw:      0.707 m^-1
Mean biotic Kw:     0.339 m^-1 (48% of total)
Mean background Kw: 0.382 m^-1 (intercept = 0.368)

NOTE: 26 of 142 background estimates were below the 0.020 m^-1 floor and
were clipped (see `$data$background_kw_raw` for the unclipped values) — this can
indicate the regression is over-attributing extinction to the biotic term on
some dates (e.g. collinearity, or a bloom event outside the fitted range).

Use `$data$background_kw` (dated) as the GLM `Kw_file` forcing when running with
AED's bioshade_feedback on. To check whether it should be static, monthly, or
fully dated, pass it on to:
  recommend_light_parameterisation(date = x$data$date, kw = x$data$background_kw)



Interpretation

Even after fixing the join (pseudo-replication), R² = 0.067 — Chla and turbidity together explain under 7% of Kd variance. Chla alone is not significant (p = 0.167); only turbidity clears p < 0.05, and its large coefficient combined with an 18% floor-clipping rate suggests the fit is being pulled around by a handful of high-turbidity events rather than reflecting a stable relationship.
aed_noncohesive is active in this AED configuration, computing its own suspended-sediment-driven extinction (Ke_ss(i) * SS_conc(i)) dynamically — so, unlike a setup with phytoplankton feedback alone, both the Chla- and turbidity-attributable terms are legitimately things AED will reconstruct, and both are fair to remove from the prescribed background. (Caveat: aed_noncohesive’s simulated SS is a mass concentration state, not the same quantity as measured NTU turbidity — the decision to exclude it is justified, but there’s no guarantee the simulated SS dynamics reproduce the same magnitude/timing the regression attributed to turbidity.)
The intercept is the one robust number here: 0.368 m⁻¹ at p = 0.0013, much better constrained than either slope, since intercepts are anchored by the bulk of the data rather than a weak covariate relationship.
The Secchi–Kd relationship was also noted as weak, reinforcing that this system’s optical signal is noisy relative to the predictors available.

title: Rotorua Light
section: Recommendation for the climate scenario runs
text:
Recommendation for the climate scenario runs
For a climate scenario parameterisation (not a historical hindcast):

Do not use observed Kd. bioshade_feedback and aed_noncohesive are both active, so a Kw already containing today’s biotic/SS signal would be double-counted against AED’s own dynamic contribution.
Do not use a dated time-varying background. There is no calendar correspondence between a historical sampling date and a future scenario year — the “use the actual dated observations” option only applies to hindcast-style runs over the sampled period.
Do not build a monthly background climatology. The Chla/turbidity regression (R² = 0.067) and the Secchi–Kd relationship are both weak; imposing monthly structure on this background signal risks encoding noise as if it were a genuine recurring seasonal driver.
Use a static background Kw, set from the regression intercept (~0.37 m⁻¹) — the most robust single number the data support. Let bioshade_feedback (phytoplankton) and aed_noncohesive (suspended sediment) supply the dynamic, climate-responsive part of the light environment, rather than freezing it to the historical record. This is also the conceptually correct setup for a scenario run: it lets the lake’s optical response evolve mechanistically under whatever the scenario does to nutrients, temperature, and hydrology, instead of repeating today’s bloom/turbidity patterns indefinitely.

&light
   light_mode       = 0
   Kw               = 0.37   ! static background Kw (regression intercept)
   n_bands          = 2
   light_extc       = 1.0, 0.5
   energy_frac      = 0.5, 0.5
   Benthic_Imin     = 10
   albedo_mode      = 1
   albedo_mean      = 0.08
   albedo_amplitude = 0.02
/

title: Rotorua Light
text:
Sensitivity check
Before committing to this, a direct sensitivity comparison is worth running: static background Kw (0.37 m⁻¹) with bioshade_feedback on, vs. the old static observed mean Kw (0.71 m⁻¹) with bioshade_feedback off. If key scenario outputs (surface temperature, stratification onset/breakdown, chlorophyll, hypolimnetic DO) are not materially different between the two, the choice matters less than the analysis above might suggest; if they diverge substantially, it’s worth investing more in constraining the background estimate (e.g. more Chla/TSS sampling, a better SS-turbidity calibration for aed_noncohesive) before running the full scenario suite.
The chunks below are scaffolding only (eval: false) — wire in your own nml paths, glm.exe invocation, and output-reading (e.g. glmtools/ncdf4) to run them.


Code

model <- "glm_aed"
model_path <- file.path(lake_dir, model) # get_model_path(aeme)
tgt_vars <- c("HYD_temp", "PHY_tchla", "LKE_photic", "HYD_thmcln")
scenarios <- list(
  `Static - feedback` = list(
    Kw = 0.37, # static background Kw (regression intercept)
    bioshade_feedback = TRUE
  ),
  `Static - no feedback` = list(
    light_mode = 0,
    Kw = 0.71, # static observed mean Kw
    bioshade_feedback = FALSE

title: Rotorua Light
text:
Summary







Question
Answer




Static vs. time-varying Kw (general)?
Time-varying is better if the seasonal signal is real and well-sampled; here, interannual variability (47% of variance) dominates over seasonality, so a pooled monthly climatology would misrepresent most years.


Does AED feedback interact with Kw?
Yes — bioshade_feedback (phytoplankton) and aed_noncohesive (suspended sediment) both add their own simulated extinction on top of the prescribed Kw, additively.


Should prescribed Kw include the biotic signal?
No, not when both feedbacks are active — it double-counts.


Can the biotic component be estimated from data?
Weakly. Kd ~ Chla + Turbidity gives R² = 0.067; only the intercept (background Kw ≈ 0.37 m⁻¹) is well-constrained.


Is calibrating AED’s biotic light coefficients a good idea?
Not as a first move — risks equifinality/circularity with growth and mortality parameters; better to fix it from the empirical estimate and reserve calibration for parameters not otherwise measurable.


What should the climate scenario runs use?
A static background Kw (~0.37 m⁻¹), with bioshade_feedback and aed_noncohesive supplying the dynamic, climate-responsive part of light extinction.

text: Simulating pH

title: Lake Rotorua Modelling
text:
The Problem
pH ignores pH_initial because it’s diagnostic, not prognostic

aed_carbon tracks DIC as a conserved state variable; pH is recomputed every timestep from DIC + Total Alkalinity via CO2SYS — pH_initial is only the solver’s first guess
Default alk_mode = 1 hardcodes a salinity regression fit to Caboolture, QLD — no general-purpose option, no way to supply real TA data
id_talk (a TA state variable ID) is declared in aed_carbon.F90 but never registered — the intended dynamic TA path was never finished


alk_mode = 0 is also broken — CO2SYS calls are commented out and the solver never converges. Modes 1–5 are all site-specific Queensland regressions. Nothing in the shipped module supports user-supplied alkalinity.

title: Lake Rotorua Modelling
text:
The Fix: alk_mode = 6
New option on branch feature/fixed-alkalinity-mode — bypasses every regression:
&aed_carbon
   alk_mode   = 6
   talk_fixed = 2200.0   !# Total Alkalinity, umol/kg
/

talk_fixed defaults to NaN — mode 6 without it fails loudly at startup
Get talk_fixed from real TA measurements, or back-solve from (DIC, observed pH) via PyCO2SYS
Observed pH becomes a validation target, not a model input
Higher TA → higher pH; response is nonlinear, steepest near pKa values (~6.3, ~10.3)
Verified with clean compile and full library build — not yet run end-to-end through GLM
If a single constant isn’t sufficient, the next step is finishing id_talk as a real dynamic state variable with a depth-varying initial profile

title: Ōhau Channel Weir and GLM Outflow Setup
text:
Note



Lake Rotorua has a single surface outflow, the Ōhau Channel, which is controlled by a weir with removable stoplogs. GLM cannot represent a two-level crest with stoplogs, so we replace it with one equivalent crest (elevation, width, and a dimensionless factor) fitted to the gauged lake level and channel discharge. This page documents the physical weir, the data used, and how the GLM parameters are derived.

title: Ōhau Channel Weir and GLM Outflow Setup
text:
1. The physical weir
The weir spans the 26 m wide Ōhau Channel. It has two crest levels:

a narrow, deep lower crest (4.6 m wide, 278.166 m) in the centre of the channel, and
a higher upper crest (279.316 m) across the remaining 21.4 m.

Up to three stoplogs, each 0.270 m high, can be stacked on the lower crest to raise the low-flow control level. Their installation and removal are tied to lake-level triggers.

title: Ōhau Channel Weir and GLM Outflow Setup
text:
3. Physical weir rating curves
For each stoplog count the discharge is the sum of the flow over the lower and the upper sections, each treated as a broad-crested rectangular weir at critical flow:
\[
Q = 1.705\, C_d \Big[\, b_{low}\,(h - z_{low})_+^{3/2} + b_{up}\,(h - z_{up})_+^{3/2} \Big]
\]
where \(1.705 = \tfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{2g/3}\) is the critical-flow broad-crested weir coefficient (SI units), \(h\) is lake level, \(z_{low} = 278.166 + n \times 0.270\) is the lower crest with \(n\) stoplogs, \(z_{up} = 279.316\), \(b_{low} = 4.6\) m, \(b_{up} = 21.4\) m, and \(C_d =\) 0.565 is an empirical discharge coefficient. This is rotorua_weir_flow() / generate_rotorua_weir_curves() in R/rotorua_weir_flow.R, as used in compare_rating_curve.R.

)

title: Ōhau Channel Weir and GLM Outflow Setup
text:
4. How GLM represents the outflow
GLM treats the lake outflow as a single rectangular broad-crested weir. When the water level \(h\) is above the crest, outflow is
\[
Q = \tfrac{2}{3}\, f_c \sqrt{2g}\; w_c\, (h - z_c)_+^{3/2}
\]
with three parameters in the .nml:








GLM parameter
Namelist entry
Meaning




Crest elevation \(z_c\)
&morphometry crest_elev
Height of the single equivalent crest (m a.s.l.)


Crest width \(w_c\)
&outflow crest_width
Width of the weir (m)


Crest factor \(f_c\)
&outflow crest_factor
Dimensionless discharge coefficient, a free scaling on flow



Because the physical weir has two crest levels and a stoplog configuration that changes through time, the GLM parameters are not measured, they are fitted so that the single crest reproduces the gauged rating.

Choices

Crest width is fixed at the full channel width, 26 m (ohau_weir_width target), so \(w_c\) is not fitted and the factor absorbs the loss in effective width.
Crest elevation and crest factor are fitted by least squares on all paired observations (flow >= 0, finite level and flow).
For any trial crest elevation \(z_c\) the best factor has a closed form. With \(q_i = \tfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{2g}\; w_c (h_i - z_c)_+^{3/2}\),

\[
f_c(z_c) = \frac{\sum q_i Q_i}{\sum q_i^2}
\]
and optimize() then searches \(z_c\) between the lower and upper physical crests (278.166–279.316 m) to minimise the sum of squared errors.
This is implemented in est_glm_weir_params() (R/est_glm_weir_params.R), run by the glm_weir_params target, and written to the model by format_weir_params().

Equivalent crest versus the real weir
The fitted crest (279.147 m) falls between the lower crest and the upper crest. This is expected: it is a flow-weighted compromise between a narrow section that passes water at low heads and a wide, higher section that dominates at high heads.


Code
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  plot_rotorua_glm_weir_comparison(crest_elev, crest_factor, n_stoplogs = 0),
  plot_rotorua_glm_weir_comparison(crest_elev, crest_factor, n_stoplogs = 2),
  ncol = 1, guides = "collect"
)





Actual weir (0 and 2 stoplogs) against the GLM single-crest approximation (dashed).




The crest factor does not move the drawn crest. It scales flow. Note the GLM equation uses \(\tfrac{2}{3}\sqrt{2g} = 2.953\) as its base coefficient, whereas the physical curves use \(1.705\,C_d\) = 0.963. Per metre of crest width at the same head, the fitted GLM coefficient is \(2.953 \times 0.362 = 1.07\), of similar magnitude to the physical 0.963. The GLM crest sits lower than the upper crest, so it compensates for the physical weir’s higher crest with a slightly higher unit coefficient over the full 26 m.


Rating comparison: physical vs GLM

Resulting namelist entries:
&morphometry
   crest_elev   = <crest_elev>      ! fitted
/
&outflow
   num_outlet   = 0                 ! surface weir only; no submerged outlet
   crest_width  = 26.0              ! channel width
   crest_factor = <crest_factor>    ! fitted
/

Caveats

One curve for all stoplog states. The fit pools all years and stoplog configurations; stoplog history is not used. The GLM rating is a compromise, so it will overpredict flow in periods when logs are in and underpredict when they are out (the scatter at a given level in the figure above shows this spread).
Pooled fit weights high flows. Least squares on flow is driven by the large discharges, so the low-head end of the rating is less well matched.
Fitted crest is an effective value. It should not be compared with a surveyed crest level, and the bounds for calibration (±0.2 m) are deliberately narrow around it.
Datum. Both level and crest elevations are in Moturiki datum, which must match the datum of the lake hypsograph used in GLM (see the crest_elev row in the config notes).

title: Overview of my Research
text:
Frequentist vs Bayes
Frequentist

There is one true value of the parameter, and we are trying to estimate it.

Bayesian

There is a distribution of possible values for the parameter, and we are trying to estimate that distribution.

title: Overview of my Research
Overview of my Research
text:
Reading the formula

Prior: what we believed before the data
Likelihood: how well each value explains the data
Posterior: our updated belief


The posterior is a compromise between the prior and the data.


The evidence term only rescales the result so the posterior integrates to 1. Spoken version: start with what you believed, weight it by how well each possibility explains the data, and renormalise.

title: Overview of my Research
text:
Bayes in lake calibration
Example parameter: sediment phosphorus release rate







Prior
Measured sediment P flux from [student]’s core incubations


Likelihood
How well simulated TP, chlorophyll-a and bottom oxygen match the lake monitoring data for each value


Posterior
The values consistent with both the experiment and the lake record




Prior: the student’s incubation experiment gives a measured release rate, with replicate-to-replicate spread. We widen it because cores are small, taken at a few sites, and incubated under controlled temperature and oxygen. Likelihood: run GLM-AED across candidate values and score the fit to monitoring data. Posterior: the combination. Do the two sources agree?

title: Overview of my Research
text:
Prior, likelihood and posterior


If the lake-only estimate and the experiment agree, we have independent support for the parameter. If they disagree, either the lab and lake conditions differ or the model is compensating for something else.

title: Overview of my Research
text:
Example: Linear regression
We have a set of data points (x, y) and we want to fit a linear model y = mx + b.
For the Frequentist approach, we would find the best-fit line that minimizes the sum of squared errors. We would then report the estimated slope (m) and intercept (b) along with confidence intervals.
For the Bayesian approach, we would specify prior distributions for m and b, and then use the data to update those priors to posterior distributions. We would then report the posterior distributions for m and b, which give us a range of plausible values for the parameters.

The likelihood is only as good as the data. It describes what the data say, not what is true. If I redid the experiment, the peak would move. The truth wouldn’t. The width tells you how much to trust the peak. A narrow curve means the data pin the slope down, and a wide one means they don’t.

            W_5 = "w_ala 5",
            `R_1.4` = "capacity x1.43 (Al:P 0.7:1)", `R_0.5` = "capacity x0.5",
            `R_0.3` = "capacity x0.3", `R_0.15` = "capacity x0.14 (Al:P 7:1)",
            `RES_0.001` = "resusp k_res 0.001", `RES_0.01` = "resusp k_res 0.01",
            `RES_0.1` = "resusp k_res 0.1", SURF = "surface dose 0.1 mmol/m2/d")

runs <- lapply(setNames(tags, tags), read_alum_run)
lake <- bind_rows(lapply(runs, `[[`, "lake")) |>
  mutate(scenario = factor(scenario, tags, labels[tags]))
zone <- bind_rows(lapply(runs, `[[`, "zone")) |>
  mutate(scenario = factor(scenario, tags, labels[tags]))
lw <- lake |> filter(Date >= WIN_START, Date <= WIN_STOP)   # analysis window

lab <- function(t) factor(labels[[t]], labels[tags])
S0 <- "S0 no alum"; S1 <- "S1 historical dose"
pal <- c("S0 no alum" = "grey35", "S1 historical dose" = "#d95f02")

title: Alum scenarios in the Lake Rotorua GLM-AED model
text:
Purpose and set-up
This page summarises the full GLM-AED output (output.nc) of the alum scenarios run by scripts/alum/01_run_scenarios.R with the calibrated stage 1–3 parameters (calibration/checkpoints/final/), the real inflow/meteorological forcing and the reconstructed alum dosing history (Puarenga and Utuhina dosing, converted to an inflow ALU_ala concentration by calc_alum_inflow()). It follows the diagnostics used in the aed_alum stress tests, but applied to the lake rather than to idealised boxes.







Scenario
What changes




S0
no alum (ALU_ala = 0 in all inflows)


S1
historical dosing, default alum parameters (w_ala = 0.5 m/d, 1 mol P capacity per mol Al)


w_ala 0.3, 1, 1.5, 5
floc settling velocity: thesis central value 0.5 m/d, plausible range 0.3–1.5, 5 as a weakly-mixed upper bound


capacity x1.43 … x0.14
P-binding capacity per Al scaled onto the dosed inflows: 1.43 = jar test (Al:P 0.7:1), 0.14 = operational field value (~7:1)


resuspension
simResuspension on (thesis recommendation) with k_res 0.001, 0.01, 0.1 d⁻¹


surface dose
no inflow dosing; whole-lake S_ala = 0.10 mmol P/m²/d (the thesis’ mean-rate equivalent)



The settling velocities of 20–100 m/d in the thesis are for individually tracked large flocs (1–3 mm) in still water. The thesis explicitly treats them as upper bounds, because wind mixing keeps flocs suspended longer, and recommends 0.5 m/d (0.3–1.5) for the model. An earlier version of this page swept w_ala up to 100 m/d, which is outside that recommendation; it has been replaced by the thesis-based set above.
: Scenarios {.striped}


Code
cat("Scenarios found:", paste(tags, collapse = ", "), "\n")








Note



Interpret differences, not absolute values. The staged calibration fits lake P poorly (stage 3 FRP KGE < 0, positive FRP/TP bias), and the TP series is still rising through the first years of each run. Everything below is therefore expressed as alum minus no-alum (S1 − S0) wherever possible.


Units: concentrations are mmol P/m³ (1 mmol P/m³ = 31 µg P/L); masses are kg P; benthic pools are summed over the four sediment zones.

title: Alum scenarios in the Lake Rotorua GLM-AED model
text:
1. Inflow loading

1.1 P and Al loads by stream


Code
il <- read_alum_inflow_loads("S1", start = WIN_START, stop = WIN_STOP) |>
  mutate(wy = as.integer(format(Date + 184, "%Y")))   # water year ending 30 June

load_tab <- il |>
  group_by(stream) |>
  summarise(`Flow (Mm3/yr)` = sum(flow_m3d) / 1e6 / N_YR,
            `FRP (t P/yr)`  = sum(frp_kgd) / 1e3 / N_YR,
            `TP (t P/yr)`   = sum(tp_kgd) / 1e3 / N_YR,
            `Alum Al (t/yr)` = sum(al_kgd) / 1e3 / N_YR,
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(`TP (t P/yr)`))
tot <- load_tab |> summarise(across(where(is.numeric), sum)) |> mutate(stream = "Total")
kable(bind_rows(load_tab, tot), digits = 1,
      caption = "Mean annual external loads over the analysis window (S1 inflow files).")




Code
ann <- il |> group_by(wy) |>
  summarise(TP = sum(tp_kgd) / 1e3, FRP = sum(frp_kgd) / 1e3,
            Al = sum(al_kgd) / 1e3, .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(-wy)
ggplot(ann, aes(wy, value, fill = name)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = NULL,
                    labels = c(Al = "Al dosed (t Al)", FRP = "FRP load (t P)",
                               TP = "TP load (t P)")) +
  labs(x = "Water year (ending 30 June)", y = "tonnes / yr")




Code
d <- il |> filter(stream %in% c("Puarenga", "Utuhina"))
conc <- d |> mutate(conc = ifelse(flow_m3d > 0, ala_kgd / MMOL_TO_KG / flow_m3d, NA))
p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(Date, al_kgd, colour = stream)) + geom_line(linewidth = .3) +
  labs(y = "kg Al / d", colour = NULL)
p2 <- ggplot(filter(conc, conc > 0), aes(Date, conc, colour = stream)) +
  geom_point(size = .4) + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(y = "ALU_ala (mmol P-capacity / m3)", colour = NULL)
p1 / p2




1.2 How much P-binding capacity is added relative to the P load?


Code
cap <- il |> summarise(
  Al_t = sum(al_kgd) / 1e3, cap_tP = sum(ala_kgd) / 1e3,
  TP_t = sum(tp_kgd) / 1e3, FRP_t = sum(frp_kgd) / 1e3)
kable(tibble(
  Quantity = c("Al dosed (t, window)", "P-binding capacity dosed (t P, 1 Al : 1 P)",
               "External TP load, all streams (t P)", "External FRP load, all streams (t P)",
               "Capacity / TP load", "Capacity / FRP load"),
  Value = c(cap$Al_t, cap$cap_tP, cap$TP_t, cap$FRP_t,
            cap$cap_tP / cap$TP_t, cap$cap_tP / cap$FRP_t)), digits = 2)


The nominal capacity added is a large multiple of the FRP actually delivered. Alum is dosed in streams that carry only part of the P load, so most capacity is expected to remain unused or be aged away (§5).

2.1 Comparison with observations
Observations are the buoy/CTD/survey data held in the Aeme object (observations()$lake), averaged by day over the epilimnion (0–5 m) or hypolimnion (15–21 m; the model lake is 21 m deep). The model is sampled over the same depth bands (volume-weighted). The real lake was dosed, so S1 is the scenario to compare with the data; S0 shows how far the no-alum counterfactual departs from what was measured.


Code
obs <- read_alum_obs() |> filter(Date >= WIN_START, Date <= WIN_STOP)
vmap <- tribble(
  ~var_aeme,   ~band, ~col,       ~scale, ~panel,
  "PHS_frp",   "epi", "frp_epi",  31,     "FRP, epilimnion (ug P/L)",
  "PHS_frp",   "hyp", "frp_hyp",  31,     "FRP, hypolimnion (ug P/L)",
  "PHS_tp",    "epi", "tp_epi",   31,     "TP, epilimnion (ug P/L)",
  "PHS_tp",    "hyp", "tp_hyp",   31,     "TP, hypolimnion (ug P/L)",
  "PHY_tchla", "epi", "chl_epi",  1,      "Chl-a, epilimnion (ug/L)",
  "CHM_oxy",   "hyp", "oxy_hyp",  1,      "Oxygen, hypolimnion (mg/L)")

  select(Date, scenario, all_of(vmap$col)) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(Date, scenario), names_to = "col") |>
  left_join(vmap, by = "col") |> mutate(value = value * scale)

  geom_line(data = mod_long, aes(Date, value, colour = scenario), linewidth = .35) +
  geom_point(data = obs_long, aes(Date, obs), size = .8, alpha = .6, colour = "black") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal, name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)

3.3 Internal FRP release and bottom-water oxygen
The sediment FRP input flux (fsed_frp, 0.003–0.010 mmol P/m²/d by zone) is not applied as-is: AED scales it by an oxygen half-saturation term, so the realised exchange PHS_frp_dsf is only a fraction of the potential SDF_Fsed_frp whenever the bottom water is oxygenated. Internal loading therefore depends on whether the bottom water goes anoxic.

4. Settling of floc: water column vs benthos


Code

  transmute(Date, `water column` = rm30(uptake_w_kgd), `settled alum (benthic)` = rm30(uptake_s_kgd)) |>

title: Alum scenarios in the Lake Rotorua GLM-AED model
section: 5. How much P does alum remove?
text:
5. How much P does alum remove?
For each scenario we integrate, over the analysis window:

Capacity dosed – ALU_ala delivered by the dosed inflows (kg P-equivalent).
P bound – FRP taken up by suspended alum (ALU_uptake_w × layer volume) plus FRP taken up by settled alum (ALU_uptake_s × zone area). These are direct model fluxes.
Where the bound P goes – GLM does not output the floc settling or burial fluxes, so they are inferred by mass closure from the pools:

exported: outflow volume × surface-layer ALU_alp;
settled to bed = water-column uptake − exported − Δ(suspended ALU_alp);
buried = settled to bed + benthic uptake − Δ(ALU_ben_alp).

As an independent check the burial implied by k_bur × ALU_ben_alp is also integrated; the ratio to the closure-implied burial should be ≈ 1.



Code
cap_by <- function(tag) {
  il <- read_alum_inflow_loads(tag, start = WIN_START, stop = WIN_STOP)
  cap <- sum(il$ala_kgd)
  if (tag == "SURF") {                       # S_ala (mmol P/m2/d) x surface area x days
    d <- lake |> filter(scenario == labels[["SURF"]], Date >= WIN_START, Date <= WIN_STOP)
    cap <- sum(0.10 * d$surface_area_m2) * MMOL_TO_KG
  }
  cap
}
bud <- lw |> group_by(scenario) |>
  arrange(Date) |>
  summarise(
    uptake_w = sum(uptake_w_kgd), uptake_s = sum(uptake_s_kgd),
    d_alp_w = last(alp_kg) - first(alp_kg),
    d_alp_s = last(ben_alp_kg) - first(ben_alp_kg),
    burial_kbur = sum(K_BUR * ben_alp_kg),
    exported = sum(overflow_m3 * alp_top) * MMOL_TO_KG,
    ala_end = last(ala_kg) + last(ben_ala_kg),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(tag = tags[match(as.character(scenario), labels[tags])]) |>
  rowwise() |> mutate(capacity = cap_by(tag)) |> ungroup() |>
  mutate(removed = uptake_w + uptake_s,
         settled = uptake_w - exported - d_alp_w,
         buried  = settled + uptake_s - d_alp_s,
         kbur_ratio = burial_kbur / buried,
         eff = removed / capacity)

bt <- bud |> filter(scenario != S0) |>
  transmute(Scenario = as.character(scenario),
            `Capacity dosed (t P)` = capacity / 1e3,
            `Uptake: water (t P)` = uptake_w / 1e3,
            `Uptake: benthic (t P)` = uptake_s / 1e3,
            `Total bound (t P)` = removed / 1e3,
            `Efficiency (bound / capacity)` = eff,
            `Exported (t P)` = exported / 1e3,
            `Settled to bed (t P)` = settled / 1e3,
            `Buried (t P)` = buried / 1e3,
            `Pool change: water (t P)` = d_alp_w / 1e3,
            `Pool change: bed (t P)` = d_alp_s / 1e3,
            `k_bur check (ratio)` = kbur_ratio)
kable(bt, digits = 2, caption = "Alum phosphorus budget over the analysis window.")








Tip



Bound P ends up almost entirely in the sediment; the closure-implied burial and the k_bur × stock estimate should agree. A ratio well above 1 would mean the benthic pool is being drained faster than the closure allows (i.e. the reported benthic mass is inconsistent with the settling that fed it) and points at the benthic bookkeeping rather than at the lake result.




Code
fb <- bud |> filter(scenario == S1) |>
  transmute(`Pool change: water` = d_alp_w, `Pool change: bed` = d_alp_s,
            Buried = buried, Exported = exported) |>
  pivot_longer(everything()) |> mutate(value = value / 1e3)
ggplot(fb, aes(reorder(name, -value), value, fill = name)) + geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") + labs(x = NULL, y = "t P")

Code

  group_by(Date) |> summarise(cap = sum(ala_kgd), .groups = "drop")

  transmute(Date, `water column` = cumsum(uptake_w_kgd) / 1e3,
            `benthic` = cumsum(uptake_s_kgd) / 1e3) |>

            by = "Date") |>
  mutate(`total bound` = `water column` + benthic) |>
  pivot_longer(-Date)
ggplot(cum, aes(Date, value, colour = name)) + geom_line() +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = NULL) + labs(y = "t P (cumulative)", x = NULL)

  summarise(`TP stock, mean (t P)` = mean(tp_kg) / 1e3,
            `FRP stock, mean (t P)` = mean(frp_kg) / 1e3,

section: 6. Sensitivity to dose and floc settling velocity
text:
6. Sensitivity to dose and floc settling velocity


Code
sens <- lw |> group_by(scenario) |>
  summarise(FRP = mean(frp_mean) * 31, TP = mean(tp_mean) * 31, Chl = mean(chl_mean),
            ben_alp_end = last(ben_alp_kg) / 1e3, .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(bud |> select(scenario, removed, eff, uptake_w, uptake_s), by = "scenario") |>
  mutate(`water-col. share` = uptake_w / removed)
s0 <- sens |> filter(scenario == S0)
kable(sens |> transmute(Scenario = scenario,
        `FRP (ug/L)` = FRP, `dFRP %` = 100 * (FRP / s0$FRP - 1),
        `TP (ug/L)` = TP, `dTP %` = 100 * (TP / s0$TP - 1),
        `dChl %` = 100 * (Chl / s0$Chl - 1),
        `Bound P (t)` = removed / 1e3, Efficiency = eff,
        `Water-col. share` = `water-col. share`, `Settled bound P, end (t)` = ben_alp_end),
      digits = 2, caption = "Scenario sensitivity (analysis-window means).")




Code
wl <- sens |> filter(grepl("^w_ala", scenario) | scenario == S1) |>
  mutate(w = ifelse(scenario == S1, 0.5, as.numeric(sub("w_ala ", "", scenario)))) |>
  filter(!duplicated(w)) |>
  mutate(dTP = 100 * (TP / s0$TP - 1), 
         dFRP = 100 * (FRP / s0$FRP - 1),
         removed_adj = removed / 1e3
         ) |> 
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c(dTP, dFRP, removed_adj, `water-col. share`), 
                      names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    label = dplyr::case_when(
      metric == "dTP" ~ "ΔTP vs S0 (%)",
      metric == "dFRP" ~ "ΔFRP vs S0 (%)",
      metric == "removed_adj" ~ "P bound by alum (t)",
      metric == "water-col. share" ~ "Water-column share of uptake"
    )
  )

p <- ggplot(wl, aes(w, value)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~label, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "w_ala (m/d)", y = NULL)

p



6.1 P-binding capacity per Al (jar test vs field)
The thesis gives Al:P = 0.7:1 in the jar test but ~7:1 in the field. This is the largest unknown in how much of the dosed Al is available to bind lake P, and it acts like a scale factor on the dosed capacity.


Code
rs <- c(S1, "capacity x1.43 (Al:P 0.7:1)", "capacity x0.5", "capacity x0.3",
        "capacity x0.14 (Al:P 7:1)")
rs <- rs[rs %in% levels(lw$scenario)]
dr <- lw |> filter(scenario %in% c(S0, rs)) |>
  select(Date, scenario, tp_mean) |> pivot_wider(names_from = scenario, values_from = tp_mean) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(Date, all_of(S0))) |>
  mutate(d = rm30(value - .data[[S0]]) * 31)
ggplot(dr, aes(Date, d, colour = name)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = .4) + scale_colour_viridis_d(name = NULL, option = "C", end = .85) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(y = "ΔTP vs S0 (ug P/L)", x = NULL)




Code
ratio_tab <- ev |>
  filter(panel %in% c("TP, epilimnion (ug P/L)", "FRP, epilimnion (ug P/L)", "Chl-a, epilimnion (ug/L)"),
         scenario %in% c(S0, rs)) |>
  group_by(panel, scenario) |> summarise(bias = mean(model - obs), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(scale = c(1.43, 0.5, 0.3, 0.143, 1, NA)[match(as.character(scenario),
           c("capacity x1.43 (Al:P 0.7:1)", "capacity x0.5", "capacity x0.3",
             "capacity x0.14 (Al:P 7:1)", S1, S0))]) |> filter(!is.na(scale))
ggplot(ratio_tab, aes(scale, bias)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line() + geom_point() + scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = "P-binding capacity per Al (relative to 1:1)", y = "Model − observed")




6.2 Resuspension
The thesis recommends resuspension on (alum is concentrated near-shore, fragile flocs), but gives no value for k_res. The runs below bracket it. Resuspension returns settled alum to the bottom water, so it should raise bottom-water alum-bound P and lower net burial.


Code
rl <- c(S1, "resusp k_res 0.001", "resusp k_res 0.01", "resusp k_res 0.1")
rl <- rl[rl %in% levels(lw$scenario)]
rr <- lw |> filter(scenario %in% rl)
pr1 <- ggplot(rr, aes(Date, ben_alp_kg / 1e3, colour = scenario)) + geom_line(linewidth = .4) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = NULL, option = "C", end = .85) + labs(y = "Settled ALU_alp (t P)", x = NULL)
pr2 <- ggplot(rr, aes(Date, alp_bot, colour = scenario)) + geom_line(linewidth = .4) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = NULL, option = "C", end = .85) + labs(y = "Bottom ALU_alp (mmol/m3)", x = NULL)
pr1 + pr2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")




6.3 Surface dose vs inflow dose
Dosing in the stream puts alum into the lake where the stream enters, with the stream discharge and P load. The surface-dose scenario applies the equivalent mean rate evenly over the lake, with the stream P load not carrying any alum. Compare the budget rows for “surface dose” and S1 above.


Code
sf <- lw |> filter(scenario %in% c(S0, S1, "surface dose 0.1 mmol/m2/d")) |>
  select(Date, scenario, frp_mean, tp_mean) |> pivot_longer(c(frp_mean, tp_mean))
ggplot(sf, aes(Date, value * 31, colour = scenario)) + geom_line(linewidth = .35) +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1,
             labeller = as_labeller(c(frp_mean = "FRP (ug P/L)", tp_mean = "TP (ug P/L)"))) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = NULL, option = "C", end = .8) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)

title: Alum scenarios in the Lake Rotorua GLM-AED model
text:
7. What to check next

Burial check – the k_bur ratio in §5 should be ≈ 1; if not, inspect the benthic bookkeeping (settling flux is not exported by GLM-AED; add a diagnostic).
w_ala – the thesis supports 0.5 m/d (0.3–1.5); the larger floc speeds it measured are quiescent upper bounds. Calibrate within about 0.3–1.5 (log scale), and only against FRP/TP in dosed years once the baseline FRP/TP bias is understood.
Capacity per Al – the jar-test (0.7:1) and field (~7:1) Al:P ratios span a factor of 10 in effective dose; this is likely a more influential unknown than w_ala and should be a calibration parameter (it scales the dosed ALU_ala).
Resuspension – recommended on by the thesis, k_res unconstrained.
pH efficiency – the thesis suggests pH_opt = 7, sigma_pH = 1, but this needs aed_carbon (for CAR_pH), which the lake configuration does not include; not tested here.
Identifiability – only lake FRP/TP/chl-a constrain the alum parameters (no Al or floc observations), so calibrate at most 3–4 parameters.
Natural experiment – Puarenga was not dosed in WY2020. The S1 − S0 response that year is a useful independent check on the dose–response.

title: Lake Rotorua — GLM Configuration
text:
This page documents the General Lake Model (GLM v4) configuration used for simulating the lake’s thermal dynamics, water balance, and nutrient cycling. The model is coupled to the Aquatic EcoDynamics (AED) library for biogeochemical processes.
The AEME package was used to retrieve and format lake characteristics, boundary conditions, and monitoring data for model configuration and validation. The glm4.nml and aed.nml files define the physical and biogeochemical model parameters, respectively, while CSV files provide time series of inflows, meteorological forcing, and phytoplankton parameters.






Note



All simulation configuration files, scripts, and outputs documented here correspond to the baseline run (run_id: aeme_base).

title: Lake Rotorua — GLM Configuration
text:
Model schematic
The schematic below shows the overall GLM–AED model configuration for Lake Rotorua, including the principal inflows, outflow, atmospheric forcing, and the biogeochemical modules activated in this simulation.






TipSchematic notes






Inflows: Four principal inflows are configured (Hamurana, Ohau, Waiowhiro, Waiteti streams). Loads are derived from monitored flow and water quality data (BoPRC).
Outflow: The Ohau Channel is the sole surface outflow; weir crest elevation set at 279.38 m a.s.l.
Meteorology: Half-hourly data from the Rotorua Airport NIWA station (agent 89894), gap-filled using ERA5 reanalysis where needed.
WWTP: Treated effluent from Rotorua WWTP is included as a point-source inflow.
AED modules active: NIT (nitrogen), PHO (phosphorus), OGM (organic matter), PHY (phytoplankton).
Sediment: 5-zone benthic configuration (benthic_mode = 2); zone-specific oxygen/N/P fluxes and sediment heat-model parameters from measured internal loading data — see the “Sediment zones” tab below.

title: Sensitivity of the CSPS Metrics to Model Parameters
text:
4 Findings by target

4.1 Polymixis
Stratification is controlled by the wind and mixing parameters: wind scaling, coef_wind_stir, the drag coefficient cd, the hypolimnetic mixing coefficient and the radiation scalings (heat input). More wind, stirring and drag reduce stratification; more long-wave radiation and warmer air increase it. Biogeochemical parameters have no meaningful effect on any mixing metric. coef_mix_shear is inert.
The wind scaling has the largest single effect, which is the reason it must not be used as a free parameter (the wind is measured on the lake): the mixing coefficients (coef_wind_stir, cd) have comparable leverage over the same metrics and are the right place for the adjustment.


4.2 Anoxia
Bottom-water oxygen and anoxic days are driven by the same mixing parameters as stratification, because the length of a stratified spell sets how long the bottom water can be drawn down. The only biogeochemical lever of comparable size is the sediment oxygen demand in the deepest zone (fsed_oxy zone 1), which also controls whether the model has anoxic years at all. The rate of oxygen decline during stratified spells (a process-level measure of oxygen demand) responds to cyanobacteria respiration and to the zone-1 oxygen demand.


4.3 Internal loading
This is the least well-controlled target. No parameter moves any loading metric by more than about 3 tolerances. Bottom-water ammonium responds to nitrification (rnitrif) and, less, to wind and the cyanobacteria nitrogen uptake. Sediment ammonium flux has a smaller effect than expected. The bottom FRP and TP gradients respond to almost nothing, including the sediment FRP flux and the P adsorption parameters.


4.4 Phytoplankton
Chlorophyll-a is controlled by the cyanobacteria group (respiration R_resp, light I_K, phosphorus half-saturation K_P, KePHY, buoyancy w_p), and by the alum rates when alum is on. A large part of the sampled space produces runaway cyanobacteria blooms (the median chlorophyll-a spans 0 to over 1,000 mg/m3), so the effect sizes for chlorophyll are dominated by those regions and overstate the sensitivity in the realistic range.

Physics and oxygen are unchanged on average (means agree to 3 figures). Individual paired runs do scatter by up to about a tolerance for some mixing metrics; this is a noise floor of the experiment (small differences amplified near stratification thresholds), so effects under one tolerance on those metrics should not be interpreted.
Phosphorus responds as expected: the 90th percentile of bottom FRP falls by about 60% and bottom TP by about 25%, and the mean simulated TLI3 is lower by about 0.8 units.
Chlorophyll-a is lower with alum in the bloom-prone parameter sets and unchanged in typical runs.
Bottom to surface contrast is larger with alum (alum removes surface phosphorus more than bottom), so the internal-loading signatures read stronger in a dosed lake.




Parameter influence with and without alum.


Parameter rankings are broadly the same (Spearman 0.69), but with alum the alum rate k_w, K_P, k_age_w, k_s and w_ala become influential for chlorophyll and phosphorus and compete with the phytoplankton and sediment parameters. This is the case for calibrating phosphorus and phytoplankton parameters with the alum module off, on years without dosing, and the alum parameters afterwards.
